title: Grade 11 daily reading
overview: A year of authentic public-domain American and modernist writing: autobiography and documentary argument (Douglass, Du Bois, Riis), scientific and philosophical prose (Darwin, Emerson, Thoreau), narrative and memoir (Sinclair, Twain), and poetry from Whitman to H.D., Eliot, and Stein. Three strands rotate nightly so that no single book dominates a week. Independent reading includes annotation and purposeful rereading, followed by evidence-based discussion; suggested total time is 25–30 minutes, adjusted to the reader. Source language is preserved, including historical viewpoints and prejudices that the discussion examines critically rather than endorses.

progression.focus: Observation, testimony, and the limits of inference
progression.rationale: Rotate Imagist lyric (H.D.), Sinclair’s opening wedding chapters, Whitman, Darwin’s introduction and domestication chapters, and the opening of Douglass’s 1855 autobiography. Each night separates observed detail, a speaker’s interpretation, and evidence sufficient for a claim.

progression.focus: Building cumulative arguments from observed and lived experience
progression.rationale: Darwin’s struggle, selection, branching, and objection chapters run beside Douglass’s literacy, escape, and first public voice, the closing chapters of Sinclair’s arrival, and the central Sea Garden poems; Emerson’s American Scholar and Du Bois’s opening chapter begin. Students trace how an argument accumulates across nights and test analogies and causal claims.

progression.focus: Modernist voice, intellectual independence, and the color line
progression.rationale: The last Sea Garden poems and Eliot’s 1917 poems meet Emerson’s Self-Reliance, Friendship, and Gifts and Du Bois on the Freedmen’s Bureau, Booker T. Washington, and a Tennessee country school. Discussion compares confident universal claims with the experience of those excluded from them.

Week 21 is given wholly to The Waste Land, its five sections read on five consecutive nights with brief recaps; around it come Eliot’s last 1917 poems, Whitman’s war and elegy poems, Emerson and Thoreau, Du Bois on leadership and education, and Twain’s piloting chapters. Students hold long structures in memory and weigh rival claims to authority.

progression.focus: Perception, expertise, and the costs of knowledge
progression.rationale: Whitman’s long poems, Thoreau’s Walden observations, Twain on learning to read the river, and Sinclair’s stockyard tour and the family’s search for work and a house ask what trained perception gains and loses and who pays for an economic system.

Stein’s Tender Buttons, Sinclair’s chapters on the house contract, speed-up, union hopes, and the close of Chapter IX on adulterated meat and workers’ injuries, the end of Twain’s piloting chapters, and Jacob Riis’s documentary study of New York tenements demand maximum independence: unconventional syntax, careful evaluation of evidence and sources, and qualified claims connecting form to social responsibility across the year.

sources.author: Walt Whitman
sources.title: Leaves of Grass
sources.edition: Philadelphia: David McKay, 1891–1892 (University of Virginia Small Special Collections copy PS3201 1892, copy 1), as encoded in the Walt Whitman Archive TEI transcription ppp.00707. Every selected poem is extracted directly from that dated witness, not from Project Gutenberg 1322, whose print exemplar is unidentified. TEI editorial notes are excluded. A print turnover inside a line is joined with a space (none after an em dash), and a word hyphenated only because it is split across a turnover takes the Archive’s regularized form (for example “returning,” not “return-ing”). Paragraph and stanza boundaries and line breaks are retained; prose layout whitespace is joined. Page numbers, running heads, and footnote callout numerals are omitted.

rights.basis: The 1891–1892 McKay printing was published before 1931; its US copyright term has expired. The Whitman Archive states that the text of the original item is in the public domain.

sources.author: T. S. Eliot
sources.title: The Waste Land
sources.edition: New York: Boni and Liveright, 1922, first American edition (copyright 1922; numbered issue of one thousand copies), Duke University Libraries copy digitized as Internet Archive wasteland01elio. The five verse sections were transcribed by collating every printed line against the facsimile page images (pp. 9–49), starting from the University of Virginia Literature in Context TEI and restoring the print’s readings, including “dont,” “wont,” “alright,” “tonight,” “smoothes,” “Oh keep the Dog,” “HURRY UP PLEASE ITS TIME,” and the printing’s own errors “Der Heimai zu,” “Od’,” and “mount in” (kept as printed: the 1928 and 1930 Liveright printings consulted read the same). One letter is supplied where type failed to print: line 135 prints “The hot w ter at ten.”; the “a” of “water” is supplied from the Horace Liveright third printing, August 1928 (Internet Archive wasteland00elio_0, p. 22). Print turnovers are joined to their lines and turnover hyphens removed; small capitals are given as capitals; italics and indentation are not reproduced; margin line numbers, running heads, Eliot’s endnotes and all editorial annotations are excluded. Stanza spaces follow the print.

rights.basis: Published in the United States in 1922; works published in 1922 entered the US public domain on January 1, 2018.

days.title: Sea Rose
days.challenge: Reconcile the damaged flower with the speaker’s comparative judgment.
days.focus: Harsh diction and the redefinition of beauty.
days.context: H.D. makes a weather-beaten flower the subject of an argument about beauty. Read aloud twice, then mark the adjectives that conventional praise might avoid.

excerpt.locator: Sea Rose; begins “Rose, harsh rose, marred and with stint of petals,”; ends “spice-rose drip such acrid fragrance hardened in a leaf?”.

questions.prompt: Why does calling the rose “more precious” surprise after the opening description?
facilitatorNotes: Thinness and damage initially seem defects; the comparison values survival and intensity rather than ornamental fullness.
evidence: more precious

questions.prompt: How do “flung,” “lifted,” and “drives” make the flower’s setting active?
facilitatorNotes: The rose is exposed to moving sand and wind, not arranged for display. The passive flower nevertheless acquires force through its surroundings.
evidence: you are flung on the sand

questions.prompt: Does the final question praise fragrance, toughness, or both? Defend the relation.
facilitatorNotes: “Acrid” resists easy sweetness while “hardened” makes scent seem concentrated and durable; other readings should account for both words.
evidence: such acrid fragrance

days.title: Origin of Species: A cautious opening (excerpt)
days.challenge: Trace the shift from autobiographical chronology to a request for reader trust; reread the qualifications before judging confidence.
days.focus: Scientific authority built through duration, collaboration, and acknowledged incompleteness.
days.context: Darwin opens his first edition by explaining the investigation and the circumstances of publishing an abstract before his larger work is complete.

excerpt.locator: Introduction, opening four paragraphs; complete source paragraphs 57–60 in the saved paragraph index; opens “When on board H.M.S. ‘Beagle,’ as naturalist, I was much struck with certain facts in the ”; closes “ears has aided me in every possible way by his large stores of knowledge and his excellent judgment.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Darwin give dates and years of work instead of beginning with the theory itself?
facilitatorNotes: The chronology answers an anticipated charge of haste: observation precedes speculation, which precedes prolonged revision. A strong response explains how this constructs credibility without treating elapsed time as proof.
evidence: I give them to show that I have not been hasty in coming to a decision.

questions.prompt: How does Wallace’s arrival at similar conclusions complicate the image of a solitary discoverer?
facilitatorNotes: Wallace independently reaches related conclusions and sends a memoir; Lyell and Hooker help arrange publication. Discuss cooperation and urgency without inventing motives not supplied in the passage.
evidence: has arrived at almost exactly the same general conclusions that I have

questions.prompt: What tension does Darwin create between asking for confidence and insisting on evidence from both sides?
facilitatorNotes: He cannot supply full references in this abstract, yet defines fairness as balancing opposing evidence. Readers may see the candor as credible or the missing detail as a limit; both positions need the specific concession.
evidence: A fair result can be obtained only by fully stating and balancing the facts and arguments on both sides of each question;

days.title: Autobiography as testimony — excerpt
days.challenge: Follow the shift from personal reluctance to an argument about public evidence.
days.focus: Autobiographical authority and the courtroom metaphor.
days.context: Douglass answers a request that he publish an account of his life. These are his own words within the editor’s preface, not the editor’s introduction.
days.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement, family separation and racist beliefs. Its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice.

excerpt.locator: Letter to the editor, dated July 2, 1855; UNC 1855 printing, pp. vi–viii; selected paragraphs corresponding to original PG indexes 27–30. Opening “DEAR FRIEND: I have long entertained, as you very well know, a somewhat positive repugnanc”; closing “as shall be best adapted to accomplish that good which you so enthusiastically anticipate.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Douglass distinguish opposition based on his own experience from opposition based on human nature?
facilitatorNotes: He insists that the wrong of slavery is universal rather than dependent on how one individual was treated. His experience will supply evidence for an already broader principle.
evidence: I have never placed my opposition to slavery on a basis so narrow as my own enslavement

questions.prompt: What roles do the system, its defenders and the public occupy in the trial metaphor?
facilitatorNotes: Slavery is the defendant, its friends enter a plea, and public opinion judges. The metaphor casts testimony as relevant evidence, not self-promotion.
evidence: this system is now at the bar of public opinion

questions.prompt: Why does the last paragraph make writing the autobiography himself especially important?
facilitatorNotes: A self-authored argument directly rebuts the claim that enslaved people cannot understand their injuries or rights. An account written by someone else would not demonstrate that capacity in the same way.
evidence: Not only is slavery on trial, but unfortunately, the enslaved people are also on trial

days.title: The Jungle: arrival at the wedding
days.challenge: Track an intrusive narrator’s changing distance from the wedding guests.
days.focus: Comic physical description, hospitality, and the narrator’s sympathy.
days.context: The novel opens at the Chicago wedding of Lithuanian immigrants Ona and Jurgis. This is a fictional scene, not a transcript of a particular immigrant family.
days.contentNote: Includes a bride under sixteen and period descriptions of ethnic appearance; discuss the narrator’s framing without treating it as a present-day norm.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 1, Wikisource 1906 Doubleday, Page transcription, chapter paragraphs 3–9; begins “It was four o'clock when the ceremony was over”; ends “the populace imbibes the sights and sounds and odors.”.
excerpt.inlineReason: The night omits the footnote callout after “married to Jurgis,” in its fourth paragraph, as its legacy edition declared (Chapter I’s pronunciation footnote and its callout not supplied); the library work keeps the callout as “[1]”. The words are otherwise identical, so the night stays inline.

blocks.text: It was four o'clock when the ceremony was over and the carriages began to arrive. There had been a crowd following all the way, owing to the exuberance of Marija Berczynskas. The occasion rested heavily upon Marija's broad shoulders—it was her task to see that all things went in due form, and after the best home traditions, and, flying wildly hither and thither, bowling everyone out of the way, and scolding and exhorting all day with her tremendous voice, Marija was too eager to see that others conformed to the proprieties to consider them herself. She had left the church last of all, and, desiring to arrive first at the hall, had issued orders to the coachman to drive faster. When that personage had developed a sill of his own in the matter, Marija had flung up the window of the carriage, and, leaning out, proceeded to tell him her opinion of him, first in Lithuanian, which he did not understand, and then in Polish, which he did. Having the advantage of her in altitude, the driver had stood his ground and even ventured to attempt to speak; and the result had been a furious altercation, which, continuing all the way down Ashland Avenue, had added a new swarm of urchins to the cortège at each side street for half a mile.

This was unfortunate, for already there was a throng before the door. The music had started up, and half a block away you could hear the dull "broom, broom" of a 'cello, with the squeaking of two fiddles which vied with each other in intricate and altitudinous gymnastics. Seeing the throng, Marija abandoned precipitately the debate concerning the ancestors of her coachman, and, springing from the moving carriage, plunged in and proceeded to clear a way to the hall. Once within, she turned and began to push the other way, roaring, meantime, "Eik! Elk! Uzdaryk-duris!" in tones which made the orchestral uproar sound like fairy music.

"Z. Graiczunas, Pasilinksminimams darzas. Vynas. Sznapsas. Wines and Liquors. Union Headquarters"—that was the way the signs ran. The reader, who perhaps has never held much converse in the language of far-off Lithuania, will be glad of the explanation that the place was the rear-room of a saloon in that part of Chicago known as "back of the yards." This information is definite and suited to the matter of fact; but how pitifully inadequate it would have seemed to one who understood that it was also the supreme hour of ecstasy in the life of one of God's gentlest creatures, the scene of the wedding-feast and the joy-transfiguration of little Ona Lukoszaite!

She stood in the doorway, shepherded by Cousin Marija, breathless from pushing through the crowd, and in her happiness painful to look upon. There was a light of wonder in her eyes and her lids trembled, and her otherwise wan little face was flushed. She wore a muslin dress, conspicuously white, and a stiff little veil coming to her shoulders. There were five pink paper-roses twisted in the veil, and eleven bright green rose-leaves. There were new white cotton gloves upon her hands, and as she stood staring about her she twisted them together feverishly. It was almost too much for her—you could see the pain of too great emotion in her face, and all the tremor of her form. She was so young—not quite sixteen—and small for her age, a mere child; and she had just been married—and married to Jurgis, of all men, to Jurgis Rudkus, he with the white flower in the button-hole of his new black suit, he with the mighty shoulders and the giant hands.

Ona was blue-eyed and fair, while Jurgis had great black eyes with beetling brows, and thick black hair that curled in waves about his ears—in short, they were one of those incongruous and impossible married couples with which Mother Nature so often wills to confound all prophets, before and after. Jurgis could take up a two-hundred-and-fifty-pound quarter of beef and carry it into a car without a stagger, or even a thought; and now he stood in a far corner, frightened as a hunted animal, and obliged to moisten his lips with his tongue each time before he could answer the congratulations of his friends.

Gradually there was effected a separation between the spectators and the guests—a separation at least sufficiently complete for working purposes. There was no time during the festivities which ensued when there were not groups of onlookers in the doorways and the corners; and if any one of these onlookers came sufficiently close, or looked sufficiently hungry, a chair was offered him, and he was invited to the feast. It was one of the laws of the veselija that no one goes hungry; and, while a rule made in the forests of Lithuania is hard to apply in the stock-yards district of Chicago, with its quarter of a million inhabitants, still they did their best, and the children who ran in from the street, and even the dogs, went out again happier. A charming informality was one of the characteristics of this celebration. The men wore their hats, or, if they wished, they took them off, and their coats with them; they ate when and where they pleased, and moved as often as they pleased. There were to be speeches and singing, but no one had to listen who did not care to; if he wished, meantime, to speak or sing himself, he was perfectly free. The resulting medley of sound distracted no one, save possibly alone the babies, of which there were present a number equal to the total possessed by all the guests invited. There was no other place for the babies to be, and so part of the preparations for the evening consisted of a collection of cribs and carriages in one corner. In these the babies slept, three or four together, or wakened together, as the case might be. Those who were still older, and could reach the tables, marched about munching contentedly at meat-bones and bologna sausages.

The room is about thirty feet square, with whitewashed walls, bare save for a calendar, a picture of a race-horse, and a family tree in a gilded frame. To the right there is a door from the saloon, with a few loafers in the doorway, and in the corner beyond it a bar, with a presiding genius clad in soiled white, with waxed black mustaches and a carefully oiled curl plastered against one side of his forehead. In the opposite corner are two tables, filling a third of the room and laden with dishes and cold viands, which a few of the hungrier guests are already munching. At the head, where sits the bride, is a snow-white cake, with an Eiffel tower of constructed decoration, with sugar roses and two angels upon it, and a generous sprinkling of pink and green and yellow candies. Beyond opens a door into the kitchen, where there is a glimpse to be had of a range with much steam ascending from it, and many women, old and young, rushing hither and thither. In the corner to the left are the three musicians, upon a little platform, toiling heroically to make some impression upon the hubbub; also the babies, similarly occupied, and an open window whence the populace imbibes the sights and sounds and odors.

questions.prompt: What contradiction makes Marija’s management of “proprieties” comic?
facilitatorNotes: Her determination to make others conform produces her own shouting and public argument. The humor also establishes protective energy.
evidence: too eager to see that others conformed to the proprieties to consider them herself

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator call the location’s factual explanation inadequate?
facilitatorNotes: A saloon’s address cannot convey Ona’s emotional transformation; external social labels and experienced significance differ.
evidence: how pitifully inadequate it would have seemed

questions.prompt: What pressure does Chicago put on the rule that nobody should go hungry?
facilitatorNotes: An open community custom meets a huge urban population. Guests still share food, making hospitality both difficult and valuable.
evidence: no one goes hungry

days.title: Origin of Species: Descent needs a mechanism (excerpt)
days.challenge: Separate the claim that species change from the explanation of how coordinated adaptations arise.
days.focus: Examples, causal demands, and a map of a scientific argument.
days.context: This excerpt follows Darwin’s account of his research. He now distinguishes a proposed history of species from a sufficient explanation of their structures and relations.
days.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and anatomical terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Introduction, final six paragraphs; complete source paragraphs 61–66 in the saved paragraph index; opens “In considering the Origin of Species, it is quite conceivable that a naturalist, reflectin”; closes “re, I am convinced that Natural Selection has been the main but not exclusive means of modification.”.

questions.prompt: Why do the woodpecker and misseltoe require more explanation than a list of climate or food conditions?
facilitatorNotes: Their structures work in coordinated relationships: the bird’s parts suit feeding, while the plant depends on trees, birds, and insects. Explain why Darwin treats coadaptation as the missing causal problem.
evidence: the structure of this parasite, with its relations to several distinct organic beings

questions.prompt: What is the argumentative purpose of studying domesticated plants and animals before nature?
facilitatorNotes: Domestication provides a more observable case of inherited variation and accumulated selection. It functions as a clue and analogy, not identical proof of every natural process.
evidence: variation under domestication, afforded the best and safest clue.

questions.prompt: How does the final sentence qualify the confidence expressed earlier in the paragraph?
facilitatorNotes: Darwin asserts that species are not immutable and identifies natural selection as the main mechanism, yet does not claim it is the only mechanism. The limitation is precise rather than a withdrawal of the larger claim.
evidence: Natural Selection has been the main but not exclusive means of modification.

days.title: Place, missing records and remembered skill — excerpt
days.challenge: Separate remembered observation, inference and openly uncertain information.
days.focus: How a life narrative uses both gaps in records and practical knowledge as evidence.
days.context: Douglass begins his life story with the place he can identify, the age he cannot know securely, and memories of his grandmother. His suggested birth year is reported historical uncertainty, not an editorial correction.
days.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement, family separation and racist beliefs. Its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, Childhood, opening five narrative paragraphs; UNC 1855 printing, pp. 33–36; selected paragraphs corresponding to original PG indexes 77–81. Opening “IN Talbot county, Eastern Shore, Maryland, near Easton, the county town of that county, th”; closing “ and as she was remembered by others, so she remembered the hungry little ones around her.”.

questions.prompt: How does Douglass qualify the explanation of the name Tuckahoe, and why does that qualification matter?
facilitatorNotes: He offers possibilities and refuses certainty. This lets readers distinguish local stories from facts he claims to know; it also builds a narrator who marks the limits of his evidence.
evidence: about this I will not be positive

questions.prompt: How does the account of age records turn a personal missing fact into an institutional criticism?
facilitatorNotes: He reports that enslaved people lack records and are forbidden to ask their ages. The absence therefore arises from power and control, not merely a faulty childhood memory.
evidence: Genealogical trees do not flourish among slaves

questions.prompt: Why does the explanation of the grandmother’s good luck change the reader’s view of her work?
facilitatorNotes: Her success comes from careful handling and frost protection, while neighbours call it luck. The details establish skill, foresight and generosity behind the reputation.
evidence: Her "good luck" was owing to the exceeding care which she took

days.title: Miracles
days.challenge: Follow a catalogue without reducing it to a list of interchangeable examples.
days.focus: Ordinary experience as wonder, from human encounters to spatial abundance.
days.context: Read once for the catalogue of ordinary sights and again for the changes in scale. The speaker uses “miracle” more broadly than an isolated supernatural event.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “Miracles”, Walt Whitman Archive ppp.00707, poem elementppp.00918; begins “WHY, who makes much of a miracle? As to”; ends “with men in them, What stranger miracles are there?”.

blocks.text: MIRACLES.

WHY, who makes much of a miracle?
As to me I know of nothing else but miracles,
Whether I walk the streets of Manhattan,
Or dart my sight over the roofs of houses toward the sky,
Or wade with naked feet along the beach just in the edge of the water,
Or stand under trees in the woods,
Or talk by day with any one I love, or sleep in the bed at night with any one I love,
Or sit at table at dinner with the rest,
Or look at strangers opposite me riding in the car,
Or watch honey-bees busy around the hive of a summer forenoon,
Or animals feeding in the fields,
Or birds, or the wonderfulness of insects in the air,
Or the wonderfulness of the sundown, or of stars shining so quiet and bright,
Or the exquisite delicate thin curve of the new moon in spring;
These with the rest, one and all, are to me miracles,
The whole referring, yet each distinct and in its place.

To me every hour of the light and dark is a miracle,
Every cubic inch of space is a miracle,
Every square yard of the surface of the earth is spread with the same,
Every foot of the interior swarms with the same.

To me the sea is a continual miracle,
The fishes that swim—the rocks—the motion of the waves—the ships with men in them,
What stranger miracles are there?

questions.prompt: Why include dinner and strangers in the same catalogue as stars and the new moon?
facilitatorNotes: The juxtaposition refuses to reserve wonder for spectacular nature; social ordinary life has equal standing.
evidence: Or look at strangers opposite me riding in the car

questions.prompt: What tension does “each distinct and in its place” preserve within the claim that everything is miraculous?
facilitatorNotes: The whole unifies experience without erasing differences. Ask whether the concrete examples keep this universal claim from becoming empty.
evidence: The whole referring, yet each distinct and in its place

questions.prompt: How does the move to inches, yards, and feet change the argument?
facilitatorNotes: Measurement usually sounds practical; here it makes abundance pervasive at every scale, preparing the challenging final question.
evidence: Every cubic inch of space is a miracle

days.title: Origin of Species: Testing explanations for variation (excerpt)
days.challenge: Distinguish observed contrasts from tentative causal claims across long, qualification-heavy sentences.
days.focus: Competing explanations and anomalous cases in scientific prose.
days.context: Darwin begins with variation among cultivated organisms. Read his 1859 explanations as hypotheses supported to different degrees by the cases he reports.
days.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and anatomical terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, opening five body paragraphs; complete source paragraphs 69–73 in the saved paragraph index; opens “When we look to the individuals of the same variety or sub-variety of our older cultivated”; closes “ colour from particular kinds of food and from light, and perhaps the thickness of fur from climate.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Darwin contrast healthy captive animals that fail to breed with weak domestic animals that breed freely?
facilitatorNotes: The contrast separates general health or tameness from reproductive success, supporting his focus on reproductive sensitivity. It does not by itself establish a complete mechanism; identify the inferential step.
evidence: though often weak and sickly, yet breeding quite freely under confinement

questions.prompt: How do sporting buds challenge an explanation that ties every variation to sexual reproduction?
facilitatorNotes: The changed bud or offset occurs without the act of generation and may be propagated by grafting. Darwin tries to relate it to reproductive tissue while acknowledging the broader implication.
evidence: variation is not necessarily connected, as some authors have supposed, with the act of generation.

questions.prompt: Why are differences among seedlings from the same fruit relevant to the direct-effects explanation?
facilitatorNotes: If shared conditions directly dictated the same change, Darwin argues, similarly exposed young should vary alike. Their differences challenge that simple account while leaving room for limited direct effects.
evidence: all would probably have varied in the same manner.

days.title: A cabin and the discovery of ownership — excerpt
days.challenge: Track the adult narrator’s analysis within a child’s changing understanding.
days.focus: The difference between a home’s emotional meaning and its legal ownership.
days.context: Douglass remembers living with his grandparents before he fully understood that another person claimed ownership of his grandmother and the children.
days.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement, family separation and racist beliefs. Its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, Childhood, cabin description through the reflection on childhood sorrow; UNC 1855 printing, pp. 36–40; selected paragraphs corresponding to original PG indexes 82–87. Opening “The dwelling of my grandmother and grandfather had few pretensions. It was a log hut, or c”; closing “e power of slavery to write indelible sorrow, at a single dash, over the heart of a child.”.

questions.prompt: How do the adult description of the cabin and the child’s judgment of it differ?
facilitatorNotes: Its materials and rough furnishings seem poor by external standards, but the child experiences ingenuity, comfort and play. Both perspectives can be true without making the home unimportant.
evidence: To my child's eye, however, it was a noble structure

questions.prompt: What sequence of discoveries makes the distant master increasingly threatening?
facilitatorNotes: The child learns that the hut belongs to someone else, then that his grandmother and the children are claimed as property, and finally that the children will be removed. The movement deepens the threat from objects to relationships.
evidence: not only the house and lot, but that grandmother herself

questions.prompt: What work does the insistence that enslaved children are children do after the account of ownership?
facilitatorNotes: It challenges readers who might discount their grief or regard separation as routine. The general claim grows from a particular attachment to his grandmother; readers may also discuss its direct address to adults.
evidence: SLAVE-children are children

days.title: The Helmsman
days.challenge: Distinguish remembered pleasure from present danger without supplying a missing plot.
days.focus: Refrain, collective voice, and the attraction of different landscapes.
days.context: An unnamed “we” remembers an inland life while appealing to an unnamed “you.” The title suggests steering at sea, but the poem leaves the addressee open.

excerpt.locator: The Helmsman; begins “O be swift-- we have always known you wanted”; ends “be swift-- we have always known you wanted us.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the inland catalogue make forgetting understandable?
facilitatorNotes: The account offers touch, taste, fruit, and varied paths; inland life genuinely enchants rather than merely distracting through weakness.
evidence: tree-resin, tree-bark

questions.prompt: How does the repeated climbing and hesitation change the poem’s pace?
facilitatorNotes: Dashes and recurring verbs interrupt smooth progress, making the boat’s unstable movement audible against the flowing memory.
evidence: our boat climbs--hesitates--drops--

questions.prompt: Does the repeated appeal imply trust, fear, or both?
facilitatorNotes: “Always known” claims an enduring relation, while “be swift” suggests urgency; the unidentified addressee prevents one fixed literal account.
evidence: we have always known you wanted us.

days.title: Origin of Species: Inheritance and the limits of knowledge (excerpt)
days.challenge: Track shifts among observed correlation, causal speculation, probability, and acknowledged ignorance.
days.focus: How a researcher argues for inheritance without claiming to know its laws.
days.context: These paragraphs move from habit and correlated traits to the importance of inheritance. The questions ask what Darwin’s reported evidence warrants within this historical argument.
days.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and anatomical terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, habit, correlation of growth, and inheritance; complete source paragraphs 74–78 in the saved paragraph index; opens “Habit also has a decided influence, as in the period of flowering with plants when transpo”; closes “bull, the greater length of horn, though appearing late in life, is clearly due to the male element.”.

questions.prompt: How does the duck comparison move from an observed difference to a proposed cause?
facilitatorNotes: The relative bone weights are offered as observation, while reduced flying and increased walking are proposed as an explanation. Attend to “presume” and “may,” and distinguish the two levels of assertion.
evidence: I presume that this change may be safely attributed to the domestic duck flying much less, and walking more

questions.prompt: Why would selecting one trait, on Darwin’s account, alter traits the breeder did not intend to change?
facilitatorNotes: He invokes correlation of growth: structural features are connected rather than independently adjustable. Readers should use a specific pair, such as pigeon beaks and feet, while evaluating the strength of universal claims in the examples.
evidence: he will almost certainly unconsciously modify other parts of the structure

questions.prompt: What role does rarity play in the parent-child argument, and what does Darwin still admit he cannot explain?
facilitatorNotes: A very rare shared deviation seems less plausibly an independent coincidence, supporting inheritance. He nevertheless declares its governing laws unknown; the inference to inheritance is distinct from an account of mechanism.
evidence: the mere doctrine of chances almost compels us to attribute its reappearance to inheritance.
The laws governing inheritance are quite unknown;

days.title: The journey away from home — excerpt
days.challenge: Read domestic detail, religious comparison and a visual anecdote as connected narrative choices.
days.focus: Power seen from a child’s position and the later narrator’s reflection on perspective.
days.context: A journey to the plantation has been arranged. His grandmother knows its purpose, while the child fears losing his home and does not know that the move is permanent.
days.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement, family separation and racist beliefs. Its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, Removed from My First Home, opening four narrative paragraphs; UNC 1855 printing, pp. 43–47; selected paragraphs corresponding to original PG indexes 93–96. Opening “THAT mysterious individual referred to in the first chapter as an object of terror among t”; closing “n. Thus early I learned that the point from which a thing is viewed is of some importance.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the long catalogue of ordinary things at the cabin matter to the account of departure?
facilitatorNotes: The well, mill, fences and squirrels establish an intricate emotional world. They explain why a materially modest place is his home and why an apparently grander plantation cannot compensate for leaving it.
evidence: was MY HOME--the only home I ever had

questions.prompt: How do the images of a demigod and priestess shape the child’s understanding of the journey?
facilitatorNotes: The master becomes an overwhelming, mysterious authority and the grandmother an unwilling intermediary leading an offering. Discuss the metaphor as a depiction of fear, not an assertion that she endorses the master’s power.
evidence: resisting, with the reserve and solemnity of a priestess

questions.prompt: What changes when the threatening beasts in the woods turn out to be logs and stumps?
facilitatorNotes: Distance and viewpoint produced an error that closer inspection corrects. The closing reflection extends this childhood discovery into a principle about interpretation and perspective.
evidence: the point from which a thing is viewed is of some importance

days.title: The Jungle: the wedding musicians
days.challenge: Separate technical musical failure from the scene’s emotional achievement.
days.focus: Narratorial repetition and the transformation of material poverty through art.
days.context: The wedding’s musicians work in Chicago’s packing industry. The narrator interrupts the feast to describe what their imperfect performance gives the guests.
days.contentNote: The passage mentions slaughterhouse work and uses patronizing ethnic and physical caricature alongside sympathy.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 1, Wikisource 1906 Doubleday, Page transcription, chapter paragraphs 12–19; begins “The musicians—how shall one begin to describe them? All”; ends “she would have to get up and run away.”.

questions.prompt: What does the repetition of “inspired man” ask us to value despite the defective instrument?
facilitatorNotes: Tamoszius’s expressive energy matters beyond correct tuning; the narrator gives comic spectacle a serious artistic dignity.
evidence: His fiddle is out of tune

questions.prompt: How does the account of the musicians’ working lives complicate the supposed “fairy place”?
facilitatorNotes: Practice follows exhausting labor and the cello player earns little; the imagined escape depends on bodies still working.
evidence: after working all day on the "killing beds

questions.prompt: Explain the connection between the music’s rough materials and the guests’ lives.
facilitatorNotes: The narrator explicitly links flawed sound to making a life from available circumstances. The remembered homeland does not erase Chicago’s conditions.
evidence: it is out of this material that they have to build their lives

days.title: Origin of Species: The pigeon as a research subject (excerpt)
days.challenge: Organize a dense catalogue into observable categories instead of trying to memorize every anatomical term.
days.focus: Specialized observation and the range of variation.
days.context: Darwin narrows his investigation to domestic pigeons. The excerpt supplies his research methods and an inventory of differences; it stops before his next classification argument.
days.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and anatomical terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, “On the Breeds of the Domestic Pigeon,” first two paragraphs; complete source paragraphs 86–87 in the saved paragraph index; opens “_On the Breeds of the Domestic Pigeon_.—Believing that it is always best to study some spe”; closes “ly, in certain breeds, the males and females have come to differ to a slight degree from each other.”.

questions.prompt: How does the opening establish that Darwin’s knowledge comes from more than reading?
facilitatorNotes: He keeps breeds, obtains skins, associates with breeders, and joins clubs. These details combine firsthand observation with distributed specialist knowledge, rather than making one method sufficient by itself.
evidence: I have associated with several eminent fanciers, and have been permitted to join two of the London Pigeon Clubs.

questions.prompt: Compare the carrier and short-faced tumbler: how does their contrast connect an obvious surface feature with internal structure?
facilitatorNotes: The conspicuous beak difference entails skull differences. A strong answer traces that connection rather than merely saying the birds look unlike each other.
evidence: wonderful difference in their beaks, entailing corresponding differences in their skulls.

questions.prompt: How does the second paragraph broaden the meaning of variation beyond the visible pigeon portraits in the first?
facilitatorNotes: It adds skeletal counts, internal structures, timing of plumage, eggs, flight, voice, and sex differences. Grouping the list shows variation in structure, development, and behavior.
evidence: The period at which the perfect plumage is acquired varies

days.title: Kinship without a shared childhood — excerpt
days.challenge: Distinguish biological relationships, lived attachment and the narrator’s explanation to his reader.
days.focus: A child’s separation as evidence of the destruction of family life.
days.context: The child reaches the plantation with his grandmother and meets siblings from whom he has been separated. The selection completes the arrival episode.
days.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement, family separation and racist beliefs. Its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, Removed from My First Home, arrival through the chapter’s closing paragraph; UNC 1855 printing, pp. 47–50; selected paragraphs corresponding to original PG indexes 97–101. Opening “As the day advanced the heat increased; and it was not until the afternoon that we reached”; closing “ so deeply. Besides, this was, in fact, my first introduction to the realities of slavery.”.

questions.prompt: Why do the words brother and sisters fail to produce immediate intimacy for Douglass?
facilitatorNotes: They have not lived or played together, so naming a relationship does not supply its emotional history. He explicitly assigns this estrangement to the system that separated them.
evidence: Brothers and sisters were by blood; but slavery had made us strangers

questions.prompt: Why do the peaches and pears not comfort him after his grandmother leaves?
facilitatorNotes: The gifts cannot replace his attachment or answer his feeling of having been deceived. His rejection does not mean the siblings are unkind; the scene includes their attempts at consolation.
evidence: I flung them away, and refused all their kindly advances

questions.prompt: How does the final paragraph defend the amount of attention given to this incident?
facilitatorNotes: He anticipates that readers may call it trivial, then grounds its importance in its deep effect on him and its introduction to slavery’s realities. Personal scale becomes part of the argument.
evidence: this was, in fact, my first introduction to the realities of slavery

days.title: Bivouac on a Mountain Side
days.challenge: Interpret a nearly still scene through shifting spatial scale and light.
days.focus: The relation between vulnerable human presence and the enduring sky.
days.context: A bivouac is a temporary military camp. Sketch the arrangement of valley, mountain, campfires, and sky before rereading the final lines.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “Bivouac on a Mountain Side”, Walt Whitman Archive ppp.00707, poem elementppp.00859; begins “I SEE before me now a traveling army halting,”; ends “out of reach, studded, breaking out, the eternal stars.”.

blocks.text: BIVOUAC ON A MOUNTAIN SIDE.

I SEE before me now a traveling army halting,
Below a fertile valley spread, with barns and the orchards of summer,
Behind, the terraced sides of a mountain, abrupt, in places rising high,
Broken, with rocks, with clinging cedars, with tall shapes dingily seen,
The numerous camp-fires scatter'd near and far, some away up on the mountain,
The shadowy forms of men and horses, looming, large-sized, flickering,
And over all the sky—the sky! far, far out of reach, studded, breaking out, the eternal stars.

questions.prompt: How do “below,” “behind,” and “over all” organize the reader’s viewpoint?
facilitatorNotes: The eye moves from the camp’s terrain to a sky exceeding the military scene; spatial orientation becomes a movement of attention.
evidence: And over all the sky—the sky

questions.prompt: What difference do the scattered fires and flickering forms make to the army’s apparent power?
facilitatorNotes: The army appears dispersed and shadowy rather than as a solid conquering mass, though its numerous fires can also suggest collective presence.
evidence: The shadowy forms of men and horses

questions.prompt: Does “far, far out of reach” offer consolation or distance?
facilitatorNotes: Both are defensible: eternal stars may endure beyond conflict, but remain inaccessible. Require attention to the doubled “far,” not an automatic peaceful moral.
evidence: far, far out of reach

days.title: Origin of Species: A cumulative case for common ancestry (excerpt)
days.challenge: Follow an argument by competing hypotheses across five long paragraphs and distinguish independent lines of evidence.
days.focus: Cumulative inference, breeding experiments, and improbable alternatives.
days.context: After cataloguing pigeon differences, Darwin argues that domestic breeds share an ancestor. He weighs an alternative involving several lost or unknown ancestral species.
days.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and anatomical terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference. The passage uses the hierarchical phrase “half-civilized man”; discuss that historical prejudice rather than adopting it.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, common origin of domestic pigeons; complete source paragraphs 89–93 in the saved paragraph index; opens “Great as the differences are between the breeds of pigeons, I am fully convinced that the ”; closes “hat all our domestic breeds have descended from the Columba livia with its geographical sub-species.”.

questions.prompt: What additional assumptions does the multiple-ancestor explanation require, according to Darwin?
facilitatorNotes: It requires several unusual ancestral species to have been domesticated successfully and then become extinct or remain unknown. Darwin argues from the combined burden, not from merely disliking an alternative.
evidence: So many strange contingencies seem to me improbable in the highest degree.

questions.prompt: Why is the blue grandchild of a white fantail and black barb especially useful to his argument?
facilitatorNotes: The offspring reappears with the rock-pigeon’s suite of marks despite neither immediate parent having them. Darwin interprets that as reversion to a shared ancestor; the answer should state the interpretation as his explanatory inference.
evidence: one grandchild of the pure white fantail and pure black barb was of as beautiful a blue colour

questions.prompt: How does the final paragraph change the reader’s task compared with judging each observation separately?
facilitatorNotes: It assembles disappearance, unusual traits, reversion, and fertility into a mutually reinforcing case. Readers can consider whether the lines are truly independent and whether one weak line would undo the whole inference.
evidence: from these several reasons, taken together, I can feel no doubt

days.title: A mother’s night journeys — excerpt
days.challenge: Distinguish the narrator’s limits of memory from his analysis of the rules surrounding parenthood.
days.focus: How legal power redirects family affection.
days.context: Douglass turns from separation from his grandmother to what he remembers of his parents, especially his mother’s visits while she worked on another farm.
days.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement, family separation and racist beliefs. Its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. The passage discusses coerced family arrangements and threatened punishment without graphic injury.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, Parentage, opening seven narrative paragraphs; UNC 1855 printing, pp. 51–54; selected paragraphs corresponding to original PG indexes 104–110. Opening “IF the reader will now be kind enough to allow me time to grow bigger, and afford me an op”; closing “senting slave. "I went to see my child," is no excuse to the ear or heart of the overseer.”.

questions.prompt: How can Douglass describe his knowledge of his mother as both scanty and distinct?
facilitatorNotes: He has few encounters to remember but vivid impressions of her appearance and actions. The distinction limits his claim while preserving the intensity of those memories.
evidence: My knowledge of my mother is very scanty, but very distinct

questions.prompt: What does the phrase about the master’s ledger reveal about the system’s treatment of childbirth?
facilitatorNotes: A new child is counted as an addition to property while the mother is denied time for reciprocal affection. The economic image interrupts the language of care and exposes incompatible priorities.
evidence: when it adds another name to a master's ledger

questions.prompt: Why does the twelve-mile distance matter beyond providing a geographical detail?
facilitatorNotes: It makes each visit a costly journey, often twenty-four miles, while she must return before sunrise under threat of punishment. The distance supplies evidence of effort against claims of maternal indifference.
evidence: I went to see my child," is no excuse to the ear or heart of the overseer

days.title: Mid-day
days.challenge: Follow an extended comparison while preserving differences between its two terms.
days.focus: Scattered thoughts, rooted trees, and a speaker’s uncertain relation to the landscape.
days.context: H.D.’s landscape and the speaker’s state of mind continually exchange qualities. Reread the seed and tree images aloud, paying attention to where the poem turns.

excerpt.locator: Mid-day; begins “The light beats upon me. I am startled-- a”; ends “on the path among the crevices of the rocks.”.

questions.prompt: What makes scattered seeds an especially precise comparison for the speaker’s thoughts?
facilitatorNotes: The seeds are dispersed, spent, and vulnerable to wind; the image joins fragmentation to exhaustion rather than simply sadness.
evidence: my thoughts are spent

questions.prompt: What changes after “yet far beyond”?
facilitatorNotes: The poem moves from damaged plants close at hand to the bright, deep-rooted poplar, introducing stability without granting it to the speaker.
evidence: the poplar is bright on the hill

questions.prompt: Does addressing the poplar resolve the speaker’s distress?
facilitatorNotes: The final contrast keeps the speaker perishing while the tree is great. Admiration is present, but no recovery is narrated.
evidence: while I perish on the path

days.title: Origin of Species: Accumulating small differences (excerpt)
days.challenge: Connect repeated comparisons to a mechanism that acts over generations rather than in a single dramatic change.
days.focus: Human purpose, expert observation, and the cumulative power of selection.
days.context: Darwin explains how breeders and gardeners direct inherited differences toward desired purposes. The domestic examples prepare an analogy with selection in nature.
days.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and anatomical terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, “Selection,” opening five paragraphs; complete source paragraphs 96–100 in the saved paragraph index; opens “_Selection_.—Let us now briefly consider the steps by which domestic races have been produ”; closes “the flowers, or the fruit, will produce races differing from each other chiefly in these characters.”.

questions.prompt: What does the contrast between an organism’s own good and human use reveal about domestic selection?
facilitatorNotes: Desired traits serve the breeder’s needs or taste and need not benefit the organism itself. Discuss how that distinction limits any simple equation between human breeding and survival in nature.
evidence: not indeed to the animal’s or plant’s own good, but to man’s use or fancy.

questions.prompt: How do the magician’s wand and connoisseur images work differently in the account of breeders?
facilitatorNotes: The wand dramatizes seemingly extraordinary transformation; the connoisseur image emphasizes patient, trained discrimination. Their tension allows discussion of spectacular results produced by ordinary repeated choices.
evidence: It is the magician’s wand
the sheep are placed on a table and are studied, like a picture by a connoisseur;

questions.prompt: Why compare cabbage leaves with cabbage flowers and gooseberry fruit with its flowers?
facilitatorNotes: Different human-valued parts vary greatly while less-selected parts remain more alike. This pattern supports directed accumulation in particular traits rather than a uniform change throughout every plant.
evidence: See how different the leaves of the cabbage are, and how extremely alike the flowers;

days.title: The heart-shaped cake and an inheritance of literacy — excerpt
days.challenge: Follow a scene into retrospective grief and a rebuttal of racial assumptions about intellectual inheritance.
days.focus: Objects, remembered actions and an incomplete family record.
days.context: The narrator recalls one visit during which his mother protected and fed him, then reflects on her death and her ability to read.
days.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement, family separation and racist beliefs. Its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Includes food deprivation, threats against a child, and a parent’s death; no graphic injury is depicted.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, Parentage, remembered visit through the account of the mother’s reading; UNC 1855 printing, pp. 54–58; selected paragraphs corresponding to original PG indexes 111–114. Opening “One of the visits of my mother to me, while at Col. Lloyd's, I remember very vividly, as a”; closing “se mental endowments it is, at present, fashionable to hold in disparagement and contempt.”.

questions.prompt: How does the heart-shaped cake mean more than the food it supplies?
facilitatorNotes: It marks the mother’s intervention and the child’s discovery that he belongs to someone emotionally, despite the surrounding property system. Its shape may reinforce the episode’s affection without requiring one fixed symbolic reading.
evidence: That night I learned the fact, that I was not only a child, but somebody's child

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator describe his remembered image of his mother as mute?
facilitatorNotes: He retains a visual presence but lacks sustained conversation, final counsel and a fuller relationship. The metaphor shows what memory preserves and what separation irreversibly withheld.
evidence: but the image is mute

questions.prompt: What argument is made by attributing his love of letters to his mother?
facilitatorNotes: Her unusual ability to read offers an intellectual inheritance he values. The attribution directly challenges a convention that would credit his white father and disparage his Black mother’s capacities.
evidence: to the native genius of my sable, unprotected, and uncultivated mother

days.title: The Jungle: the wedding debt
days.challenge: Distinguish a character’s reassuring belief from evidence that challenges it.
days.focus: Social trust, unequal sacrifice, and the limits of individual effort.
days.context: Near the end of the wedding, family members calculate what unpaid contributions and the saloon bill will mean. Earlier guests were expected to help the couple begin married life.
days.contentNote: Includes poverty and corrupt dealings; the narrator’s broad claims about urban life should be evaluated as the novel’s rhetoric.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 1, Wikisource 1906 Doubleday, Page transcription, chapter paragraphs 34–37; begins “In the meantime there was going on in another”; ends “all problems, and who was so big and strong!”.

questions.prompt: Why call the wedding agreement a compact “not expressed”?
facilitatorNotes: Custom creates a shared obligation without a written contract. Its breakdown leaves the hosts financially exposed and morally bewildered.
evidence: a compact not expressed

questions.prompt: How does the account of Aniele’s chickens change the meaning of a small contribution?
facilitatorNotes: The narration measures money through labor, vigilance, and dependence; a donation’s monetary size cannot express its cost to the giver.
evidence: Money could not tell the value of these chickens

questions.prompt: What evidence invites doubt about “I will work harder” even as Ona finds comfort in it?
facilitatorNotes: The earlier passport and lodging scams show exploitation that strength cannot prevent; repeating the phrase creates sympathy and dramatic irony.
evidence: I will work harder

days.title: Origin of Species: When classifications become uncertain (excerpt)
days.challenge: Identify circular definitions and distinguish observed intermediate forms from intermediates inferred by analogy.
days.focus: Classification, expert judgment, and uncertainty in categories.
days.context: Darwin moves from domestic variation to organisms in nature. The passage questions supposedly secure boundaries between species, varieties, and individual differences.
days.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and anatomical terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, opening five body paragraphs; complete source paragraphs 117–121 in the saved paragraph index; opens “Before applying the principles arrived at in the last chapter to organic beings in a state”; closes “nown varieties can be named which have not been ranked as species by at least some competent judges.”.

questions.prompt: Why is “important organs never vary” potentially circular as used by the authors Darwin criticizes?
facilitatorNotes: If importance is defined by lack of variation, any varying organ is automatically excluded from the important category. The claim then protects itself from counterexamples instead of testing a substantive definition.
evidence: these same authors practically rank that character as important

questions.prompt: What changes when a naturalist has not found intermediate forms but assumes that they exist or once existed?
facilitatorNotes: A classification moves from direct linking evidence toward analogy and conjecture. Darwin does not prohibit inference, but marks the increased uncertainty explicitly.
evidence: a wide door for the entry of doubt and conjecture is opened.

questions.prompt: Does the final appeal to experienced naturalists remove disagreement? Explain the role of the majority.
facilitatorNotes: Expert judgment is offered as the available guide, yet competent judges still differ; majority decision is a practical response rather than a proof that a boundary is clear in nature.
evidence: We must, however, in many cases, decide by a majority of naturalists

days.title: The plantation as a closed public world — excerpt
days.challenge: Trace a qualified concession through a concrete institutional counterexample.
days.focus: Public opinion, closed information systems and unchecked authority.
days.context: Douglass examines a claim that Maryland slavery was moderated by proximity to free states, then considers the isolation of the plantation he knew.
days.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement, family separation and racist beliefs. Its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. References to cruelty and killing are general, not graphic.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, A General Survey of the Slave Plantation, opening seven narrative paragraphs; UNC 1855 printing, pp. 61–64; selected paragraphs corresponding to original PG indexes 124–130. Opening “IT is generally supposed that slavery, in the state of Maryland, exists in its mildest for”; closing “ands; full three hundred years behind the age, in all that relates to humanity and morals.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Douglass first concede that public opinion can restrain cruelty?
facilitatorNotes: The concession narrows his disagreement: he questions whether humane outside opinion can actually reach this plantation. It makes the argument conditional rather than simply denying every regional distinction.
evidence: whenever and wherever it can reach them

questions.prompt: How does the account of ships and commerce support the larger argument about isolation?
facilitatorNotes: The owner controls transport in both directions and owns nearly everyone aboard. Even trade, which might bring outsiders and scrutiny, travels through a controlled channel.
evidence: everything brought to the plantation, comes through the same channel

questions.prompt: What is the effect of listing the overseer as accuser, judge, jury, advocate and executioner?
facilitatorNotes: The list collapses institutions that should check one another into one authority. The enslaved person has no voice or independent recourse, so the plantation’s order cannot be equated with justice.
evidence: The overseer is generally accuser, judge, jury, advocate and executioner

days.title: Pursuit
days.challenge: Audit the changing confidence of a speaker who interprets physical traces.
days.focus: Observation and imaginative reconstruction in a lyric pursuit.
days.context: The speaker reconstructs another person’s movement from marks on plants and earth. Attend to each shift between seeing, inferring, questioning, and claiming certainty.

excerpt.locator: Pursuit; begins “What do I care that the stream is trampled,”; ends “trace of you in the larch-cones and the underbrush.”.

questions.prompt: Which details are physical traces, and which are the speaker’s reconstructions?
facilitatorNotes: A snapped stalk and turned grass are visible; speed, bodily injury, and prayer are interpretations built upon them. Distinguish plausible inference from certainty.
evidence: a wild-hyacinth stalk is snapped

questions.prompt: Why does “This is clear” become unstable when followed by questions?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker claims a fall and injury, then asks about gaze and speech that traces cannot establish. Confidence and desire outrun available evidence.
evidence: This is clear--

questions.prompt: Does the disappearance prove the wood-daemon’s help?
facilitatorNotes: It explains the loss of tracks poetically but is not independently demonstrated. An ending of uncertainty is supported by the last statement.
evidence: I can find no trace of you

days.title: Origin of Species: What struggle means (excerpt)
days.challenge: Hold a technical metaphor apart from its everyday sense and reconstruct the link between variation and selection.
days.focus: Definition, reproductive success, and hidden competition.
days.context: Darwin introduces the struggle for existence after establishing variation. His definition explicitly includes dependence and reproductive success, not only direct combat.
days.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and anatomical terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, opening five body paragraphs; complete source paragraphs 142–146 in the saved paragraph index; opens “Before entering on the subject of this chapter, I must make a few preliminary remarks, to ”; closes “w increasing, more or less rapidly, in numbers, all cannot do so, for the world would not hold them.”.

questions.prompt: Why is variation alone, in Darwin’s argument, insufficient to explain adaptation?
facilitatorNotes: Variation supplies differences, but selection explains which differences tend to be preserved through survival and offspring. Trace both steps rather than treating any difference as automatically advantageous.
evidence: the mere existence of individual variability and of some few well-marked varieties

questions.prompt: How do drought and missletoe extend struggle beyond two animals fighting for food?
facilitatorNotes: Drought shows dependence on physical conditions; missletoe involves hosts, neighboring plants, and dispersing birds. The metaphor gathers different relations under one heading and should not make every relation literal combat.
evidence: I use the term Struggle for Existence in a large and metaphorical sense

questions.prompt: What does the scene of singing birds expose about a casual observer’s view of nature?
facilitatorNotes: A pleasant surface hides continual feeding on other life and destruction of eggs or young. The passage asks readers to revise perception, not merely accept an abstract population proposition.
evidence: We behold the face of nature bright with gladness

days.title: Beauty and power at the Great House — excerpt
days.challenge: Hold sensory pleasure and institutional condemnation together without flattening either perspective.
days.focus: The distinction between enjoying a landscape and owning people or property.
days.context: After analysing the plantation’s isolation, Douglass describes its landscape, buildings and organisation from the intertwined perspectives of a child and an adult.
days.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement, family separation and racist beliefs. Its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Includes historical ghost stories, references to punishment and the sale of enslaved people.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, A General Survey of the Slave Plantation, outward appearance through the work of the surrounding farms; UNC 1855 printing, pp. 64–69; selected paragraphs corresponding to original PG indexes 131–138. Opening “This, however, is not the only view that the place presents. Civilization is shut out, but”; closing “l" was the shoemaker; and all these had hands to assist them in their several departments.”.

questions.prompt: How does the opening paragraph make room for the child’s pleasure without retracting the criticism of the plantation?
facilitatorNotes: It explicitly separates outward appearance and natural beauty from impunity and coercion. Adaptation is a response to having no way to leave, not evidence that the system is benign.
evidence: Civilization is shut out, but nature cannot be

questions.prompt: What distinction is compressed into the statement that the Lloyds occupied the house while he enjoyed it?
facilitatorNotes: Legal possession and sensory or imaginative access are different. The child claims an experience of beauty that ownership cannot monopolise; students may also note how precarious that access remains.
evidence: They occupied it; I enjoyed it

questions.prompt: How does the closing inventory of work alter the earlier image of ornamental wealth?
facilitatorNotes: The craftsmen and farms expose the labour and ownership structure sustaining the estate. Beauty rests beside an account that reduces people to a replenishing stock, creating an ethical contrast.
evidence: the home plantation merely groaned at a removal of the young increase, or human crop

days.title: To a Stranger
days.challenge: Separate a speaker’s assured language from externally confirmed knowledge.
days.focus: Imagined recognition, bodily reciprocity, and the paradox of silent address.
days.context: The speaker addresses a passerby without actually speaking to that person. Distinguish the encounter that occurs from the intimacy the speaker imagines.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “To a Stranger”, Walt Whitman Archive ppp.00707, poem elementppp.00767; begins “PASSING stranger! you do not know how longingly I”; ends “see to it that I do not lose you.”.

blocks.text: TO A STRANGER.

PASSING stranger! you do not know how longingly I look upon you,
You must be he I was seeking, or she I was seeking, (it comes to me as of a dream,)
I have somewhere surely lived a life of joy with you,
All is recall'd as we flit by each other, fluid, affectionate, chaste, matured,
You grew up with me, were a boy with me or a girl with me,
I ate with you and slept with you, your body has become not yours only nor left my body mine only,
You give me the pleasure of your eyes, face, flesh, as we pass, you take of my beard, breast, hands, in return,
I am not to speak to you, I am to think of you when I sit alone or wake at night alone,
I am to wait, I do not doubt I am to meet you again,
I am to see to it that I do not lose you.

questions.prompt: What does “as of a dream” do to the claim of having shared a former life?
facilitatorNotes: It qualifies the seeming certainty with a dreamlike comparison; the poem can evoke intense recognition without proving literal previous acquaintance.
evidence: as of a dream

questions.prompt: How does the exchange of bodily details make looking reciprocal?
facilitatorNotes: “You give” and “you take” imagine mutual participation; the stranger’s actual perspective remains unavailable, an important limit to the speaker’s claim.
evidence: you take of my beard, breast, hands

questions.prompt: Why end with future intention after saying the speaker will not speak?
facilitatorNotes: The encounter becomes an inward commitment to memory and possible reunion, not a completed relationship. The repeated “I am to” makes that intention emphatic.
evidence: I am not to speak to you

days.title: Origin of Species: Growth, checks, and the crowded surface (excerpt)
days.challenge: Separate hypothetical unchecked growth, reported field cases, and a closing spatial metaphor.
days.focus: Models of increase and the distinction between fertility and actual abundance.
days.context: Darwin develops the consequences of reproduction under limited conditions. Treat his historical numerical scenarios as arguments with assumptions rather than verified modern population forecasts.
days.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and anatomical terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, geometrical increase and reproductive checks; complete source paragraphs 147–151 in the saved paragraph index; opens “There is no exception to the rule that every organic being naturally increases at so high ”; closes “n inwards by incessant blows, sometimes one wedge being struck, and then another with greater force.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Darwin move from theoretical calculations to introduced animals and plants?
facilitatorNotes: The observed expansions offer a second form of evidence for growth potential when checks weaken. His transition acknowledges that hypothetical calculations alone are not the strongest available support.
evidence: better evidence on this subject than mere theoretical calculations

questions.prompt: What do the condor, ostrich, and petrel examples challenge about using egg counts to predict abundance?
facilitatorNotes: Higher fertility does not directly determine the number surviving in a region; survival and environmental checks intervene. The text explicitly makes average population depend only indirectly on eggs or seeds.
evidence: the average number of any animal or plant depends only indirectly on the number of its eggs or seeds.

questions.prompt: What does the image of ten thousand wedges help readers imagine, and where might its simplification become a limitation?
facilitatorNotes: It makes crowding and interconnected displacement vivid: a push on one affects space for others. Readers may note that a mechanical image compresses different living relations; support either its usefulness or its limit with the actual comparison.
evidence: ten thousand sharp wedges packed close together and driven inwards by incessant blows

days.title: Who may interpret the facts? — excerpt
days.challenge: Distinguish goodwill, restrictive expectations and the practical danger of proving an identity.
days.focus: Authority over one’s own narrative and the costs of public evidence.
days.context: Douglass has begun lecturing against slavery. He describes tensions with sympathetic organisers who want personal testimony while reserving interpretation for themselves.
days.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement, family separation and racist beliefs. Its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXIII, Introduced to the Abolitionists, speaking assignments through the decision to publish his first narrative; UNC 1855 printing, pp. 360–363; selected paragraphs corresponding to original PG indexes 536–538. Opening “Among the first duties assigned me, on entering the ranks, was to travel, in company with ”; closing “own in Maryland, and I had reason to believe that an effort would be made to recapture me.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the distinction between facts and philosophy become restrictive for Douglass?
facilitatorNotes: His allies value testimony but try to limit his role to recounting personal events. His reading and thinking produce arguments that exceed the assigned role, so the distinction allocates intellectual authority unequally.
evidence: Give us the facts," said Collins, "we will take care of the philosophy

questions.prompt: How does the advice to be himself contradict the advice to retain a plantation manner of speech?
facilitatorNotes: He is developing through reading and public work, yet listeners expect a fixed performance that matches their idea of an enslaved person. Their expectation makes growth seem less authentic.
evidence: Besides, I was growing, and needed room

questions.prompt: What dilemma does the decision to publish names and dates create?
facilitatorNotes: Specific information permits independent checking and rebuts accusations of imposture, but also helps those who might recapture him. More verifiable testimony carries a personal cost in an unequal legal system.
evidence: I had reason to believe that an effort would be made to recapture me

days.title: The Jungle: the promise of America
days.challenge: Read a retrospective account for discrepancies between expectation and evidence.
days.focus: Strength, hearsay, and the economic assumptions beneath an immigrant dream.
days.context: Chapter II turns backward from the wedding to the family’s decision to emigrate. Watch how confidence draws support from limited experience.
days.contentNote: Includes treating marriage as a purchase, coercive labor, and a brief threat of violence. These are features of the novel’s historical world.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 2, Wikisource 1906 Doubleday, Page transcription, chapter paragraphs 2–8; begins “Jurgis talked lightly about work, because he was young.”; ends “odd jobs, and sleeping always with one eye open.”.

questions.prompt: Why is being chosen quickly for work weak proof that everyone can avoid starvation?
facilitatorNotes: Jurgis treats his exceptional physical strength and luck as a universal explanation, dismissing the men left waiting rather than testing their history.
evidence: the line always moved too slowly for him

questions.prompt: What is missing when Jurgis calculates American wages?
facilitatorNotes: He uses prices in Lithuania; the apparent fortune depends on an unsupported assumption about living costs.
evidence: with prices as they were where he lived

questions.prompt: How does the railroad episode both support and threaten his confidence?
facilitatorNotes: He survives through endurance and restraint, but employers and gamblers try to take his money and life. Personal discipline succeeds amid structural danger.
evidence: sleeping always with one eye open

days.title: Origin of Species: Cats, clover, and indirect causes (excerpt)
days.challenge: Diagram the causal chains while distinguishing counted observations from hypothetical consequences.
days.focus: Ecological interdependence and the limits of a simple causal story.
days.context: Darwin turns from general population pressure to examples in which distant organisms affect one another through intermediate relationships.
days.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and anatomical terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, interconnected checks and relations; complete source paragraphs 158–160 in the saved paragraph index; opens “Many cases are on record showing how complex and unexpected are the checks and relations b”; closes “ the intervention first of mice and then of bees, the frequency of certain flowers in that district!”.

questions.prompt: What changes when Darwin looks closely beneath the heath rather than surveying it from a distance?
facilitatorNotes: He discovers suppressed seedlings where he initially sees no fir trees. The thirty-two trees in a square yard make the point that apparent absence can mask persistent life checked by browsing.
evidence: I counted thirty-two little trees

questions.prompt: Where does the Paraguay account move from a reported observation into a conditional chain?
facilitatorNotes: The fly’s effect on newborn animals is presented through named observers; the increase of birds and subsequent shifts are expressed through “if” and “would.” Readers should mark the change in evidentiary status.
evidence: if certain insectivorous birds

questions.prompt: Trace the proposed connection between cats and flowers. Why does Darwin describe it as credible rather than a direct observation?
facilitatorNotes: Cats reduce mice, mice destroy bee nests, and bees fertilize certain plants. The final abundance claim combines links and must be distinguished from personally observing the whole chain.
evidence: through the intervention first of mice and then of bees

days.title: A child before he is property — excerpt
days.challenge: Follow a long paragraph whose immediate gratitude is repeatedly qualified by hindsight.
days.focus: The corrosive effects of power on domestic affection.
days.context: The young Douglass adjusts to Baltimore and to Sophia Auld’s initial kindness. The adult narrator already knows that her behaviour will change.
days.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement, family separation and racist beliefs. Its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice.
