excerpt.locator: Chapter X, Life in Baltimore, first narrative paragraph; UNC 1855 printing, pp. 141–145; selected paragraphs corresponding to original PG indexes 215–215. Opening “ONCE in Baltimore, with hard brick pavements under my feet, which almost raised blisters, ”; closing “e first seven years I lived with her, occasional returns of her former kindly disposition.”.

questions.prompt: How do the hostile streets and the welcoming household complicate the promise of the move to Baltimore?
facilitatorNotes: The city initially overwhelms and threatens him, while the household offers protection and recognition. The contrast prevents a simple equation of a new location with immediate happiness.
evidence: My country eyes and ears were confused and bewildered here

questions.prompt: What changes are condensed into the comparison between being treated as a pig and as a child?
facilitatorNotes: Material improvements accompany permission to look up, receive affection and behave without crouching. The comparison makes recognition of humanity as important as food or bedding.
evidence: I had been treated as a pig on the plantation; I was treated as a child now

questions.prompt: Why does the repeated qualification for a time matter to the portrait of Sophia Auld?
facilitatorNotes: It interrupts the welcoming scene with knowledge of later corruption. Her initial recognition of a child is described as natural, while treating him as property must be learned.
evidence: This latter thought was a thing of conventional growth

days.title: The Jungle: reaching Packingtown
days.challenge: Track sensory description alongside changing knowledge of the city.
days.focus: The gap between legal forms, practical access, and a welcoming community.
days.context: The emigrating family arrives in Chicago without English. Their destination gradually becomes a landscape of smoke, sound, expense, and recognizable neighbors.
days.contentNote: Includes fraud, poverty, and a narrator’s condescending generalizations about immigrant experience.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 2, Wikisource 1906 Doubleday, Page transcription, chapter paragraphs 10–17; begins “There were twelve in all in the party, five”; ends “prices that the railroad people asked them for food.”.

questions.prompt: What does the sentence about the hotel rate card expose about formal protection?
facilitatorNotes: A posted price may satisfy a law yet offer little usable information to a reader who cannot understand it; the irony concerns access to protection.
evidence: it does not say that it shall be in Lithuanian

questions.prompt: How does the stockyards’ sound delay recognition of its source?
facilitatorNotes: It first resembles bees and forest whispers, then resolves into thousands of animals. Familiar natural comparisons make the industrial scale newly strange.
evidence: the distant lowing of ten thousand cattle

questions.prompt: Why is finding Jokubas a “happy ending” that does not restore the dream of wealth?
facilitatorNotes: He offers language, food, and practical knowledge, but high prices have already disproved the family’s simple wage calculation.
evidence: a land of high prices

days.title: Origin of Species: Nature as a selector (excerpt)
days.challenge: Analyze the difference between a stated mechanism and the personification used to explain it.
days.focus: Analogy, scale, and the rhetorical force of natural selection.
days.context: Darwin applies his earlier accounts of variation and competition to natural selection, contrasting the mechanism with human breeding.
days.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and anatomical terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, opening five body paragraphs; complete source paragraphs 171–175 in the saved paragraph index; opens “How will the struggle for existence, discussed too briefly in the last chapter, act in reg”; closes “ogical ages, that we only see that the forms of life are now different from what they formerly were.”.

questions.prompt: According to the first paragraph, what happens to variations that are neither useful nor harmful?
facilitatorNotes: They are not affected by selection in the stated account and remain fluctuating. This qualification prevents treating every difference as an adaptation and clarifies what the mechanism is said to act upon.
evidence: Variations neither useful nor injurious would not be affected by natural selection

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of comparing an open country with an island or barrier-bounded country?
facilitatorNotes: Immigration changes which organisms can occupy places; barriers alter the possibilities for local descendants. The comparison presents conditions under which selection operates, not proof that isolation is always required.
evidence: into which new and better adapted forms could not freely enter

questions.prompt: How might the verbs scrutinising, rejecting, and preserving help and mislead a reader?
facilitatorNotes: They make a slow nonhuman process vivid by resembling an active breeder’s choices. Readers should connect them to differential survival rather than infer conscious intention from the personification.
evidence: natural selection is daily and hourly scrutinising

days.title: An unintended lesson about freedom — excerpt
days.challenge: Analyse irony when one speaker’s intended warning becomes another person’s argument for resistance.
days.focus: Education, the control of knowledge and the agency of a listener.
days.context: Sophia Auld has begun teaching Douglass to read. Her husband intervenes, explaining why he thinks literacy incompatible with enslavement.
days.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement, family separation and racist beliefs. Its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Contains a racial slur in Hugh Auld’s quoted speech; the quotation is evidence of his dehumanising reasoning. The complete 1855 paragraph includes an additional racist assertion omitted by the earlier Gutenberg transcription.

excerpt.locator: Chapter X, Life in Baltimore, the reading lessons and Hugh Auld’s prohibition; UNC 1855 printing, pp. 145–147; selected paragraphs corresponding to original PG indexes 216–217. Opening “The frequent hearing of my mistress reading the bible--for she often read aloud when her h”; closing “and by the other; believing, that but for my mistress, I might have grown up in ignorance.”.

questions.prompt: What makes the reading lessons initially seem ordinary and desirable to Sophia Auld?
facilitatorNotes: Her own Bible reading awakens curiosity, and she takes pride in the child’s progress. She expects her husband to share that pride before encountering the rules of ownership.
evidence: My mistress seemed almost as proud of my progress, as if I had been her own child

questions.prompt: Why does Douglass call Hugh Auld’s speech his first anti-slavery lecture?
facilitatorNotes: Auld means to defend slavery by explaining its dependence on ignorance. Douglass accepts the connection but rejects the goal, treating knowledge as a route out of bondage.
evidence: His discourse was the first decidedly antislavery lecture

questions.prompt: How does the final acknowledgment of both adults avoid treating them as equivalent teachers?
facilitatorNotes: Sophia supplies the alphabet and encouragement, while Hugh unintentionally supplies strategic understanding through opposition. The narrator distinguishes their intentions while tracing effects neither fully controlled.
evidence: I do not owe quite as much to the opposition of my master, as to the kindly assistance of my amiable mistress

days.title: The Jungle: an economical arrangement
days.challenge: Identify dramatic irony without confusing it with a character’s explicit belief.
days.focus: Pollution, distant spectators, and industrial power viewed as opportunity.
days.context: Jurgis and Ona explore the streets around the stockyards. Their hopeful conclusions often differ from the narrator’s implications.
days.contentNote: Depicts children scavenging and environmental contamination.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 2, Wikisource 1906 Doubleday, Page transcription, chapter paragraphs 21–25; begins “Later that afternoon he and Ona went out to”; ends “"To-morrow I shall go there and get a job!"”.

questions.prompt: Why compare the streets to a topographical map?
facilitatorNotes: Exaggerated mountains, valleys, and rivers make neglected infrastructure physically visible; the scene is difficult terrain rather than an ordinary roadway.
evidence: a miniature topographical map

questions.prompt: What is the effect of the visitors debating children’s scavenging without going down to ask?
facilitatorNotes: Their curiosity becomes detached spectatorship. The narrator exposes an avoidable gap between observing suffering and investigating it.
evidence: Apparently none of them ever went down to find out

questions.prompt: How does the final sunset alter Packingtown without changing its material conditions?
facilitatorNotes: Light converts smoke into a vision of power, while the earlier hazards remain. Hope comes through the couple’s perspective rather than proof of safety.
evidence: in the twilight it was a vision of power

days.title: Origin of Species: Imagined flowers, observed pollen (excerpt)
days.challenge: Track when the argument enters an imaginary case, supplies observation, and returns to hypothesis.
days.focus: Evidence embedded in a model of reciprocal adaptation.
days.context: This selection develops a hypothetical relationship between nectar-producing flowers and insects. Darwin temporarily interrupts it with an account of examining holly flowers.
days.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and anatomical terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, complex illustrations of natural selection; complete source paragraphs 185–188 in the saved paragraph index; opens “Let us now take a more complex case. Certain plants excrete a sweet juice, apparently for ”; closes “ontinued creation of new organic beings, or of any great and sudden modification in their structure.”.

questions.prompt: Why might destruction of much pollen still be compatible with a gain to the plant in the imagined case?
facilitatorNotes: Some pollen reaches another flower and enables crossing, whose benefits Darwin argues may outweigh the loss. The reasoning compares consequences rather than treating any material loss as decisive.
evidence: although nine-tenths of the pollen were destroyed, it might still be a great gain to the plant

questions.prompt: How do the distance between holly trees, microscope examination, and wind direction support his inference about insects?
facilitatorNotes: The evidence establishes pollen on separated female flowers and argues against transport by the prevailing wind. Discuss what the observations support without claiming that the whole imagined evolutionary sequence has thereby been observed.
evidence: the pollen could not thus have been carried.

questions.prompt: Why does the final paragraph bring in coast-waves and valleys?
facilitatorNotes: It uses a geological analogy: small repeated actions over long periods can yield large structures. The analogy answers an objection to scale, while the conditional “if it be a true principle” leaves the mechanism’s truth to evidence.
evidence: the coast-waves, called a trifling and insignificant cause

days.title: Too late to stop the lessons — excerpt
days.challenge: Read two short paragraphs slowly, tracing how a proverb and a concrete exchange carry an argument about irreversible learning.
days.focus: Surveillance that arrives too late, and the exchange of bread for literacy.
days.context: Recap: in Baltimore, Sophia Auld began teaching the young Douglass the alphabet until her husband forbade it, and she then turned against the lessons herself. These two paragraphs describe the household’s watchfulness and the strategies Douglass used to keep learning.
days.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement, family separation and racist beliefs. Its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XI, A Change Came O’er the Spirit of My Dream, two contiguous paragraphs; UNC 1855 printing; opens “Mrs. Auld was an apt woman, and the advice of her husband”; closes “that they lived on Philpot street, very near Durgin & Bailey's shipyard.”.

questions.prompt: Douglass says the household’s watchfulness came “entirely too late.” What does his proverb of the “inch” and the “ell” claim about how learning works, and why does he locate the decisive step “in the days of her simplicity and kindness”?
facilitatorNotes: An ell was an old cloth measure much longer than an inch; the proverb says a small concession invites a far larger claim. Douglass presents literacy as self-propelling: once the alphabet is known, no ordinary precaution can reverse it. The irony that kindness, not design, began his escape from ignorance is central; some students may also read the line as a challenge to the slaveholders’ belief that control can be complete.
evidence: The first, and never to be retraced, step had been taken.
my mistress had given me the "inch," and now, no ordinary precaution could prevent me from taking the "ell."

questions.prompt: In the first paragraph, what does the household’s surveillance (“I was sure to be suspected of having a book”) reveal about how the Aulds understood the power of reading, and how does Douglass use their own conviction as evidence?
facilitatorNotes: The suspicion treats a book as contraband and reading as a threat to the institution itself. Douglass lets the slaveholders’ conclusion that “education and slavery are incompatible” stand as their admission, not merely his claim. Students may alternatively emphasize fear, or the pragmatic logic of control; ask which words show the narrator’s irony.
evidence: education and slavery are incompatible with each other
I was sure to be suspected of having a book, and was at once called upon to give an account of myself

questions.prompt: Why is the bread-for-lessons exchange more complex than a simple purchase, and what does Douglass’s refusal to name the boys add?
facilitatorNotes: Bread answers the boys’ hunger while lessons answer his denied intellectual need, and “a lesson more valuable to me than bread” inverts the market value; some teach without payment. His refusal to name them shows the unequal risks surrounding the exchange: helping a slave toward freedom was “almost an unpardonable offense.”
evidence: I generally paid my tuition fee to the boys, with bread
For a single biscuit, any of my hungry little comrades would give me a lesson more valuable to me than bread.
prudence forbids

days.title: The Gift
days.challenge: Follow revisions and denials within an intimate argument rather than inventing its backstory.
days.focus: The poem as gift and the paradox of beauty that overwhelms.
days.context: An intimate speaker sends a written statement instead of jewelry. The preceding encounter remains unspecified; the poem supplies its own argument about unbearable beauty.

excerpt.locator: The Gift; begins “Instead of pearls--a wrought clasp-- a bracelet--will you accept”; ends “I send no string of pearls, no bracelet--accept this.”.

questions.prompt: How does the broken necklace connect the speaker’s longing to the street-child?
facilitatorNotes: Both grasp after something dropped by the addressee. The comparison acknowledges desire and unequal access rather than presenting detached judgment.
evidence: as the street-child clutched

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker reject the image of someone who calls ripe pears bitter?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker denies that this is simple resentment or incapacity for pleasure; later descriptions insist that beauty is excessively intense.
evidence: Do not dream that I speak

questions.prompt: What does the imagined bare landscape offer that the garden cannot?
facilitatorNotes: Stillness and contrast relieve relentless sensation; the requested gift may be understanding rather than another beautiful object.
evidence: stones, stones, bare rocks

days.title: Origin of Species: Why differences might widen (excerpt)
days.challenge: Compare a breeder analogy, a hypothetical animal, an experiment, and a small-area observation.
days.focus: Divergence as an explanation linking variety, competition, and occupation of different places.
days.context: Darwin asks why small differences among varieties might become larger differences among species. He moves between domestic selection and relationships in nature.
days.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and anatomical terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “Divergence of Character,” opening five paragraphs; complete source paragraphs 212–216 in the saved paragraph index; opens “_Divergence of Character_.—The principle, which I have designated by this term, is of high”; closes “ch other most closely, shall, as a general rule, belong to what we call different genera and orders.”.

questions.prompt: How do the horse and pigeon examples explain the disappearance of intermediate forms under human selection?
facilitatorNotes: Different breeders repeatedly prefer different extremes; animals that satisfy neither preference are neglected. The account provides an analogy of divergence, not an assertion that nature has identical human preferences.
evidence: fanciers do not and will not admire a medium standard, but like extremes

questions.prompt: Why does the hypothetical carnivore need new habits or places if the country already supports its full average number?
facilitatorNotes: Additional descendants must use opportunities not already filled in the same way, such as different prey, water, or trees. Connect this condition to the proposed advantage of diversified descendants.
evidence: only by its varying descendants seizing on places at present occupied by other animals

questions.prompt: What do the mixed-grass plot and tiny turf observation each contribute, and what is not directly observed?
facilitatorNotes: The experiment compares production in mixed and single plantings; the turf shows diversity in a small place. Neither directly observes the entire many-generation formation of species, so the final connection remains an inference.
evidence: supported twenty species of plants, and these belonged to eighteen genera and to eight orders

days.title: Conversations, a schoolbook and arguments for liberty — excerpt
days.challenge: Separate the narrator’s lived conversations from the dialogue he summarises inside the memoir.
days.focus: The possibilities and limits of persuasion under unequal power.
days.context: Douglass can now read and talks with white playmates about their different futures. He describes a purchased schoolbook whose dialogue offers a model of argument.
days.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement, family separation and racist beliefs. Its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XI, A Change Came O’er the Spirit of My Dream, conversations with boys and the Columbian Orator dialogue; UNC 1855 printing, pp. 155–158; selected paragraphs corresponding to original PG indexes 229–230. Opening “Although slavery was a delicate subject, and very cautiously talked about among grown up p”; closing “made by the slave to the master, in this instance, would find their counterpart in myself.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the comparison with the boys’ freedom at twenty-one sharpen Douglass’s question about rights?
facilitatorNotes: The boys expect an end to dependency, while his legal condition is lifelong. Their similarity as children exposes the arbitrary difference in their futures.
evidence: but I am a slave for life. Have I not as good a right to be free as you have

questions.prompt: Why does increased knowledge make his condition more painful even as the book becomes a treasure?
facilitatorNotes: Learning expands his sense of possible freedom and the arguments supporting it, but does not itself end enslavement. The emotional burden and intellectual resource develop together.
evidence: every increase of knowledge, especially respecting the FREE STATES, added something to the almost intolerable burden

questions.prompt: How does the schoolbook’s dialogue both inspire him and differ from his actual situation?
facilitatorNotes: The fictional master permits debate and accepts defeat by emancipating the speaker. Douglass imagines using such answers himself, but the passage has already shown that real power can prevent an effective response.
evidence: the well-directed answers made by the slave to the master

days.title: Sheltered Garden
days.challenge: Interpret violent imperatives without reducing their figurative possibilities to one moral.
days.focus: Protection, strength, and the cost of cultivated beauty.
days.context: The speaker rejects a carefully protected garden. Test whether the wish for damage is literal gardening advice, an aesthetic argument, or a metaphorical demand.

excerpt.locator: Sheltered Garden; begins “I have had enough. I gasp for breath.”; ends “find a new beauty in some terrible wind-tortured place.”.

questions.prompt: How do covered pears and melons turn protection into confinement?
facilitatorNotes: Wadding and straw exclude the light and exposure that the speaker values; “smothered” changes care into suffocation.
evidence: smothered in straw

questions.prompt: Why prefer fruit marked by frost?
facilitatorNotes: Tartness and a russet coat signify having endured conditions on its own terms. The preference challenges smoothness as the measure of worth.
evidence: test their own worth

questions.prompt: What tension remains in the wish for broken trees?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker seeks strength through exposure but imagines real destruction; the final beauty is “terrible,” so the poem does not make this a painless remedy.
evidence: showing the fight was valiant

days.title: Origin of Species: The branching tree (excerpt)
days.challenge: Translate conditional reasoning and nested classification into the parts of an extended metaphor.
days.focus: A summary argument embodied in the tree of life.
days.context: Darwin closes the natural-selection chapter. A previously discussed diagram is mentioned but is not needed here: the final paragraph supplies a self-contained verbal tree model.
days.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and anatomical terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “Summary of the Chapter” through the closing tree simile; complete source paragraphs 237–240 in the saved paragraph index; opens “_Summary of the Chapter_.—If during the long course of ages and under varying conditions o”; closes “ the crust of the earth, and covers the surface with its ever branching and beautiful ramifications.”.

questions.prompt: How does the opening paragraph’s sequence of if-clauses connect assumptions with the principle of preservation?
facilitatorNotes: It assembles variation, excess reproduction, and complex relations before drawing a survival-and-inheritance conclusion. Name the premises and the conclusion instead of reading the paragraph as one undifferentiated assertion.
evidence: But if variations useful to any organic being do occur

questions.prompt: Why does Darwin reject a single-file arrangement of living groups?
facilitatorNotes: Nested affinities involve different branches and levels of relation rather than one linear ranking. The clustering description prepares the tree’s ability to show shared origins and diverging descendants.
evidence: cannot be ranked in a single file

questions.prompt: What do green twigs, old branches, and broken branches each represent, and how does the tree include both survival and loss?
facilitatorNotes: Living tips represent existing species; earlier branching joins descendants to past forms; dead limbs represent extinct groups. The metaphor explains relationships while making extinction integral to the visible pattern.
evidence: fills with its dead and broken branches the crust of the earth

days.title: Learning to write from the shipyard — excerpt
days.challenge: Connect a practical motive for literacy to an account of self-designed learning.
days.focus: Risk, ingenuity and the conversion of available objects into educational tools.
days.context: Douglass encounters men who advise escape and then explains how he acquired writing skills from work, play and borrowed materials.
days.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement, family separation and racist beliefs. Its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Includes fear of kidnapping and threatened punishment, without graphic description.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XII, Religious Nature Awakened, the Irish workers through the writing practice; UNC 1855 printing, pp. 169–172; selected paragraphs corresponding to original PG indexes 241–243. Opening “I went, one day, on the wharf of Mr. Waters; and seeing two Irishmen unloading a large sco”; closing “ver executed his threat to whip me, for having thus, innocently, employed my leisure time.”.

questions.prompt: Why does he hide his interest in the Irishmen’s advice while still remembering it?
facilitatorNotes: He believes they may be sincere but knows that apparent helpers can profit from betrayal. His guarded response distinguishes the value of advice from certainty about a speaker’s motives.
evidence: I, however, pretended not to be interested in what they said, for I feared they might be treacherous

questions.prompt: How do the markings on ship timbers become a writing lesson?
facilitatorNotes: He connects letters to the purposes and positions of pieces, then copies the forms. The workplace supplies an accessible system of signs when ordinary instruction is denied.
evidence: I soon learned these letters, and for what they were placed on the timbers

questions.prompt: What does the catalogue of fences, pavements, chalk and copybooks show about agency under constraint?
facilitatorNotes: He reorganises the materials and encounters available to him into instruction, including playful competition and secret copying. This ingenuity does not remove the risks that make the learning necessary.
evidence: With playmates for my teachers, fences and pavements for my copy books, and chalk for my pen and ink

days.title: Garden
days.challenge: Follow impossible physical descriptions as representations of blocked motion.
days.focus: Conditional power, hard flowers, and an appeal to wind.
days.context: Two numbered sections turn a rose and summer heat into resistant physical materials. Read the conditional sentences and the commands with different emphasis.

excerpt.locator: Garden; begins “I”; ends “it, turning it on either side of your path.”.

questions.prompt: How does the rock comparison change a conventional image of the rose?
facilitatorNotes: A delicate flower becomes hard and resistant; scraping color replaces admiring soft petals and prepares the desire to break it.
evidence: O rose, cut in rock

questions.prompt: Why does “If I could stir” revise the previous claim about breaking a tree?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker’s imagined force depends on the very movement that is unavailable, exposing a gap between potential and action.
evidence: If I could stir

questions.prompt: What does ploughing the heat achieve that merely cooling the air would not?
facilitatorNotes: Heat becomes an obstructing substance that can be divided and displaced. The verb gives the wind an active path and a bodily force.
evidence: plough through it

days.title: Origin of Species: The difficult example of the eye (excerpt)
days.challenge: Read a concession in the context of the conditional argument that follows it, rather than isolating a striking sentence.
days.focus: Reason, imagination, analogy, and the evidence for possible intermediate structures.
days.context: Darwin confronts the complexity of the eye as a difficulty for his theory. The selection presents his admission, reasoning, evidence limitations, and revised telescope analogy.
days.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and anatomical terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, “Organs of extreme perfection and complication,” opening five paragraphs; complete source paragraphs 325–329 in the saved paragraph index; opens “_Organs of extreme perfection and complication_.—To suppose that the eye, with all its ini”; closes “t might thus be formed as superior to one of glass, as the works of the Creator are to those of man?”.

questions.prompt: Why would quoting only Darwin’s claim that the idea seems absurd misrepresent this passage?
facilitatorNotes: The admission introduces a conditional explanation based on useful gradations, inherited variation, and changing conditions. A fair reading follows the “Yet” into that argument rather than treating the concession as his final position.
evidence: Yet reason tells me, that if numerous gradations

questions.prompt: What difference does Darwin make between studying lineal ancestors and studying related living species?
facilitatorNotes: Ancestors would directly show a historical sequence but are usually inaccessible. Related species can show possible grades of structure; possibility is not the same as having observed the exact ancestry.
evidence: in order to see what gradations are possible

questions.prompt: How does he revise the telescope comparison to avoid simply assuming a human-style designer?
facilitatorNotes: He imagines slight tissue changes, multiplication, preservation, and replacement across immense time instead of a single act of human planning. Readers may debate the persuasiveness while accurately identifying the revised process.
evidence: In living bodies, variation will cause the slight alterations, generation will multiply them almost infinitely

days.title: Freedom and insecurity in New York — excerpt
days.challenge: Follow rapid tonal changes without assuming that legal geography guarantees practical safety.
days.focus: The limits of language for joy and the continuing dangers facing fugitives.
days.context: Douglass has escaped and arrived in New York. He tells readers the outcome without supplying operational details of the escape, then describes the first experience of a free state.
days.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement, family separation and racist beliefs. Its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Discusses recapture, loneliness and fear without depicting physical injury.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXII, Liberty Attained, opening five narrative paragraphs; UNC 1855 printing, pp. 335–339; selected paragraphs corresponding to original PG indexes 504–508. Opening “THERE is no necessity for any extended notice of the incidents of this part of my life. Th”; closing “money, and without any definite knowledge of which way to go, or where to look for succor.”.

questions.prompt: How does the balloon image shape the transition between the enslaved and free portions of the story?
facilitatorNotes: It conveys peril and uncertainty while allowing the narrator to announce where he landed rather than narrating the route. Its playful form also addresses a reader’s suspense.
evidence: knowing not where I should land--whether in slavery or in freedom

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator claim joy is hard to describe and then offer several images for it?
facilitatorNotes: The images try to approximate an experience declared beyond adequate language. Readers may see productive tension between the claim of ineffability and the vivid work of narration.
evidence: joy and gladness, like the rainbow of promise, defy alike the pen and pencil

questions.prompt: How does the encounter with William Dixon change the meaning of being surrounded by people?
facilitatorNotes: The crowd first appears as a dazzling new world, then as possible informants and kidnappers. Dixon’s own fear limits his help, leaving social proximity without reliable belonging.
evidence: In the midst of thousands of my fellow-men, and yet a perfect stranger

days.title: Orchard
days.challenge: Explain a paradoxical plea using its contrasting images.
days.focus: Beauty as assault and offering as an attempt to negotiate it.
days.context: The speaker makes an offering to an orchard god while asking to be spared the orchard’s beauty. The ritual is a literary scene, not evidence of one documented ancient ceremony.

excerpt.locator: Orchard; begins “I saw the first pear as it fell-- the”; ends “figs and quinces untouched, I bring you as offering.”.

questions.prompt: How are the speaker and the bees first alike and then divided?
facilitatorNotes: Both rush toward fruit, but the bees continue while the speaker collapses; the same abundance nourishes one and overwhelms the other.
evidence: I alone was prostrate

questions.prompt: Why appeal specifically to a rough-hewn, unbeautiful god?
facilitatorNotes: That figure offers a possible counterweight to the injurious loveliness of blossoms; the appeal depends on difference rather than more beauty.
evidence: do you, alone unbeautiful

questions.prompt: Do the rich offerings support or undermine the wish to escape beauty?
facilitatorNotes: They can show that the speaker remains drawn into sensuous abundance even while seeking relief. The poem leaves desire entangled with refusal.
evidence: pomegranates already broken

days.title: Origin of Species: What would a missing link connect? (excerpt)
days.challenge: Distinguish direct intermediates between living forms from branches leading back to a common ancestor.
days.focus: An acknowledged objection and a clarification of what evidence the theory predicts.
days.context: Darwin begins his geological-record discussion by admitting the force of missing transitional evidence and clarifying the kinds of intermediate forms his account requires.
days.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and anatomical terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IX, opening four body paragraphs; complete source paragraphs 468–471 in the saved paragraph index; opens “In the sixth chapter I enumerated the chief objections which might be justly urged against”; closes “ in all cases the new and improved forms of life will tend to supplant the old and unimproved forms.”.

questions.prompt: What makes the geological record a more serious objection than the absence of intermediates living today?
facilitatorNotes: Extinction can explain the present absence, but a long history should have contained many intermediates. Their scarcity in strata therefore raises a distinct evidence problem that Darwin explicitly calls grave.
evidence: the most obvious and gravest objection which can be urged against my theory

questions.prompt: Why need a form halfway between the fantail’s tail and the pouter’s crop not have existed?
facilitatorNotes: Each breed may connect separately to the rock-pigeon ancestor. A branch relationship does not require a direct blend of the two descendant extremes.
evidence: forms intermediate between each species and a common but unknown progenitor

questions.prompt: What extra condition would a direct horse-from-tapir history require in Darwin’s account?
facilitatorNotes: One form would remain largely unchanged while descendants altered greatly; he presents that as possible but rare under his competition argument. Avoid converting the illustrative possibility into an established ancestry claim.
evidence: one form had remained for a very long period unaltered

days.title: A new name and a different organisation of labour — excerpt
days.challenge: Examine how particular observations challenge a general economic assumption.
days.focus: Naming, free labour and the revision of inherited ideas.
days.context: With assistance, Douglass has reached New Bedford and found shelter with Nathan Johnson. He now compares what he sees with assumptions formed while enslaved.
days.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement, family separation and racist beliefs. Its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. Includes historical racial and class insults as the narrator recounts assumptions he revises.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXII, Liberty Attained, naming in New Bedford through civic possibilities; UNC 1855 printing, pp. 342–347; selected paragraphs corresponding to original PG indexes 514–517. Opening “Once initiated into the new life of freedom, and assured by Mr. Johnson that New Bedford w”; closing “olored people themselves were of the best metal, and would fight for liberty to the death.”.

questions.prompt: Why are the changes of name not presented as evidence of dishonesty in Douglass himself?
facilitatorNotes: Different names protect him from people who would return him to bondage. He locates the dishonesty in a social order that makes honest identification unsafe for fugitives.
evidence: but toward fugitives, Americans are not honest

questions.prompt: How does Nathan Johnson’s household challenge the belief that slavery is necessary for wealth?
facilitatorNotes: Johnson is a Black working man with books, knowledge and domestic comfort exceeding many slaveholders. His example directly contradicts the narrator’s earlier model of prosperity.
evidence: Regarding slavery as the basis of wealth, I fancied that no people could become very wealthy without slavery

questions.prompt: Why does the unloading of oil matter to an argument larger than the efficiency of one dock?
facilitatorNotes: A small group using an ox and equipment shows how skill and organisation replace forced expenditure of human strength. The example supports his emerging contrast between systems of labour, while remaining an observation rather than a complete economic study.
evidence: Main strength, unassisted by skill, is slavery's method of labor

days.title: Sea Gods
days.challenge: Track changes of pronoun, tense, and confidence across a lyric argument.
days.focus: Collective faith answered in the imagined movement of water.
days.context: Three sections move from reported hopelessness through an offering to a prediction of return. Distinguish a community’s conviction from an event the poem actually narrates.

excerpt.locator: Sea Gods; begins “I”; ends “lie of men's thoughts, and cherish and shelter us.”.

questions.prompt: Who claims that there is no hope, and why does that attribution matter?
facilitatorNotes: The repeated “They say” distances the speaker from a pessimistic report; it is not an uncontested statement of fact.
evidence: They say there is no hope

questions.prompt: Why spend an entire section naming kinds of violets?
facilitatorNotes: The abundance and specificity of the offering actively counter the opening wreckage; a fragile flower becomes a collective resource.
evidence: violets tugged from rocks

questions.prompt: Does the final section show the gods returning?
facilitatorNotes: It predicts “you will” repeatedly. The imagined waves give conviction sensory force, but the grammar preserves future expectation.
evidence: you will answer our taut hearts

days.title: Origin of Species: From an imperfect record to an entangled bank (excerpt)
days.challenge: Evaluate a conclusion that combines evidentiary caution, future prediction, theological language, and lyrical synthesis.
days.focus: How scientific exposition ends with a vision of connected life.
days.context: These are the closing paragraphs of the 1859 first edition. They move from the incompleteness of geological evidence toward future research and the famous entangled-bank image.
days.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and anatomical terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XIV, final four paragraphs; complete source paragraphs 762–765 in the saved paragraph index; opens “The noble science of Geology loses glory from the extreme imperfection of the record. The ”; closes “imple a beginning endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved.”.

questions.prompt: How does the contrast between a well-filled museum and a poor collection change what readers should expect from fossils?
facilitatorNotes: It presents the record as selectively and irregularly preserved rather than complete. Darwin then cautions against overrating organic change as a clock, preserving a limit within his broader confidence.
evidence: not be looked at as a well-filled museum, but as a poor collection made at hazard and at rare intervals.

questions.prompt: Where does the passage move beyond describing past evidence into predicting future developments or progress?
facilitatorNotes: The psychology sentence and claims about future descendants and perfection project beyond current observations. A strong discussion identifies this shift and separates the persuasive vision from directly supplied proof.
evidence: all corporeal and mental endowments will tend to progress towards perfection.

questions.prompt: How does the final bank scene gather the argument’s beauty and violence into one image?
facilitatorNotes: Plants, birds, insects, and worms provide a visible community, while struggle, extinction, famine, and death enter its explanation. The grandeur comes through a claimed relationship between these forces, not by excluding loss from the scene.
evidence: Thus, from the war of nature, from famine and death

days.title: An unexpected public voice — excerpt
days.challenge: Distinguish the remembered sensations of a speech from its later historical significance.
days.focus: Public testimony, persuasion and retrospective qualification of youthful confidence.
days.context: In 1841 Douglass attends an antislavery convention seeking a brief rest from work. An invitation to speak begins a new public role.
days.contentNote: This historical autobiography describes enslavement, family separation and racist beliefs. Its historical terminology and reported prejudices belong to the source, not to the site’s voice. A quoted introduction alludes to the bodily marks of enslavement without graphic description.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXIII, Introduced to the Abolitionists, opening four narrative paragraphs; UNC 1855 printing, pp. 357–360; selected paragraphs corresponding to original PG indexes 532–535. Opening “IN the summer of 1841, a grand anti-slavery convention was held in Nantucket, under the au”; closing “ers were not yet passed; and that the life now before me, had shadows as well as sunbeams.”.

questions.prompt: Why is the narrator’s inability to remember his words significant rather than merely a missing detail?
facilitatorNotes: He remembers bodily fear and the audience’s response more clearly than sentences. This emphasises the transition into public speaking and leaves room for the possibility that visible vulnerability carried persuasive force.
evidence: I am not sure that my embarrassment was not the most effective part of my speech

questions.prompt: What does the account of a meeting becoming a single individuality suggest about Garrison’s rhetoric?
facilitatorNotes: The metaphor presents an audience temporarily united in feeling and purpose by an orator. Students may discuss both its admiration for collective mobilisation and its striking language of control.
evidence: a public meeting is transformed, as it were, into a single individuality

questions.prompt: How does the ending revise the belief that a just cause must quickly triumph?
facilitatorNotes: Douglass contrasts his early certainty with later knowledge of continued danger and hardship. The cause’s moral strength is not denied, but neither is it treated as a guarantee of easy progress.
evidence: the life now before me, had shadows as well as sunbeams

days.title: Acon
days.challenge: Use context for unfamiliar names while grounding interpretation in the poem’s actions.
days.focus: A petition that asks divine reciprocity for a suffering person.
days.context: A speaker seeks healing for Hyella through herbs, offerings, and appeals to nature spirits. Dictaeus and Erymanthus locate the poem in an imagined ancient Greek landscape; dryads and nereids are woodland and water nymphs.
days.contentNote: Depicts serious illness and a plea for relief; ancient ritual imagery is part of the poem, not health guidance.

excerpt.locator: Acon; begins “I”; ends “iris, and a branch of shrub, and frail-headed poppies.”.

questions.prompt: What does the list of herbs establish before the gods are directly petitioned?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker searches and chooses material remedies, so care takes practical form as well as prayer.
evidence: all-healing herbs

questions.prompt: Why remind the spirits of Hyella’s earlier offerings?
facilitatorNotes: The appeal makes past devotion a reason for reciprocal aid; it challenges the opening claim that no god pities her.
evidence: which she once brought to your altars

questions.prompt: How does the hyacinth comparison represent more than mere paleness?
facilitatorNotes: A hidden flower dying on burnt grass combines fading vitality, isolation, and an inhospitable setting; it makes urgent care necessary.
evidence: perishes upon burnt grass

days.title: The American Scholar: A person larger than a profession (excerpt)
days.challenge: Follow the changing body metaphor from useful division of labor to damaging fragmentation.
days.focus: Intellectual independence and the difference between a whole person and a social function.
days.context: Emerson opens an address to a literary gathering by asking what an American scholar should become. He turns from national aspirations to an account of divided human work.
days.contentNote: This 1907 transcription retains nineteenth-century gendered language and bracketed reference numbers. The source’s editorial endnotes are not included; the questions depend on the supplied essay text.

excerpt.locator: The American Scholar, opening seven prose paragraphs; complete source paragraphs 80–86 in the saved paragraph index; opens “I greet you on the recommencement of our literary year. Our anniversary is one of hope, an”; closes “ege. Let us see him in his school, and consider him in reference to the main influences he receives.”.

questions.prompt: How does the image of foreign harvests characterize intellectual dependence?
facilitatorNotes: It makes inherited learning resemble food that has dried out rather than fresh nourishment. Readers can distinguish his call for new expression from a simple claim that every foreign work is worthless.
evidence: the sere remains of foreign harvests.

questions.prompt: At what point does the division into fingers stop being a beneficial image and become a damaging one?
facilitatorNotes: The initial hand gains usefulness through distinct fingers, but the later amputated parts lose relation to the whole. The transition criticizes specialization without larger human awareness, not necessarily all cooperative labor.
evidence: a good finger, a neck, a stomach, an elbow, but never a man.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes Man Thinking from a parrot of other people’s thought?
facilitatorNotes: The first exercises a whole, active mind in relation to life; the second repeats inherited ideas as a narrow function. Link that contrast to the farmer who sees only a bushel and cart.
evidence: the parrot of other men's thinking.

days.title: The veil and double-consciousness — excerpt
days.challenge: Follow an abstract concept as it emerges from a particular scene and expands across several occupations.
days.focus: The strain of identity measured through a hostile social gaze.
days.context: Du Bois opens his inquiry into Black American life by moving from everyday encounters and a childhood memory to the concepts of the veil and double-consciousness.
days.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement. Historical racial terminology, generalisations and the author’s reported viewpoints are retained for critical reading, not adopted as the site’s voice.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, Of Our Spiritual Strivings, opening five prose paragraphs; UNC transcription of second edition, June1,1903, pp. 1–5; selected paragraphs corresponding to original PG indexes 25–29. Opening “BETWEEN me and the other world there is ever an unasked question: unasked by some through ”; closing “means of salvation, and at times has even seemed about to make them ashamed of themselves.”.

questions.prompt: How do the opening speakers avoid asking the question Du Bois says they really mean?
facilitatorNotes: They offer acquaintances, military service or indignation instead of directly acknowledging his experience. Their apparent sympathy can still cast him as a social problem rather than an individual.
evidence: How does it feel to be a problem

questions.prompt: Why does the rejected visiting-card become an important event despite its small material value?
facilitatorNotes: The exchange abruptly makes an exclusion visible within an otherwise shared childhood. The veil names the separation he discovers, not an innate difference the card creates.
evidence: refused my card,--refused it peremptorily, with a glance

questions.prompt: Does merging the double self require abandoning either Black identity or American belonging in this passage?
facilitatorNotes: No. He explicitly rejects losing either older self and seeks the freedom to inhabit both without exclusion. The occupational examples show the costs of demands that remain unreconciled.
evidence: In this merging he wishes neither of the older selves to be lost

days.title: Night
days.challenge: Infer an emotional effect from repetitive syntax and personification.
days.focus: Time as methodical separation rather than restful shelter.
days.context: Night acts upon a rose as if it possessed hands. Listen for the repeated directions and the pace of the unfolding action.

excerpt.locator: Night; begins “The night has cut each from each and curled”; ends “core of the rose to perish on the branch.”.

questions.prompt: What does repeating “under” and “back” make the reader experience?
facilitatorNotes: The directional pattern enacts steady stripping or folding, less a single dramatic blow than persistent action.
evidence: under at an unfaltering pace

questions.prompt: How do “unfaltering” and “grave” qualify the violence?
facilitatorNotes: They make it measured and inexorable, possibly solemn, rather than frantic. A reading of grief should account for this controlled tempo.
evidence: under at a grave pace

questions.prompt: Why leave the core on the branch instead of ending when petals fall?
facilitatorNotes: The remaining center prolongs exposure and loss; personified night both removes parts and abandons what survives.
evidence: leave the stark core

days.title: The American Scholar: Nature and the unifying mind (excerpt)
days.challenge: Reread the movement from scientific classification to a spiritual claim and distinguish analogy from demonstrated identity.
days.focus: The mind’s search for order and its proposed kinship with nature.
days.context: This complete section within the larger address identifies nature as the scholar’s first influence. Its compressed metaphors invite slow reading rather than memorization of a single doctrine.
days.contentNote: This 1907 transcription retains nineteenth-century gendered language and bracketed reference numbers. The source’s editorial endnotes are not included; the questions depend on the supplied essay text.

excerpt.locator: The American Scholar, section I on nature, complete two-paragraph section; complete source paragraphs 88–89 in the saved paragraph index; opens “I. The first in time and the first in importance of the influences upon the mind is that o”; closes “cient precept, "Know thyself," and the modern precept, "Study nature," become at last one maxim.”.

questions.prompt: What changes as the young mind moves from one object to two, three, and three thousand?
facilitatorNotes: It finds shared relations instead of isolated things and develops classification. The escalating numbers enact the expanding impulse to connect, which Emerson calls both an instinct and a kind of tyranny.
evidence: tyrannized over by its own unifying instinct

questions.prompt: How do geometry and chemistry support the claim that nature is intelligible to the mind?
facilitatorNotes: They provide examples of order expressed through mental forms and proportions. Discuss whether they demonstrate full spiritual unity or serve as analogies preparing that larger philosophical step.
evidence: geometry, a pure abstraction of the human mind, is the measure of planetary motion.

questions.prompt: What does the seal-and-print image add to the closing merger of Know thyself and Study nature?
facilitatorNotes: It pictures corresponding forms as impressions of a shared order. Readers may interpret this as a claim of deep kinship rather than literal sameness, but should explain how the image supports the merged maxim.
evidence: One is seal and one is print.

days.title: Work, culture and liberty together — excerpt
days.challenge: Trace the movement from a difficult educational journey to a synthesis of several public goals.
days.focus: How material deprivation and social prejudice shape the meaning of progress.
days.context: After surveying successive hopes for freedom, political power and education, Du Bois considers why each isolated solution has proved incomplete.
days.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement. Historical racial terminology, generalisations and the author’s reported viewpoints are retained for critical reading, not adopted as the site’s voice. Includes references to sexual exploitation under slavery and racial violence, without graphic description.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, Of Our Spiritual Strivings, educational striving through the chapter’s end; UNC transcription of second edition, June1,1903, pp. 8–12; selected paragraphs corresponding to original PG indexes 36–41. Opening “Up the new path the advance guard toiled, slowly, heavily, doggedly; only those who have w”; closing “mphasis and deeper detail, that men may listen to the striving in the souls of black folk.”.

questions.prompt: What can the cold statistician record, and what does the climbing metaphor add to that record?
facilitatorNotes: Statistics register increments and setbacks; the metaphor represents fatigue, limited visibility and perseverance. The passage asks readers to consider lived effort alongside measured outcomes.
evidence: The cold statistician wrote down the inches of progress

questions.prompt: Why does Du Bois reject the choice between work, education and freedom rather than reject those goals themselves?
facilitatorNotes: He argues that each goal pursued alone is incomplete and depends on the others. Economic activity needs protection, education needs opportunity, and freedom must include the capacity to work and think.
evidence: not singly but together, not successively but together

questions.prompt: How does the closing description of the republic turn a supposedly separate problem into a national test?
facilitatorNotes: The treatment of Black citizens becomes evidence of whether the republic’s principles actually apply. The claim asks readers to evaluate national ideals through their concrete operation.
evidence: a concrete test of the underlying principles of the great republic

days.title: Prisoners
days.challenge: Reconstruct a relationship and immediate danger from an incomplete letter.
days.focus: Silence as protection and a last glimpse as a source of strength.
days.context: A condemned prisoner sends hurried instructions to a beloved in another cell. No historical prison is named: interpret this as a dramatic lyric situation.
days.contentNote: A prisoner anticipates execution; includes confinement and remembered violence without graphic detail.

excerpt.locator: Prisoners; begins “It is strange that I should want this sight”; ends “you tried to shield me as the horsemen passed.”.

questions.prompt: Why must the beloved reach the gate but not speak?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker seeks recognition while fearing attention that might endanger the other prisoner; intimacy requires restraint.
evidence: you may yet be released

questions.prompt: How do gold and the spearsman establish the cost of this letter?
facilitatorNotes: The messenger expects payment and the writer has given everything; the request depends on precarious exchange, not free communication.
evidence: I gave all I had left.

questions.prompt: Why desire the unkempt face when beautiful memories already exist?
facilitatorNotes: The actual reciprocal glance may confirm presence more powerfully than remembered banquets or dreams. The repeated question makes this need urgent, not fully explained.
evidence: your eyes and my eyes may meet.

days.title: The American Scholar: Books that inspire and books that govern (excerpt)
days.challenge: Track a reversal from praise of books to criticism of their authority without reducing the argument to an anti-reading slogan.
days.focus: Creative reading versus submission to inherited genius.
days.context: Emerson turns from nature to the influence of the past, chiefly through books. The excerpt develops both the nobility of writing and the risk of turning a record into unquestioned authority.
days.contentNote: This 1907 transcription retains nineteenth-century gendered language and bracketed reference numbers. The source’s editorial endnotes are not included; the questions depend on the supplied essay text.

excerpt.locator: The American Scholar, section II, first seven paragraphs; complete source paragraphs 91–97 in the saved paragraph index; opens “II. The next great influence into the spirit of the scholar is the mind of the Past,--in w”; closes “ation bear me witness. The English dramatic poets have Shakespearized now for two hundred years.”.

questions.prompt: What does the repeated “It came” and “It went” pattern suggest about a writer’s work?
facilitatorNotes: The paired clauses transform lived events into truth, poetry, and lasting thought. The rhythm presents authorship as active remaking, not passive storage of facts.
evidence: It came to him business; it went from him poetry.

questions.prompt: How does a guide become a tyrant in the passage?
facilitatorNotes: Reverence for the writer’s creative act transfers to an assumption that the book is perfect. Subsequent readers accept the record instead of seeing principles themselves, replacing kinship with domination.
evidence: The guide is a tyrant. We sought a brother, and lo, a governor.

questions.prompt: What difference does the satellite image establish between influence and inspiration?
facilitatorNotes: Inspiration energizes an active soul’s own creation; becoming a satellite makes one orbit someone else’s mind. A defensible response can discuss how difficult that boundary is while keeping Emerson’s distinction clear.
evidence: made a satellite instead of a system.

days.title: From wartime emergency to a national obligation — excerpt
days.challenge: Separate changing policy, immediate humanitarian needs and the emergence of a larger administrative problem.
days.focus: How practical events force a denied question into public policy.
days.context: Du Bois begins a historical account of the Freedmen’s Bureau by tracing the responses to people escaping slavery during the Civil War. Dates, figures and characterisations are his historical account, available for critical evaluation.
days.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement. Historical racial terminology, generalisations and the author’s reported viewpoints are retained for critical reading, not adopted as the site’s voice. Describes wartime displacement, hunger and historical dehumanising labels; no graphic injury.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, Of the Dawn of Freedom, opening seven prose paragraphs; UNC transcription of second edition, June1,1903, pp. 13–18; selected paragraphs corresponding to original PG indexes 46–52. Opening “THE problem of the twentieth century is the problem of the color-line,--the relation of th”; closing “fter that terribly picturesque march to the sea, thousands of the wretched camp followers.”.

questions.prompt: How do the arrival of fugitives and the differing military orders challenge the claim that the war has nothing to do with slavery?
facilitatorNotes: The armies must decide whether to return, employ or recognise people as free. These decisions make slavery unavoidable in practice despite declarations that the war concerns other matters.
evidence: The war has naught to do with slaves

questions.prompt: What does the change from a stream to a flood convey, and what information does the metaphor leave unspecified?
facilitatorNotes: It stresses increasing numbers and pressure on existing arrangements. It does not by itself provide a count or explain each person’s circumstances; those limits matter when imagery supports historical argument.
evidence: The stream of fugitives swelled to a flood

questions.prompt: Why does the passage move from relief supplies to wages, contracts, land and schools?
facilitatorNotes: Food and shelter answer emergencies but cannot establish durable freedom and livelihoods. The expanding list shows why the response becomes a national institutional task.
evidence: this was no ordinary matter of temporary relief, but a national crisis

days.title: Storm
days.challenge: Connect repeated consonants with a sharply changing physical image.
days.focus: A moving leaf transformed into a weighted object.
days.context: This compact poem addresses a storm directly. Reread it for sound, then trace the leaf’s trajectory rather than treating the scene as a general description of bad weather.

excerpt.locator: Storm; begins “You crash over the trees, you crack the live”; ends “hurled out, whirls up and sinks, a green stone.”.

questions.prompt: What does “crash” beside “crack” contribute beyond naming damage?
facilitatorNotes: The repeated hard consonants make impacts audible, while one verb describes broad collision and the other a local break.
evidence: You crash over the trees

questions.prompt: How does the leaf’s path resist a simple downward fall?
facilitatorNotes: It is first hurled and whirls upward before sinking; the sequence gives the storm unstable directional force.
evidence: whirls up and sinks

questions.prompt: Why end by calling the leaf “a green stone”?
facilitatorNotes: Weight and hardness replace expected lightness. The impossible identity compresses the soaked leaf’s changed movement into a final image.
evidence: a green stone.

days.title: The American Scholar: Experience becomes language (excerpt)
days.challenge: Connect multiple transformation metaphors and evaluate the delay between living an event and understanding it.
days.focus: Action as the raw material of thought and speech.
days.context: The address’s third influence is action. Emerson challenges the idea that a scholar should remain detached from work, difficulty, and ordinary experience.
days.contentNote: This 1907 transcription retains nineteenth-century gendered language and bracketed reference numbers. The source’s editorial endnotes are not included; the questions depend on the supplied essay text. The opening uses femininity as a stereotype of weakness; that prejudice is available for critical discussion, not endorsement.

excerpt.locator: The American Scholar, section III, first six paragraphs; complete source paragraphs 103–108 in the saved paragraph index; opens “III. There goes in the world a notion that the scholar should be a recluse, a valetudinari”; closes “ to learn grammar. Colleges and books only copy the language which the field and the work-yard made.”.

questions.prompt: How does the opening answer the practical person who treats speculation as useless?
facilitatorNotes: Emerson refuses the separation: action is necessary for thought to ripen, while lived experience gives words force. The passage criticizes a diminished scholarly life rather than abandoning reflection.
evidence: Without it thought can never ripen into truth.

questions.prompt: Why can a recent event be harder to contemplate than childhood experience?
facilitatorNotes: The recent deed is still embedded in feeling and practical activity; later it can detach and become an object of thought. The ripe-fruit and winged-grub images emphasize a process that cannot be forced ahead of time.
evidence: The new deed is yet a part of life

questions.prompt: What does “Life is our dictionary” imply about the relation between work and formal education?
facilitatorNotes: Life supplies the concrete language and perceptions that institutions later record. Use the field and work-yard ending to discuss the claim’s force, while allowing a reader to question whether all learning must be firsthand.
evidence: Colleges and books only copy the language which the field and the work-yard made.

days.title: A vast commission with limited resources — excerpt
days.challenge: Compare a declared mission with the resources and personnel available to carry it out.
days.focus: Institutional design, implementation and qualified judgments of success.
days.context: The Freedmen’s Bureau has been established. Du Bois examines its responsibilities, the appointment of Oliver Howard and obstacles to turning a legal mandate into effective work.
days.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement. Historical racial terminology, generalisations and the author’s reported viewpoints are retained for critical reading, not adopted as the site’s voice. References to war, suffering and dispossession are non-graphic.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, Of the Dawn of Freedom, the new Bureau and Howard’s first year; UNC transcription of second edition, June1,1903, pp. 21–25; selected paragraphs corresponding to original PG indexes 58–62. Opening “Thus did the United States government definitely assume charge of the emancipated Negro as”; closing “ did their work well. In that first year they taught one hundred thousand souls, and more.”.

questions.prompt: How does the opening description distinguish the size of the mission from the means supplied for it?
facilitatorNotes: Millions of lives and a hostile postwar setting create enormous responsibilities, while powers are indefinite and funding absent or limited. The contrast prepares a judgment that cannot rest only on the ambition of the mandate.
evidence: vast responsibilities, indefinite powers, and limited resources

questions.prompt: Why do the two difficulties involving land and personnel alter the theory as well as the execution of the Bureau’s work?
facilitatorNotes: Restored land undermines the plan for ownership, while ill-suited or scarce agents undermine fair local administration. These obstacles weaken the mechanisms through which freedom was supposed to become sustainable.
evidence: two grave difficulties appeared which changed largely the theory and outcome of Bureau work

questions.prompt: What does the shift from field guns to the rhythm of the alphabet suggest about the teachers’ role?
facilitatorNotes: Education is represented as another campaign following military conflict, with different instruments and aims. Students may consider both the praise of courage and the religious or martial implications of the crusade metaphor.
evidence: after the hoarse mouthings of the field guns rang the rhythm of the alphabet

days.title: Hermes of the Ways
days.challenge: Relate mythic address to specific geography and changes of scale.
days.focus: A threshold between dangerous sea and imperfect refuge.
days.context: Hermes is associated with roads, travelers, and boundaries. Here a shore and a small orchard surround his waiting presence. Read the rough terrain without assuming shelter must be comfortable.

excerpt.locator: Hermes of the Ways; begins “The hard sand breaks, and the grains of it”; ends “but you have waited, were sea-grass tangles with shore-grass.”.

questions.prompt: What does facing three ways suggest about Hermes’s role?
facilitatorNotes: The figure attends a crossroads and welcomes travelers arriving from different directions; “dubious” leaves orientation unsettled.
evidence: facing three ways

questions.prompt: Why include small, late apples and twisted branches in a place of refuge?
facilitatorNotes: Shelter is battered and imperfect, but distinct from torn sails at sea. The contrast is relative safety rather than luxurious restoration.
evidence: twisted by many bafflings

questions.prompt: How does the ending locate divine help at a boundary?
facilitatorNotes: Hermes waits where two grasses meet; the poem places welcome between environments, after a sea figured as a hostile mouth.
evidence: sea-grass tangles with

days.title: Self-Reliance: The cost of surrendering judgment (excerpt)
days.challenge: Test how agricultural, musical, prison, and financial images develop one argument.
days.focus: Private judgment and the social pressures that make people distrust it.
days.context: Emerson begins with the experience of recognizing an original thought that one had previously dismissed.
days.contentNote: This 1907 transcription retains nineteenth-century gendered language and bracketed reference numbers. The source’s editorial endnotes are not included; the questions depend on the supplied essay text.

excerpt.locator: Self-Reliance, first six prose paragraphs; complete source paragraphs 191–196 in the saved paragraph index; opens “I read the other day some verses written by an eminent painter which were original and not”; closes “nformity. Self-reliance is its aversion. It loves not realities and creators, but names and customs.”.

questions.prompt: Why does a work of genius sometimes return our own thoughts with an alienated majesty?
facilitatorNotes: The reader rejected an intuition until another person expressed it with authority. Emerson makes this recognition evidence of misplaced dependence, while leaving room to ask whether every private intuition deserves trust.
evidence: our own rejected thoughts

questions.prompt: How does the boy’s freedom differ from the successful adult’s prison?
facilitatorNotes: The boy judges without protecting an established public role; the adult becomes bound by others’ expectations after a conspicuous success. The prison is consciousness of reputation rather than literal confinement.
evidence: clapped into jail by his consciousness.

questions.prompt: What exchange does the joint-stock company metaphor accuse society of making?
facilitatorNotes: Security and shared provision are purchased by surrendering liberty and self-development. Evaluate the bargain using the contrast between creators and accepted names, rather than assuming cooperation itself is impossible.
evidence: to surrender the liberty and culture of the eater.

days.title: Labour, land and schools: an institutional balance sheet — excerpt
days.challenge: Compare several kinds of evidence without assuming that money totals alone measure success.
days.focus: Different standards for relief, property, labour rights and education.
days.context: Du Bois turns from the Bureau’s difficult setting to a review of its practical work. The passage supplies his figures and evaluations rather than a present-day statistical report.
days.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement. Historical racial terminology, generalisations and the author’s reported viewpoints are retained for critical reading, not adopted as the site’s voice. Includes general references to racist violence against education, without graphic detail.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, Of the Dawn of Freedom, the seven fields of Bureau work through soldiers’ payments; UNC transcription of second edition, June1,1903, pp. 30–33; selected paragraphs corresponding to original PG indexes 69–73. Opening “Here, then, was the field of work for the Freedmen's Bureau; and since, with some hesitati”; closing “ put needed capital in the hands of practical paupers, and some, at least, was well spent.”.

questions.prompt: What difference does Du Bois draw between the rules for free labour and their local implementation?
facilitatorNotes: The central instructions protect choice and prohibit forced labour, but changing agents with unequal capacity produce uneven results. A sound rule and a successful implementation are distinct claims.
evidence: the outcome was necessarily varied

questions.prompt: How does the land discussion challenge an explanation of poverty based only on individual effort?
facilitatorNotes: The text describes a lost or withdrawn opportunity for landholding despite work and expectations. It also credits later ownership to thrift, distinguishing personal effort from institutional support.
evidence: it was by grace of his thrift rather than by bounty of the government

questions.prompt: Why does Du Bois partly concede that education is dangerous?
facilitatorNotes: He treats dissatisfaction with existing conditions as an enduring effect of learning, not a reason to withhold it. The concession turns the opponents’ fear into evidence of education’s transformative power.
evidence: education among all kinds of men always has had, and always will have, an element of danger and revolution

days.title: Pear Tree
days.challenge: Connect color, scale, and future possibility in a brief apostrophe.
days.focus: Blossom as both overwhelming present beauty and the promise of fruit.
days.context: The pear tree’s flowers appear first as a rising mass of silver. Track how the poem moves from what is visible now to fruit that has not arrived.

excerpt.locator: Pear Tree; begins “Silver dust lifted from the earth, higher than my”; ends “bring summer and ripe fruits in their purple hearts.”.

questions.prompt: Why repeat that the blossom reaches higher than the speaker’s arms?
facilitatorNotes: The tree exceeds bodily grasp, turning observation into a relation of scale and wonder.
evidence: higher than my arms reach

questions.prompt: What does “staunch” add to the white flower?
facilitatorNotes: It attributes firmness or steadfastness to a normally delicate object, joining beauty with strength.
evidence: so staunch a white leaf

questions.prompt: How can flower-tufts already “bring” ripe fruit?
facilitatorNotes: The present blossom holds the potential of a later season. The verb telescopes time without claiming the fruit is physically ripe now.
evidence: bring summer and ripe fruits

days.title: Self-Reliance: Integrity, performance, and exclusion (excerpt)
days.challenge: Separate a critique of performative goodness from the prejudices and ethical risks in its examples.
days.focus: The moral promise and limits of independence from public approval.
days.context: Emerson argues that goodness cannot be established by a label or a respectable performance. His examples also invite scrutiny of whose needs and judgments he dismisses.
days.contentNote: This 1907 transcription retains nineteenth-century gendered language and bracketed reference numbers. The source’s editorial endnotes are not included; the questions depend on the supplied essay text. Contains racialized language, contemptuous class descriptions, and a gender stereotype. Analyze these limitations alongside the argument about integrity.

excerpt.locator: Self-Reliance, nonconformity through the world’s displeasure; complete source paragraphs 197–201 in the saved paragraph index; opens “Whoso would be a man must be a nonconformist. He who would gather immortal palms must”; closes “w, it needs the habit of magnanimity and religion to treat it godlike as a trifle of no concernment.”.

questions.prompt: How does Emerson distinguish a life lived for itself from virtues performed as penances?
facilitatorNotes: Publicly legible good deeds can become compensation for a distrusted life rather than expressions of conviction. Readers should explain this criticism without assuming the passage proves that all organized charity is dishonest.
evidence: Their virtues are penances.

questions.prompt: Why does he compare a partisan preacher to a retained attorney pretending to be a judge?
facilitatorNotes: The preacher’s conclusion is fixed by affiliation before inquiry begins. The legal image exposes the mismatch between advocacy and the appearance of impartial judgment.
evidence: a retained attorney

questions.prompt: Where could independence become indifference to others in this argument?
facilitatorNotes: The refusal of obligations to the poor and contempt for classed or gendered opponents provide concrete grounds for critique. A response may defend personal integrity while rejecting the assumption that another person’s need or criticism is irrelevant.
evidence: Are they _my_ poor?

days.title: Public trust, institutional failure and the ballot — excerpt
days.challenge: Track distinctions between legal responsibility, practical association and broader political alternatives.
days.focus: How a qualified institutional judgment can lead to a claim about citizenship.
days.context: After considering conflicting courts and the Bureau’s errors, Du Bois argues against assigning every postwar failure to a single institution. He then discusses investigations, the Freedmen’s Bank and voting rights.
days.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement. Historical racial terminology, generalisations and the author’s reported viewpoints are retained for critical reading, not adopted as the site’s voice.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, Of the Dawn of Freedom, retrospective judgment through the argument for suffrage; UNC transcription of second edition, June1,1903, pp. 35–38; selected paragraphs corresponding to original PG indexes 75–80. Opening “All this is easy, but it is neither sensible nor just. Some one had blundered, but that wa”; closing “on the altar of national integrity; and some felt and feel only indifference and contempt.”.

questions.prompt: How does Du Bois assign causes to the Bureau’s successes and failures without making either list disappear?
facilitatorNotes: He names labour, philanthropy and Black striving as sources of achievement, while distinguishing local misconduct, difficult conditions and national neglect as causes of failure. The balance resists total vindication or total condemnation.
evidence: Its failures were the result of bad local agents, the inherent difficulties of the work, and national neglect

questions.prompt: Why does the bank’s collapse damage more than the amount of money lost?
