facilitatorNotes: The institution carried governmental prestige, so financial loss undermines belief in saving and trust in institutions and people. The author also distinguishes its practical association with the Bureau from a legal connection.
evidence: all the faith in saving went too, and much of the faith in men

questions.prompt: How does the passage turn opposition to guardianship into an argument for the ballot?
facilitatorNotes: If national protection is rejected, people require political power to protect their own interests. Du Bois identifies both justice and political calculation in this reasoning rather than attributing it to a single pure motive.
evidence: to make those wards their own guardians by arming them with the ballot

days.title: Cities
days.challenge: Evaluate a speculative origin story that repeatedly questions its own premises.
days.focus: Urban ugliness, inherited beauty, and a contested future.
days.context: The speaker imagines a maker who replaces magnificent ancient cities with crowded modern streets. The extended hive metaphor raises questions about who belongs and whose beauty counts.
days.contentNote: The speaker describes people through a hierarchical hive metaphor and invokes a “strong race”; evaluate this exclusionary language as part of the poem’s argument.

excerpt.locator: Cities; begins “Can we believe--by an effort comfort our hearts: it”; ends “the old splendour, await the new beauty of cities?”.

questions.prompt: Why does the poem repeatedly ask whether “we” can believe its story?
facilitatorNotes: The story consoles but is not established; recurring questions keep the explanation of ugly cities provisional.
evidence: Can we believe--by an effort

questions.prompt: How does the hive metaphor divide old and new inhabitants?
facilitatorNotes: The older voices become rare honey and pollen, while newer lives are larvae and cells. This preserves art but also risks devaluing living people.
evidence: not honey but seething life

questions.prompt: Does the ending choose the old city over every possible new one?
facilitatorNotes: It recalls old splendor while awaiting new beauty. The imagined conflict does not eliminate hope for a future the speaker cannot yet see.
evidence: await the new beauty of cities?

days.title: Self-Reliance: Consistency and the zigzag voyage (excerpt)
days.challenge: Distinguish superficial consistency from the deeper continuity the author still values.
days.focus: Changing one’s mind without losing an honest character.
days.context: Emerson now considers the fear of contradicting a former public opinion. Several metaphors suggest how change might coexist with integrity.
days.contentNote: This 1907 transcription retains nineteenth-century gendered language and bracketed reference numbers. The source’s editorial endnotes are not included; the questions depend on the supplied essay text.

excerpt.locator: Self-Reliance, the terror of consistency through cumulative character; complete source paragraphs 202–206 in the saved paragraph index; opens “The other terror that scares us from self-trust is our consistency; a reverence ”; closes “pendent, self-derived, and therefore of an old immaculate pedigree, even if shown in a young person.”.

questions.prompt: What does calling memory a corpse suggest about relying on yesterday’s judgment?
facilitatorNotes: A past opinion can become dead weight when it substitutes for present perception. Emerson does not erase memory; he denies it automatic authority over a new honest judgment.
evidence: Why drag about this corpse of your memory

questions.prompt: Does the claim that great thinkers were misunderstood establish that every misunderstood person is great?
facilitatorNotes: No. The examples challenge fear of misunderstanding, but the inference cannot simply be reversed. A strong answer distinguishes the rhetorical encouragement from a sufficient test of greatness.
evidence: To be great is to be misunderstood.

questions.prompt: How does the ship’s zigzag reconcile changing actions with a coherent character?
facilitatorNotes: Individual tacks differ while the voyage viewed at a distance has direction. Emerson locates agreement in actions that are honest in their own circumstances, rather than in repeated surface positions.
evidence: a zigzag line of a hundred tacks.

days.title: Admiration and the right to criticise a leader — excerpt
days.challenge: Notice concessions, shifts in audience and the distinction between popular approval and open deliberation.
days.focus: Leadership, tact and democratic criticism.
days.context: Du Bois introduces Booker T. Washington’s prominence and acknowledges his achievements before explaining why sincere criticism remains necessary. This is one participant’s argument in a debate, not a neutral summary of every position.
days.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement. Historical racial terminology, generalisations and the author’s reported viewpoints are retained for critical reading, not adopted as the site’s voice.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, Of Mr. Booker T. Washington and Others, opening eight prose paragraphs; UNC transcription of second edition, June1,1903, pp. 41–46; selected paragraphs corresponding to original PG indexes 89–96. Opening “EASILY the most striking thing in the history of the American Negro since 1876 is the asce”; closing “vance be relative retrogression. All this is the social student's inspiration and despair.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Du Bois connect Washington’s rise with the nation’s interest in dollars?
facilitatorNotes: He presents the programme’s success as partly a fit with the era’s priorities, not simply the result of personal qualities. That context also prepares his criticism of reducing education and citizenship to material aims.
evidence: was concentrating its energies on Dollars

questions.prompt: How could different Southern audiences approve the same Atlanta statement for different reasons?
facilitatorNotes: Some hear surrender of equality, while others hear a workable basis for cooperation. The same language permits incompatible expectations, so applause does not establish shared meaning.
evidence: The South interpreted it in different ways

questions.prompt: Why does silencing honest critics harm the community even if its recognised leader achieves useful results?
facilitatorNotes: Du Bois argues that selecting and evaluating leaders is itself an education in democratic judgment. Silence can produce passivity or destructive outbursts instead of accountable debate.
evidence: this is the soul of democracy and the safeguard of modern society

days.title: Preludes
days.challenge: Follow shifting pronouns and scale without forcing the four scenes into one continuous plot.
days.focus: Routine, fragmented bodies, and an interrupted gesture of compassion.
days.context: Four urban miniatures move from evening to morning and inward to consciousness. Read once for scenes, then chart who seems to perceive each one.

excerpt.locator: Complete individual poem, 1917 collection, Preludes; begins “I”; ends “revolve like ancient women Gathering fuel in vacant lots.”.

questions.prompt: What changes when morning itself “comes to consciousness”?
facilitatorNotes: The city seems to wake as a body, while muddy feet and hands fragment its actual inhabitants into routine actions.
evidence: The morning comes to consciousness

questions.prompt: How does the private room in section III complicate the public street?
facilitatorNotes: The person’s soul is made of urban images yet has a vision the street cannot understand; inward experience exceeds outward routine.
evidence: As the street hardly understands

questions.prompt: Does the final comparison erase the preceding “infinitely gentle” possibility?
facilitatorNotes: The abrupt command to laugh can undercut compassion, while the laboring women may also renew it. Require explanation of the tonal turn, not one settled verdict.
evidence: some infinitely gentle

days.title: Self-Reliance: What travels with the traveler? (excerpt)
days.challenge: Read an emphatic prohibition alongside its qualifications and concrete examples.
days.focus: Original work, local conditions, and the fantasy of escaping oneself.
days.context: Emerson examines travel as a promise of renewal, then connects imported architectural styles with borrowed habits of thought.
days.contentNote: This 1907 transcription retains nineteenth-century gendered language and bracketed reference numbers. The source’s editorial endnotes are not included; the questions depend on the supplied essay text.

excerpt.locator: Self-Reliance, travel and imitation; complete source paragraphs 230–234 in the saved paragraph index; opens “2. It is for want of self-culture that the superstition of Traveling, whose idols are Ital”; closes “le and noble regions of thy life, obey thy heart, and thou shalt reproduce the Foreworld again.”.

questions.prompt: What kinds of travel does Emerson explicitly permit, and why does that qualification matter?
facilitatorNotes: He accepts travel for art, study, and benevolence. The target is dependence on place to supply missing self-culture, so treating the passage as a literal ban on crossing borders misses its distinction.
evidence: for the purposes of art, of study, and benevolence

questions.prompt: What does the giant in Naples represent?
facilitatorNotes: It represents the unchanged self and its unresolved sadness. A new setting cannot by itself produce the transformation the traveler expects.
evidence: My giant goes with me wherever I go.

questions.prompt: How does the architecture example clarify the demand never to imitate?
facilitatorNotes: Buildings should answer local climate, materials, needs, and people rather than reproduce prestigious foreign forms automatically. Discuss how learning from predecessors could differ from allowing their finished forms to dictate one’s work.
evidence: what is imitation but the traveling of the mind?

days.title: The three paradoxes of economic advancement — excerpt
days.challenge: Follow parallel numbered lists and distinguish a causal claim from a qualified association.
days.focus: Whether economic security can be separated from political rights and higher education.
days.context: Du Bois lays out the elements he believes Washington’s programme asks people to postpone, then tests the relationship between those concessions and economic progress.
days.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement. Historical racial terminology, generalisations and the author’s reported viewpoints are retained for critical reading, not adopted as the site’s voice. Includes period racial hierarchies within the author’s argument; these categories should be examined critically.

excerpt.locator:
Chapter III, Of Mr. Booker T. Washington and Others, the programme’s economic emphasis through the numbered paradoxes; UNC transcription of second edition, June1,1903, pp. 50–52; selected paragraphs corresponding to original PG indexes 103–114. Opening “Mr. Washington represents in Negro thought the old attitude of adjustment and submission; ”; closing “ a day were it not for teachers trained in Negro colleges, or trained by their graduates.
”.

questions.prompt: How do the three things to be postponed prepare the later three paradoxes?
facilitatorNotes: Political power, civil rights and higher education return as supports that economic work and common schools require. The matching structure makes the criticism an argument about internal dependence.
evidence: First, political power

questions.prompt: What qualification does Du Bois make before connecting Washington’s programme with recent losses of rights?
facilitatorNotes: He says these changes are not direct results of the teachings, while arguing that the programme helped them happen faster. Students should preserve that distinction rather than restate the claim as sole causation.
evidence: These movements are not, to be sure, direct results of Mr. Washington's teachings

questions.prompt: Why is the teachers’ training an especially concrete example of the third paradox?
facilitatorNotes: Industrial and common schools need teachers produced by higher institutions. The example identifies an existing dependence within the educational programme being defended.
evidence: were it not for teachers trained in Negro colleges, or trained by their graduates

days.title: Rhapsody on a Windy Night
days.challenge: Distinguish clock sequence from associative mental movement.
days.focus: Mechanical commands, damaged images, and a return home that offers little release.
days.context: A night walker encounters speaking streetlamps and disordered memories. “La lune ne garde aucune rancune” means that the moon keeps no grudge; its sound also links the poem’s English and French phrases.
days.contentNote: Includes illness imagery, sexual suggestion, and a figurative knife; the walker’s descriptions are a limited and sometimes dehumanizing viewpoint.

excerpt.locator: Complete individual poem, 1917 collection, Rhapsody on a Windy Night; begins “Twelve o'clock. Along the reaches of the street Held”; ends “The last twist of the knife.”.

questions.prompt: How can the clock times organize a poem whose memory loses “clear relations”?
facilitatorNotes: The hours supply an external order while images jump associatively. This conflict keeps a chronological walk from becoming a coherent inner narrative.
evidence: Dissolve the floors of memory

questions.prompt: What unites the branch and the broken factory spring?
facilitatorNotes: Both are twisted remnants from which vitality or force has gone; natural and manufactured objects become comparable residues.
evidence: the form that the strength has left

questions.prompt: Why might “prepare for life” be followed by the final knife image?
facilitatorNotes: The ordinary return promises rest but also compulsory repetition. The ending makes routine feel injurious rather than restorative.
evidence: The last twist of the knife

days.title: Friendship: The imagined stranger (excerpt)
days.challenge: Notice where affectionate imagination enlarges perception and where it invents its object.
days.focus: Unspoken affection and the capacities awakened by another person.
days.context: The essay begins with everyday goodwill and develops an extended scene of a household awaiting a praised stranger.
days.contentNote: This 1907 transcription retains nineteenth-century gendered language and bracketed reference numbers. The source’s editorial endnotes are not included; the questions depend on the supplied essay text.

excerpt.locator: Friendship, numbered paragraphs 1–5; complete source paragraphs 243–247 in the saved paragraph index; opens “1. We have a great deal more kindness than is ever spoken. Barring all the selfishness tha”; closes “ affinity will exert its energy on whomsoever is as noble as these men and women, wherever I may be.”.

questions.prompt: How do ether and fire make unseen affection perceptible?
facilitatorNotes: Ether imagines love as a surrounding medium; fire makes its inward warmth and animation felt. Both images enlarge apparently minor encounters beyond spoken declarations.
evidence: like a fine ether.

questions.prompt: Why does the stranger initially improve everyone’s conversation, and what ends that effect?
facilitatorNotes: The household projects an ideal humanity onto the guest and rises toward that ideal. Particular prejudices and defects break the projection, suggesting that the initial energy belongs partly to expectation.
evidence: He stands to us for humanity.

questions.prompt: How can the speaker embrace solitude and still be grateful for friendship?
facilitatorNotes: He distinguishes compulsory society from affinities that deepen his own thought. The final social web is made through recognition, not simply through constant company.
evidence: we weave social threads of our own

days.title: Criticism as a responsibility to the nation — excerpt
days.challenge: Analyse a position that combines cooperation, dissent, patience and firm claims to rights.
days.focus: The difference between reconciliation and the abandonment of equal citizenship.
days.context: Having identified what he calls three paradoxes in Washington’s programme, Du Bois distinguishes groups of critics and explains the commitments of those with whom he aligns himself.
days.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement. Historical racial terminology, generalisations and the author’s reported viewpoints are retained for critical reading, not adopted as the site’s voice. Includes references to imperial violence and period assumptions about social hierarchy.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, Of Mr. Booker T. Washington and Others, the two groups of critics through the warning about reconciliation; UNC transcription of second edition, June1,1903, pp. 52–56; selected paragraphs corresponding to original PG indexes 115–121. Opening “This triple paradox in Mr. Washington's position is the object of criticism by two classes”; closing “ the inevitable seeds are sown for a harvest of disaster to our children, black and white.”.

questions.prompt: Why do the quieter critics hesitate to speak, and why does Du Bois argue that they cannot remain silent?
facilitatorNotes: They do not want principled disagreement to become a pretext for petty attacks on a useful leader. Fundamental rights nevertheless impose a responsibility greater than protecting unity or reputation.
evidence: an excuse for a general discharge of venom from small-minded opponents

questions.prompt: How does the passage distinguish patience about achieving rights from surrendering the claim to them?
facilitatorNotes: The critics recognise that prejudice will not vanish immediately, but regard abandoning the demand as undermining its eventual achievement. Courtesy and continued insistence can coexist.
evidence: the way for a people to gain their reasonable rights is not by voluntarily throwing them away

questions.prompt: Why is opposition to an unequal reconciliation described as patriotic rather than disloyal?
facilitatorNotes: The argument treats equal citizenship as part of the nation’s moral responsibility. A reunion purchased through another group’s civic exclusion would damage the shared country and future generations.
evidence: a responsibility to this nation,--this common Fatherland

days.title: The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock
days.challenge: Track conditional speech, self-correction, and allusion across a sustained dramatic monologue.
days.focus: The social imagination as both expressive power and an obstacle to action.
days.context: The Italian epigraph comes from Dante’s Inferno: a speaker answers because he believes the listener cannot return to report him. Read Prufrock as a dramatic voice, not a direct confession by Eliot; mark imagined reactions separately from spoken events.
days.contentNote: Contains sexual suggestion, beheading and drowning imagery, and anxiety about aging; no literal act of self-harm is established.

excerpt.locator: Complete individual poem, 1917 collection, The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock; begins “S'io credesse che mia risposta fosse A persona che”; ends “brown Till human voices wake us, and we drown.”.
excerpt.inlineReason: The night’s stanza divisions differ from the library work at two page breaks of the transcription: it joins the row of asterisks ending page 14 to the stanza “No! I am not Prince Hamlet” opening page 15 (the transcription marks a stanza break there, and the night keeps the poem’s other two asterisk rows as their own stanzas), and it divides “I have seen them riding seaward on the waves” from “We have lingered in the chambers of the sea” across the break from page 15 to 16, where the transcription marks none. The words and lines are otherwise identical, so the night stays inline.

blocks.text: The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock

S'io credesse che mia risposta fosse
A persona che mai tornasse al mondo,
Questa fiamma staria senza piu scosse.
Ma perciocche giammai di questo fondo
Non torno vivo alcun, s'i'odo il vero,
Senza tema d'infamia ti rispondo.

Let us go then, you and I,
When the evening is spread out against the sky
Like a patient etherized upon a table;
Let us go, through certain half-deserted streets,
The muttering retreats
Of restless nights in one-night cheap hotels
And sawdust restaurants with oyster-shells:
Streets that follow like a tedious argument
Of insidious intent
To lead you to an overwhelming question. . . .
Oh, do not ask, "What is it?"
Let us go and make our visit.

In the room the women come and go
Talking of Michelangelo.

The yellow fog that rubs its back upon the window-panes,
The yellow smoke that rubs its muzzle on the window-panes,
Licked its tongue into the corners of the evening,
Lingered upon the pools that stand in drains,
Let fall upon its back the soot that falls from chimneys,
Slipped by the terrace, made a sudden leap,
And seeing that it was a soft October night,
Curled once about the house, and fell asleep.

And indeed there will be time
For the yellow smoke that slides along the street,
Rubbing its back upon the window-panes;
There will be time, there will be time
To prepare a face to meet the faces that you meet;
There will be time to murder and create,
And time for all the works and days of hands
That lift and drop a question on your plate;
Time for you and time for me,
And time yet for a hundred indecisions,
And for a hundred visions and revisions,
Before the taking of a toast and tea.

In the room the women come and go
Talking of Michelangelo.

And indeed there will be time
To wonder, "Do I dare?" and, "Do I dare?"
Time to turn back and descend the stair,
With a bald spot in the middle of my hair—
(They will say: "How his hair is growing thin!")
My morning coat, my collar mounting firmly to the chin,
My necktie rich and modest, but asserted by a simple pin—
(They will say: "But how his arms and legs are thin!")
Do I dare
Disturb the universe?
In a minute there is time
For decisions and revisions which a minute will reverse.

For I have known them all already, known them all:
Have known the evenings, mornings, afternoons,
I have measured out my life with coffee spoons;
I know the voices dying with a dying fall
Beneath the music from a farther room.
So how should I presume?

And I have known the eyes already, known them all—
The eyes that fix you in a formulated phrase,
And when I am formulated, sprawling on a pin,
When I am pinned and wriggling on the wall,
Then how should I begin
To spit out all the butt-ends of my days and ways?
And how should I presume?

And I have known the arms already, known them all—
Arms that are braceleted and white and bare
(But in the lamplight, downed with light brown hair!)
Is it perfume from a dress
That makes me so digress?
Arms that lie along a table, or wrap about a shawl.
And should I then presume?
And how should I begin?

Shall I say, I have gone at dusk through narrow streets
And watched the smoke that rises from the pipes
Of lonely men in shirt-sleeves, leaning out of windows? . . .

I should have been a pair of ragged claws
Scuttling across the floors of silent seas.

And the afternoon, the evening, sleeps so peacefully!
Smoothed by long fingers,
Asleep . . . tired . . . or it malingers,
Stretched on the floor, here beside you and me.
Should I, after tea and cakes and ices,
Have the strength to force the moment to its crisis?
But though I have wept and fasted, wept and prayed,
Though I have seen my head (grown slightly bald) brought in upon a platter,
I am no prophet—and here's no great matter;
I have seen the moment of my greatness flicker,
And I have seen the eternal Footman hold my coat, and snicker,
And in short, I was afraid.

And would it have been worth it, after all,
After the cups, the marmalade, the tea,
Among the porcelain, among some talk of you and me,
Would it have been worth while,
To have bitten off the matter with a smile,
To have squeezed the universe into a ball
To roll it toward some overwhelming question,
To say: "I am Lazarus, come from the dead,
Come back to tell you all, I shall tell you all"—
If one, settling a pillow by her head,
Should say: "That is not what I meant at all;
That is not it, at all."

And would it have been worth it, after all,
Would it have been worth while,
After the sunsets and the dooryards and the sprinkled streets,
After the novels, after the teacups, after the skirts that trail along the floor—
And this, and so much more?—
It is impossible to say just what I mean!
But as if a magic lantern threw the nerves in patterns on a screen:
Would it have been worth while
If one, settling a pillow or throwing off a shawl,
And turning toward the window, should say:
"That is not it at all,
That is not what I meant, at all."

I grow old . . . I grow old . . .
I shall wear the bottoms of my trousers rolled.

Shall I part my hair behind? Do I dare to eat a peach?
I shall wear white flannel trousers, and walk upon the beach.
I have heard the mermaids singing, each to each.
I do not think that they will sing to me.

I have seen them riding seaward on the waves
Combing the white hair of the waves blown back
When the wind blows the water white and black.

We have lingered in the chambers of the sea
By sea-girls wreathed with seaweed red and brown
Till human voices wake us, and we drown.

questions.prompt: How does “there will be time” change from reassurance into a mechanism of delay?
facilitatorNotes: The available time fills with preparations, indecisions, and revisions. The repetition licenses postponement rather than establishing an action actually taken.
evidence: a hundred visions and revisions

questions.prompt: How do coffee spoons and the specimen pinned to a wall give different forms to his fear?
facilitatorNotes: The spoons measure life into trivial repetitions; the pin represents being fixed and judged by another’s label. Both reduce a fluid self.
evidence: sprawling on a pin

questions.prompt: What does denying he is Hamlet reveal about his sense of role?
facilitatorNotes: He assigns himself a cautious supporting part, then slides toward the Fool. This self-diminishment is also a highly artful performance, not a neutral diagnosis.
evidence: No! I am not Prince Hamlet

days.title: Friendship: Truth and tenderness (excerpt)
days.challenge: Reconcile lofty metaphors with ordinary practical demands.
days.focus: Two equally necessary elements of a durable friendship.
days.context: These two paragraphs name truth and tenderness as the essay’s central conditions for friendship.
days.contentNote: This 1907 transcription retains nineteenth-century gendered language and bracketed reference numbers. The source’s editorial endnotes are not included; the questions depend on the supplied essay text.

excerpt.locator: Friendship, numbered paragraphs 12–13; complete source paragraphs 257–258 in the saved paragraph index; opens “12. I do not wish to treat friendships daintily, but with roughest courage. When they are ”; closes “usual and settled, but should be alert and inventive, and add rhyme and reason to what was drudgery.”.

questions.prompt: What does the contrast between frost-work and solidity suggest about testing a friendship?
facilitatorNotes: A real bond should withstand difficulty rather than require delicate protection from every challenge. The contest with time, want, and danger gives that durability concrete trials.
evidence: not glass threads or frost-work

questions.prompt: How does the image of removing garments describe sincerity?
facilitatorNotes: Courtesy and concealment become layers one can remove before an equal. Emerson values a relation in which a person can think aloud, though readers may question whether every courtesy is hypocrisy.
evidence: Before him, I may think aloud.

questions.prompt: Why must friendship have feet as well as eloquence?
facilitatorNotes: Tenderness needs practical fidelity, justice, punctuality, and care. The passage rejects both useful exchanges without intimacy and beautiful declarations without ordinary responsibility.
evidence: friendship should have feet, as well as eyes and eloquence.

days.title: Hunting for a country school — excerpt
days.challenge: Read comic storytelling, remembered landscape and sudden social exclusion within the same episode.
days.focus: Educational aspiration amid material scarcity and segregation.
days.context: As a Fisk student, Du Bois seeks summer teaching work in rural Tennessee. Josie, a young woman eager to learn, helps him find a community that needs a school.
days.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement. Historical racial terminology, generalisations and the author’s reported viewpoints are retained for critical reading, not adopted as the site’s voice.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, Of the Meaning of Progress, the opening through the schoolhouse description; UNC transcription of second edition, June1,1903, pp. 60–64; selected paragraphs corresponding to original PG indexes 132–138. Opening “ONCE upon a time I taught school in the hills of Tennessee, where the broad dark vale of t”; closing “ne virtue of making naps dangerous,-- possibly fatal, for the floor was not to be trusted.”.

questions.prompt: How does comparing the search for a school with hunting alter the account of exhaustion?
facilitatorNotes: The playful comparison makes the search adventurous, while the repeated long roads and refusals reveal its difficulty. Humour does not cancel the teacher’s physical and emotional weariness.
evidence: the pleasures of the chase

questions.prompt: What details make Josie central to the narrative before she becomes a pupil?
facilitatorNotes: She identifies the need for a school, expresses her own desire to learn and works continuously for her family. The narrator’s portrait connects personal ambition with service rather than treating her as merely a recipient of teaching.
evidence: make life broader, deeper, and fuller for her and hers

questions.prompt: Why is the apparently hospitable meal with the commissioner interrupted by the image of the Veil?
facilitatorNotes: Approval of the teaching certificate and a dinner invitation do not prevent segregated eating. The abrupt final detail exposes a boundary beneath friendly manners.
evidence: for they ate first, then I--alone

days.title: Morning at the Window
days.challenge: Evaluate the limits of a detached observer’s imaginative sympathy.
days.focus: Fog, class distance, and a smile detached from its owner.
days.context: The observer looks down from a window at working people and passing faces. Read aloud slowly, then distinguish what can be seen from what the speaker claims about interior lives.

excerpt.locator: Complete individual poem, 1917 collection, Morning at the Window; begins “They are rattling breakfast plates in basement kitchens, And”; ends “air And vanishes along the level of the roofs.”.

questions.prompt: Which concrete details locate the housemaids socially and physically?
facilitatorNotes: Basement kitchens, plates, and area gates place domestic work below the observer’s window and at the edges of the street.
evidence: breakfast plates in basement kitchens

questions.prompt: What is gained and risked by imagining “damp souls” sprouting?
facilitatorNotes: The image extends the wet environment inward and suggests inhibited growth, but it also presumes knowledge of strangers’ feelings.
evidence: damp souls of housemaids

questions.prompt: How does the smile’s movement differ from the passerby’s?
facilitatorNotes: The smile seems torn free, hovering up to roof level and vanishing. The brief connection is fleeting and mediated by the observer’s metaphor.
evidence: An aimless smile that hovers in the air

days.title: Friendship: The beautiful enemy (excerpt)
days.challenge: Trace the paradox that closeness requires distance and independence.
days.focus: Conversation, difference, and the limits of possessing a friend.
days.context: Emerson considers why a person may speak brilliantly with one companion but remain silent with another, then asks how friendship preserves distinct selves.
days.contentNote: This 1907 transcription retains nineteenth-century gendered language and bracketed reference numbers. The source’s editorial endnotes are not included; the questions depend on the supplied essay text.

excerpt.locator: Friendship, numbered paragraphs 14–19; complete source paragraphs 259–264 in the saved paragraph index; opens “14. Friendship may be said to require natures so rare and costly, each so well-tempered, a”; closes “between two spirits, never mutual respect until, in their dialogue, each stands for the whole world.”.

questions.prompt: How does the sundial explain conversational ability?
facilitatorNotes: A dial needs sunlight, as a speaker needs an enabling relation. Eloquence is relational rather than a fixed possession available with every audience.
evidence: a dial in the shade.

questions.prompt: Why is a nettle preferable to an echo?
facilitatorNotes: Respectful resistance preserves the friend’s independent mind; automatic agreement erases the difference that makes friendship valuable. Neither constant hostility nor compliance fulfills the stated ideal.
evidence: Better be a nettle in the side of your friend, than his echo.

questions.prompt: What tension does the beautiful enemy image preserve?
facilitatorNotes: Admiration and affinity coexist with otherness that cannot be owned or reduced to convenience. Readers can assess whether his insistence on distance strengthens friendship or neglects ordinary intimacy.
evidence: a sort of beautiful enemy

days.title: The school and the worlds beyond the hill — excerpt
days.challenge: Connect attendance and aspiration with household labour, economic pressure and differences between generations.
days.focus: A teacher’s intimacy with a community and the limits of his judgments.
days.context: The school opens, and Du Bois describes its pupils, his visits to their homes and the circumstances affecting attendance. His portraits include period judgments that readers should evaluate as part of his narrative stance.
days.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement. Historical racial terminology, generalisations and the author’s reported viewpoints are retained for critical reading, not adopted as the site’s voice. The narrator uses disparaging descriptions of appearance, poverty and family status; discuss their effect rather than treating them as neutral facts.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, Of the Meaning of Progress, the school’s first day through generational responses to isolation; UNC transcription of second edition, June1,1903, pp. 64–68; selected paragraphs corresponding to original PG indexes 139–145. Opening “It was a hot morning late in July when the school opened. I trembled when I heard the patt”; closing “outh, of life; at last, in dangerous moments, against everything that opposed even a whim.”.

questions.prompt: What different explanations does the narrator discover for pupils’ absences?
facilitatorNotes: Children work in crops, care for babies or stay away because parents doubt book learning. The variety prevents absence from being explained by one lack of interest.
evidence: the crops needed the boys

questions.prompt: How does the account of sleeping arrangements complicate any assumption that poor housing means a lack of hospitality?
facilitatorNotes: Families carefully manage privacy and share what they have to accommodate the teacher. Their consideration is visible despite scarce rooms and resources.
evidence: embarrassment was very deftly avoided

questions.prompt: Why does the final paragraph call this community both a world and a group with only partly shared consciousness?
facilitatorNotes: Isolation and common barriers unite it, but generations interpret their conditions through different memories, beliefs and expectations. Shared hardship does not produce one uniform response.
evidence: these, when ripe for speech, were spoken in various languages

days.title: Cousin Nancy
days.challenge: Read domestic objects and literary names as parts of a compact cultural argument.
days.focus: Social change, uncertainty, and the authority of a bookshelf.
days.context: Nancy’s behavior challenges her New England aunts. “Matthew and Waldo” points to Matthew Arnold and Ralph Waldo Emerson as authors whose books stand on the shelves; the final line echoes Meredith’s poem Lucifer in Starlight.

excerpt.locator: Complete individual poem, 1917 collection, Cousin Nancy; begins “Miss Nancy Ellicot Strode across the hills and broke”; ends “guardians of the faith, The army of unalterable law.”.

questions.prompt: Why describe Nancy as breaking the hills when she rides across them?
facilitatorNotes: The repeated exaggeration makes physical movement seem a violation of inherited order; the landscape participates in the social conflict.
evidence: Strode across the hills and broke them

questions.prompt: What is precise about the aunts knowing an action is modern but not knowing their own feelings?
facilitatorNotes: Classification arrives before judgment. Their uncertainty complicates a simple opposition between rebellion and settled disapproval.
evidence: not quite sure how they felt about it

questions.prompt: How do the books become guardians, and is their power convincing?
facilitatorNotes: Personification makes the shelf a watchful authority, but stationary books face Nancy’s movement. An ironic reading can question how unalterable their law really is.
evidence: guardians of the faith

days.title: Gifts
days.challenge: Follow an argument that revises its rules and ends by limiting rule-making itself.
days.focus: Giving as expression, obligation, and a possible threat to independence.
days.context: This complete essay asks why choosing and receiving presents can be difficult even when generosity is welcome.
days.contentNote: This 1907 transcription retains nineteenth-century gendered language and bracketed reference numbers. The source’s editorial endnotes are not included; the questions depend on the supplied essay text. The essay uses historical religious generalizations and gendered occupational examples.

excerpt.locator: Gifts, epigraph and complete six-paragraph essay; complete source paragraphs 334–342 in the saved paragraph index; opens “Gifts of one who loved me-- 'Twas high time they came; When he ceased to love me, Time the”; closes “ke apples, and leave you out. But love them, and they feel for you, and delight in you all the time.”.

questions.prompt: Why can both a needed pair of shoes and a flower be fitting gifts?
facilitatorNotes: Necessity removes uncertainty in one case; beauty beyond utility justifies the other. Emerson’s criteria are plural and depend on the relationship and occasion.
evidence: if the man at the door have no shoes

questions.prompt: What separates a portion of oneself from an expensive purchased object?
facilitatorNotes: A gift can express the giver’s work, experience, or talent instead of merely transferring wealth. Examine the occupational examples and the danger of treating a price as a measure of affection.
evidence: The only gift is a portion of thyself.

questions.prompt: How does the ending qualify the essay’s earlier prescriptions?
facilitatorNotes: Love may give kingdoms or leaves, resisting rigid rules. The ultimate distinction concerns felt affinity rather than a transaction that obliges gratitude or purchases attachment.
evidence: Let him give kingdoms or flower-leaves indifferently.

days.title: Returning to the families: interrupted hopes — excerpt
days.challenge: Read compressed life histories in which a brief sentence can disclose a major loss.
days.focus: The tension between educational hope, family duties and the passage of time.
days.context: Ten years after teaching in the community, Du Bois returns to learn what has happened to his former pupils. Earlier he had portrayed Josie as hardworking and eager for further education.
days.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement. Historical racial terminology, generalisations and the author’s reported viewpoints are retained for critical reading, not adopted as the site’s voice. Includes death, imprisonment, a child born outside marriage and judgmental historical language about disability and sexuality; no graphic detail.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, Of the Meaning of Progress, the return after ten years through the young wife’s planned farm; UNC transcription of second edition, June1,1903, pp. 68–70; selected paragraphs corresponding to original PG indexes 146–149. Opening “The ten years that follow youth, the years when first the realization comes that life is l”; closing “he tale of her thrifty husband, the horse and cow, and the farm they were planning to buy.”.

questions.prompt: How does the abrupt announcement of Josie’s death change the emotional direction of the return?
facilitatorNotes: Nostalgia and curiosity are immediately confronted with irreversible loss. The following account reconstructs the labour and family pressures concealed by the brief announcement.
evidence: Josie was dead

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator imagine another future for Jim under different family and social conditions?
facilitatorNotes: He distinguishes Jim’s energy from the opportunities and support available to direct it. The counterfactual challenges the idea that the resulting life simply reveals an inherent lack of ability.
evidence: With a cultured parentage and a social caste to uphold him

questions.prompt: How does the final young wife’s pride prevent the passage from becoming only a catalogue of defeat?
facilitatorNotes: She describes domestic order, a thrifty husband and plans for ownership. These hopes exist alongside worry and the preceding losses; readers need not choose an entirely hopeful or entirely bleak interpretation.
evidence: the farm they were planning to buy

days.title: Conversation Galante
days.challenge: Use dialogue structure to test the self-importance of a speaker’s rhetoric.
days.focus: Wit, evasion, and uncertainty about whether a conversation is serious.
days.context: The title suggests elegant courtly conversation. Two speakers trade elaborate comparisons and brisk responses; read their lines with distinct voices. Prester John was a legendary ruler, not a person identified in this scene.

excerpt.locator: Complete individual poem, 1917 collection, Conversation Galante; begins “I observe: "Our sentimental friend the moon! Or possibly”; ends “mad poetics to confute—" And—"Are we then so serious?"”.

questions.prompt: How does the woman’s first reply change the effect of the moon comparisons?
facilitatorNotes: Her short accusation of digression punctures his elaborate performance and asks what it has to do with their actual conversation.
evidence: How you digress

questions.prompt: What happens when she asks whether “vacuity” refers to her?
facilitatorNotes: The abstract aesthetic claim becomes a social risk, and he hastily assigns inanity to himself. The exchange exposes rhetoric as interpersonal maneuver.
evidence: Does this refer to me

questions.prompt: Does the final question simply defeat the man, or also evade him?
facilitatorNotes: It can puncture grand flattery while refusing to state her own position. The dialogue permits mutual evasion as well as a one-sided comic correction.
evidence: Are we then so serious

days.title: Nature: Leaving the knapsack of custom (excerpt)
days.challenge: Read sensory description as an argument about habit, attention, and healing.
days.focus: The forest’s power to interrupt inherited social measures.
days.context: Emerson opens this essay with an unusually harmonious autumn day and the altered perception of someone entering the woods.
days.contentNote: This 1907 transcription retains nineteenth-century gendered language and bracketed reference numbers. The source’s editorial endnotes are not included; the questions depend on the supplied essay text.

excerpt.locator: Nature, numbered paragraphs 1–2; complete source paragraphs 345–346 in the saved paragraph index; opens “1. There are days which occur in this climate, at almost any season of the year, wher”; closes “rse with Gabriel and Uriel, the upper sky would be all that would remain of our furniture.”.

questions.prompt: What falls away with the knapsack of custom?
facilitatorNotes: City assumptions about importance, wisdom, and foolishness cease to be unquestioned measures. The metaphor makes habit a burden that can be temporarily removed.
evidence: The knapsack of custom falls off his back

questions.prompt: How does a perpetual morning describe an effect rather than a literal time?
facilitatorNotes: The woods seem renewing and stimulating throughout the visit. The image connects changing attention with the possibility of beginning again.
evidence: like a perpetual morning

questions.prompt: Why compare rock and ground with water for thirst?
facilitatorNotes: The senses require physical scope and contact as the body requires water. This supports the claim that nature’s ordinary pleasures can heal, before the paragraph rises to spiritual imagination.
evidence: as water to our thirst

days.title: How shall progress be measured? — excerpt
days.challenge: Balance material gains with human costs and attend to the force of a brief closing detail.
days.focus: The difficulty of measuring a community’s progress through property alone.
days.context: Continuing the return visit, Du Bois examines the school and several families before asking what counts as progress. The earlier section has disclosed Josie’s death after years of work and deferred schooling.
days.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement. Historical racial terminology, generalisations and the author’s reported viewpoints are retained for critical reading, not adopted as the site’s voice. Contains a racial slur in reported speech, threatened mob violence, domestic abuse and deaths, without graphic injuries.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, Of the Meaning of Progress, the changed schoolhouse through the chapter’s final sentence; UNC transcription of second edition, June1,1903, pp. 70–74; selected paragraphs corresponding to original PG indexes 150–156. Opening “My log schoolhouse was gone. In its place stood Progress; and Progress, I understand, is n”; closing “Thus sadly musing, I rode to Nashville in the Jim Crow car.”.

questions.prompt: How does the new schoolhouse both support and trouble the idea of progress?
facilitatorNotes: There is a permanent county site and regular school, but broken glass and backless benches complicate the improvement. The narrator’s pleasure and hesitation coexist rather than cancel one another.
evidence: I felt glad, very glad, and yet

questions.prompt: Why does the account of Ben matter to the narrator’s credibility as an observer?
facilitatorNotes: He admits that his prediction of failure was wrong. Ben’s later work and care for his sister require a revision of a judgment based on the household he came from.
evidence: But this is an odd world; for Ben is a busy farmer

questions.prompt: How do the bushel-of-wheat question and the final segregated railway carriage work together?
facilitatorNotes: The question resists converting suffering into a simple economic balance sheet. The carriage shows that a public system of racial exclusion remains around the local gains and losses.
evidence: How many heartfuls of sorrow shall balance a bushel of wheat

days.title: La Figlia Che Piange
days.challenge: Follow shifts of tense and mood to locate the speaker’s control over another person’s grief.
days.focus: Aesthetic arrangement and the emotional cost of a memorable pose.
days.context: The Italian title means “the girl who weeps.” The speaker arranges a parting scene and later remembers its image; separate commands, imagined alternatives, and the event finally reported.

excerpt.locator: Complete individual poem, 1917 collection, La Figlia Che Piange; begins “Stand on the highest pavement of the stair— Lean”; ends “still amaze The troubled midnight and the noon's repose.”.

questions.prompt: What power does the opening series of commands give the speaker?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker directs posture, flowers, expression, and light like a stage manager or artist; the woman initially appears as an arranged image.
evidence: Clasp your flowers to you

questions.prompt: What does “would have had” reveal about the scene’s status?
facilitatorNotes: It marks a preferred arrangement rather than an uncomplicated record. The speaker’s desired version must be distinguished from what occurred.
evidence: So I would have had her stand and grieve

questions.prompt: Why is imagining the couple together a threat to a “gesture and a pose”?
facilitatorNotes: Reunion would remove the aesthetically satisfying separation. The poem makes the speaker’s artistic gain potentially conflict with the people’s happiness.
evidence: I should have lost a gesture and a pose

days.title: Nature: One material, many forms (excerpt)
days.challenge: Distinguish scientific observation, analogy, and philosophical inference.
days.focus: Change, continuity, and the claim that artificial life remains natural.
days.context: Emerson turns from landscape’s appearance to the processes that produce forms, drawing on nineteenth-century science and his own philosophy.
days.contentNote: This 1907 transcription retains nineteenth-century gendered language and bracketed reference numbers. The source’s editorial endnotes are not included; the questions depend on the supplied essay text. Historical scientific and developmental claims are objects of rhetorical analysis, not a current science lesson.

excerpt.locator: Nature, numbered paragraphs 6–10; complete source paragraphs 350–354 in the saved paragraph index; opens “6. But taking timely warning, and leaving many things unsaid on this topic, but not longer”; closes “vy and Black, is the same common sense which made the arrangements which now it discovers.”.

questions.prompt: Why does geology require a change of perspective?
facilitatorNotes: Rock formation, soil, and successive life forms require timescales far beyond everyday measures. Emerson makes this expanded scale part of his account of gradual transformation.
evidence: We know nothing rightly, for want of perspective.

questions.prompt: What does the repeated one stuff claim accomplish?
facilitatorNotes: It holds underlying continuity together with astonishing variety. The cup, shell, and stars become analogies for shared processes; readers should distinguish their suggestive force from a scientific demonstration of every claim.
evidence: it is still one stuff

questions.prompt: How does the mason example challenge an easy city-versus-nature opposition?
facilitatorNotes: Humans and their capacities arise in nature, so their buildings do too. The conclusion questions the belief that camping or eating roots automatically makes a person wiser or more natural.
evidence: Nature, who made the mason, made the house.

days.title: Atlanta and the golden apples — excerpt
days.challenge: Follow an extended mythic analogy while distinguishing qualified praise from criticism.
days.focus: When necessary economic development becomes an inadequate final aim.
days.context: Du Bois personifies Atlanta as a city recovering from war and compares its pursuit of prosperity with the classical story of Atalanta, which he retells in the passage.
days.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement. Historical racial terminology, generalisations and the author’s reported viewpoints are retained for critical reading, not adopted as the site’s voice. Includes idealised descriptions of the old Southern elite and period class insults that invite critical scrutiny.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, Of the Wings of Atalanta, opening nine prose paragraphs; UNC transcription of second edition, June1,1903, pp. 75–79; selected paragraphs corresponding to original PG indexes 161–169. Opening “SOUTH of the North, yet north of the South, lies the City of a Hundred Hills, peering out ”; closing “finally, instead of Truth, Beauty, and Goodness, wealth as the ideal of the Public School.”.

questions.prompt: How does personifying Atlanta as a working widow complicate the later criticism of wealth-seeking?
facilitatorNotes: The city’s labour is shown as an earnest response to loss and necessity. The warning is not that rebuilding is wrong, but that its means can displace broader purposes.
evidence: the city rose like a widow and cast away her weeds, and toiled for her daily bread

questions.prompt: What exactly do the golden apples stand for in the analogy, and why are they dangerous?
facilitatorNotes: They represent material rewards that distract a runner from a larger goal. The text recognises their attraction and utility but rejects treating them as the purpose of the race.
evidence: golden apples are the goal of racing, and not mere incidents by the way

questions.prompt: Why does the final list repeat wealth in relation to social problems and schools?
facilitatorNotes: The repetition imitates a universal prescription applied to distinct needs. Ending with the public school reveals the cost when Truth, Beauty and Goodness are replaced by one monetary standard.
evidence: wealth as the ideal of the Public School

days.title: Prudence: Will it bake bread? (excerpt)
days.challenge: Analyze a writer’s admission of weakness and a hierarchy of competing values.
days.focus: Practical needs as necessary means rather than the whole purpose of life.
days.context: Emerson admits limited practical skill before arguing that material prudence has a legitimate but subordinate place.
days.contentNote: This 1907 transcription retains nineteenth-century gendered language and bracketed reference numbers. The source’s editorial endnotes are not included; the questions depend on the supplied essay text.

excerpt.locator: Prudence, opening five paragraphs; complete source paragraphs 397–401 in the saved paragraph index; opens “What right have I to write on Prudence, whereof I have little, and that of the negative so”; closes “or pleasures for their own sake, he may be a good wheel or pin, but he is not a cultivated man.”.

questions.prompt: How does admitting an untidy garden help establish the essay’s method?
facilitatorNotes: He claims aspiration and awareness of a lack can motivate thought, not only mastery. The admission can build candor while inviting scrutiny of his authority.
evidence: We write from aspiration and antagonism

questions.prompt: What distinguishes utility, taste, and spiritual perception in his three classes?
facilitatorNotes: They value the usefulness of a symbol, its beauty, and what it signifies. The hierarchy asks readers to see material objects as capable of more than one kind of meaning.
evidence: The first class have common sense; the second, taste; and the third, spiritual perception.

questions.prompt: Why is the bread question insufficient even though bodily needs matter?
facilitatorNotes: It turns a necessary means into the only standard of value. The wheel-or-pin image makes a capable specialist seem incomplete when utility consumes the whole person.
evidence: Will it bake bread?

days.title: The university as another horizon — excerpt
days.challenge: Track a turn from warning and repeated questions to the concrete description of a learning community.
days.focus: A liberal education’s purposes beyond earning a living.
days.context: Du Bois extends his warning about golden apples from Atlanta’s general culture to Black communities, then describes Atlanta University. The concluding German line means, in brief, that one must practise renunciation; this orientation is outside the source text.
days.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement. Historical racial terminology, generalisations and the author’s reported viewpoints are retained for critical reading, not adopted as the site’s voice. Includes paternalistic period descriptions and idealisations of the past.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, Of the Wings of Atalanta, the Black World’s changing ideals through the quoted German line; UNC transcription of second edition, June1,1903, pp. 79–83; selected paragraphs corresponding to original PG indexes 170–174. Opening “Not only is this true in the world which Atlanta typifies, but it is threatening to be tru”; closing “"Entbehren sollst du, sollst entbehren."”.

questions.prompt: How does the wheel-within-a-wheel image explain the relationship between the Black community and the wider society?
facilitatorNotes: The smaller world has distinct barriers but also parallel struggles over leadership, money and ideals. Its choices will eventually affect the larger world, so its apparent invisibility does not make it unimportant.
evidence: like a wheel within a wheel

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the succession of questions beginning What if?
facilitatorNotes: They project possible consequences rather than report them as accomplished facts. Their accumulation presses readers to judge what would be lost if monetary aims displaced justice and knowledge.
evidence: What if the Negro people be wooed from a strife for righteousness, from a love of knowing

questions.prompt: How do the university’s buildings, sounds and curriculum provide an answer to the earlier warning?
facilitatorNotes: The ordered and restful scene makes intellectual pursuit tangible, while its studies range across literature, science and history. The university asks what life is for rather than treating subsistence as its sole purpose.
evidence: not to earn meat, but to know the end and aim of that life which meat nourishes

days.title: Circles: Beyond the latest boundary (excerpt)
days.challenge: Track one geometric image through nature, institutions, personal growth, and debate.
days.focus: The provisional character of apparently final knowledge.
days.context: The essay begins with the eye and horizon, then imagines every established circle as capable of being surrounded by another.
days.contentNote: This 1907 transcription retains nineteenth-century gendered language and bracketed reference numbers. The source’s editorial endnotes are not included; the questions depend on the supplied essay text. Includes a gender stereotype about understanding property and historical generalizations about cultures.

excerpt.locator: Circles, opening six paragraphs; complete source paragraphs 420–425 in the saved paragraph index; opens “The eye is the first circle; the horizon which it forms is the second; and throughout natu”; closes “man in the world as he is a suggestion of that he should be. Men walk as prophecies of the next age.”.

questions.prompt: Why is a new dawn at noon a useful paradox for this argument?
facilitatorNotes: It imagines renewal arriving when completeness seems already achieved. The circle can be a real accomplishment while remaining open to a larger understanding.
evidence: another dawn risen on mid-noon

questions.prompt: How do the granite tower and changing technologies challenge permanence?
facilitatorNotes: Structures depend on the thoughts and practices that made them; new capacities can supersede them. Apparent stability therefore varies with scale and knowledge.
evidence: that which builds is better than that which is built.

questions.prompt: What happens when another speaker draws a circle around a seemingly final explanation?
facilitatorNotes: The first statement becomes a limited contribution within a broader account. Emerson extends this process inward: people can also revise their own convictions.
evidence: only a first speaker.

days.title: Roots, wings and an educational system — excerpt
days.challenge: Separate a defence of an educational principle from approval of every institution claiming its name.
days.focus: Different forms of training within a common human purpose.
days.context: Du Bois has presented universities as a protection against reducing life to material gain. He now criticises actual institutions while defending a connected system of education.
days.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement. Historical racial terminology, generalisations and the author’s reported viewpoints are retained for critical reading, not adopted as the site’s voice. Contains elitist period assumptions about ability and occupational roles; the questions invite examination rather than automatic endorsement.

Opening “They made their mistakes, those who planted Fisk and Howard and Atlanta before the smoke o”; closing “Atalanta pausing over her golden apples. Fly, my maiden, fly, for yonder comes Hippomenes!”.

questions.prompt: Which mistakes does Du Bois attribute to early educational builders, and which criticism does he reject?
facilitatorNotes: He criticises haste, weak foundations and inflated university labels, but rejects the idea that beginning with advanced teacher training was inherently wrong. The distinction concerns quality and implementation, not merely institutional names.
evidence: some dozen poorly equipped high schools and miscalled them universities

questions.prompt: How does the roots-and-leaves analogy support his account of a whole system?
facilitatorNotes: Advanced knowledge supports teachers and schools, which in turn support other forms of training. The image presents mutual dependence across levels, rather than a contest in which one kind of schooling must eliminate the others.
evidence: The roots of the tree, rather than the leaves, are the sources of its life

questions.prompt: What tension exists between the division of workers and thinkers and the insistence that the final product is a person?
facilitatorNotes: He assigns different talents to different paths while insisting on a common human end beyond occupation. Students may defend the differentiation or question whether the hierarchy restricts people too early, using both parts of the argument.
evidence: the final product of our training must be neither a psychologist nor a brickmason, but a man

days.title: The Waste Land I: The Burial of the Dead
days.challenge: Track distinct voices and recurring motifs across abrupt transitions.
days.focus: Rebirth made painful, failed prediction, and the city as a crowd of the dead.
days.context: The poem opens by splicing seasonal reflection, memory, prophecy, and a London crowd. Marie’s German line asserts Lithuanian origin and German identity; the Wagner fragments evoke longing and an empty sea. Read for recurring images before trying to resolve every allusion.
days.contentNote: Includes death, a corpse imagined in a garden, and religious allusions. Foreign-language fragments are given as printed in the 1922 edition, including its misprints “Der Heimai zu,” and “Od’.”

excerpt.locator: Complete verse section I. THE BURIAL OF THE DEAD, 1922 Boni and Liveright edition; begins “APRIL is the cruellest month, breeding Lilacs out of”; ends “dig it up again! “You! hypocrite lecteur!—mon semblable,—mon frère!””.

blocks.text: I. THE BURIAL OF THE DEAD

APRIL is the cruellest month, breeding
Lilacs out of the dead land, mixing
Memory and desire, stirring
Dull roots with spring rain.
Winter kept us warm, covering
Earth in forgetful snow, feeding
A little life with dried tubers.
Summer surprised us, coming over the Starnbergersee
With a shower of rain; we stopped in the colonnade,
And went on in sunlight, into the Hofgarten,
And drank coffee, and talked for an hour.
Bin gar keine Russin, stamm’ aus Litauen, echt deutsch.
And when we were children, staying at the archduke’s,
My cousin’s, he took me out on a sled,
And I was frightened. He said, Marie,
Marie, hold on tight. And down we went.
In the mountains, there you feel free.
I read, much of the night, and go south in the winter.

What are the roots that clutch, what branches grow
Out of this stony rubbish? Son of man,
You cannot say, or guess, for you know only
A heap of broken images, where the sun beats,
And the dead tree gives no shelter, the cricket no relief,
And the dry stone no sound of water. Only
There is shadow under this red rock,
(Come in under the shadow of this red rock),
And I will show you something different from either
Your shadow at morning striding behind you
Or your shadow at evening rising to meet you;
I will show you fear in a handful of dust.

Frisch weht der Wind
Der Heimai zu,
Mein Irisch Kind,
Wo weilest du?

“You gave me hyacinths first a year ago;
“They called me the hyacinth girl.”
—Yet when we came back, late, from the Hyacinth garden,
Your arms full, and your hair wet, I could not
Speak, and my eyes failed, I was neither
Living nor dead, and I knew nothing,
Looking into the heart of light, the silence.
Od’ und leer das Meer.

Madame Sosostris, famous clairvoyante,
Had a bad cold, nevertheless
Is known to be the wisest woman in Europe,
With a wicked pack of cards. Here, said she,
Is your card, the drowned Phoenician Sailor,
(Those are pearls that were his eyes. Look!)
Here is Belladonna, the Lady of the Rocks,
The lady of situations.
Here is the man with three staves, and here the Wheel,
And here is the one-eyed merchant, and this card,
Which is blank, is something he carries on his back,
Which I am forbidden to see. I do not find
The Hanged Man. Fear death by water.
I see crowds of people, walking round in a ring.
Thank you. If you see dear Mrs. Equitone,
Tell her I bring the horoscope myself:
One must be so careful these days.

Unreal City,
Under the brown fog of a winter dawn,
A crowd flowed over London Bridge, so many,
I had not thought death had undone so many.
Sighs, short and infrequent, were exhaled,
And each man fixed his eyes before his feet.
Flowed up the hill and down King William Street,
To where Saint Mary Woolnoth kept the hours
With a dead sound on the final stroke of nine.
There I saw one I knew, and stopped him, crying: “Stetson!
“You who were with me in the ships at Mylae!
“That corpse you planted last year in your garden,
“Has it begun to sprout? Will it bloom this year?
“Or has the sudden frost disturbed its bed?
“Oh keep the Dog far hence, that’s friend to men,
“Or with his nails he’ll dig it up again!
“You! hypocrite lecteur!—mon semblable,—mon frère!”

questions.prompt: Why can spring be cruel while winter seems protective?
facilitatorNotes: Spring stirs memory and desire that winter’s covering allowed to remain dormant. Renewal requires confronting what was suppressed.
evidence: Winter kept us warm

questions.prompt: How does Madame Sosostris’s ordinary cold complicate her prophetic reputation?
facilitatorNotes: The bodily detail and practical closing message puncture solemn authority without making all her images irrelevant; water and crowds return elsewhere.
evidence: Had a bad cold

questions.prompt: What does asking whether a planted corpse will bloom do to the opening seasonal pattern?
facilitatorNotes: The grotesque garden collapses burial and growth, making renewal frightening rather than simply hopeful. The direct address implicates a reader rather than leaving the scene distant.
evidence: Has it begun to sprout

days.title: The Waste Land II: A Game of Chess
days.challenge: Compare unequal social settings while evaluating the pressures inside quoted dialogue.
days.focus: Luxury, failed conversation, and demands placed on women’s bodies.
days.context: Recap of Part I: the poem moved from April’s painful renewal through memories, a fortune-teller’s cards, and a crowd flowing over London Bridge. After Part I’s fractured public voices, two interiors expose troubled relationships. The myth of Philomela concerns sexual violence and transformation into a bird. A pub’s closing call interrupts the second conversation; distinguish its quoted speaker from the poem’s author. The 1922 printing’s own readings are kept, including “dont,” “wont,” and “HURRY UP PLEASE ITS TIME.” In “The hot water at ten” the first printing shows a blank where the “a” failed to print; the letter is supplied from the Horace Liveright third printing of August 1928.
days.contentNote: Includes allusions to rape, reproductive coercion, abortion, and dangerous childbirth. Discussion should analyze the text without asking for personal disclosure.

excerpt.locator: Complete verse section II. A GAME OF CHESS, 1922 Boni and Liveright edition; begins “THE Chair she sat in, like a burnished throne,”; ends “ladies, good night, sweet ladies, good night, good night.”.

blocks.text: II. A GAME OF CHESS

THE Chair she sat in, like a burnished throne,
Glowed on the marble, where the glass
Held up by standards wrought with fruited vines
From which a golden Cupidon peeped out
(Another hid his eyes behind his wing)
Doubled the flames of sevenbranched candelabra
Reflecting light upon the table as
The glitter of her jewels rose to meet it,
From satin cases poured in rich profusion;
In vials of ivory and coloured glass
Unstoppered, lurked her strange synthetic perfumes,
Unguent, powdered, or liquid—troubled, confused
And drowned the sense in odours; stirred by the air
That freshened from the window, these ascended
In fattening the prolonged candle-flames,
Flung their smoke into the laquearia,
Stirring the pattern on the coffered ceiling.
Huge sea-wood fed with copper
Burned green and orange, framed by the coloured stone,
In which sad light a carvèd dolphin swam.
Above the antique mantel was displayed
As though a window gave upon the sylvan scene
The change of Philomel, by the barbarous king
So rudely forced; yet there the nightingale
Filled all the desert with inviolable voice
And still she cried, and still the world pursues,
“Jug Jug” to dirty ears.
And other withered stumps of time
Were told upon the walls; staring forms
Leaned out, leaning, hushing the room enclosed.
Footsteps shuffled on the stair.
Under the firelight, under the brush, her hair
Spread out in fiery points
Glowed into words, then would be savagely still.

“My nerves are bad tonight. Yes, bad. Stay with me.
“Speak to me. Why do you never speak. Speak.
“What are you thinking of? What thinking? What?
“I never know what you are thinking. Think.”

I think we are in rats’ alley
Where the dead men lost their bones.

“What is that noise?”
The wind under the door.
“What is that noise now? What is the wind doing?”
Nothing again nothing.
“Do
“You know nothing? Do you see nothing? Do you remember
“Nothing?”
I remember
Those are pearls that were his eyes.
“Are you alive, or not? Is there nothing in your head?”
But
O O O O that Shakespeherian Rag—
It’s so elegant
So intelligent
“What shall I do now? What shall I do?”
“I shall rush out as I am, and walk the street
“With my hair down, so. What shall we do tomorrow?
“What shall we ever do?”
The hot water at ten.
And if it rains, a closed car at four.
And we shall play a game of chess,
Pressing lidless eyes and waiting for a knock upon the door.

When Lil’s husband got demobbed, I said—
I didn’t mince my words, I said to her myself,
HURRY UP PLEASE ITS TIME
Now Albert’s coming back, make yourself a bit smart.
He’ll want to know what you done with that money he gave you
To get yourself some teeth. He did, I was there.
You have them all out, Lil, and get a nice set,
He said, I swear, I can’t bear to look at you.
And no more can’t I, I said, and think of poor Albert,
He’s been in the army four years, he wants a good time,
And if you dont give it him, there’s others will, I said.
Oh is there, she said. Something o’ that, I said.
Then I’ll know who to thank, she said, and give me a straight look.
HURRY UP PLEASE ITS TIME
If you dont like it you can get on with it, I said,
Others can pick and choose if you can’t.
But if Albert makes off, it wont be for lack of telling.
You ought to be ashamed, I said, to look so antique.
(And her only thirty-one.)
I can’t help it, she said, pulling a long face,
It’s them pills I took, to bring it off, she said.
(She’s had five already, and nearly died of young George.)
The chemist said it would be alright, but I’ve never been the same.
You are a proper fool, I said.
Well, if Albert wont leave you alone, there it is, I said,
What you get married for if you dont want children?
HURRY UP PLEASE ITS TIME
Well, that Sunday Albert was home, they had a hot gammon,
And they asked me in to dinner, to get the beauty of it hot—
HURRY UP PLEASE ITS TIME
HURRY UP PLEASE ITS TIME
Goonight Bill. Goonight Lou. Goonight May. Goonight.
Ta ta. Goonight. Goonight.
Good night, ladies, good night, sweet ladies, good night, good night.

questions.prompt: Why does the richly furnished room feel oppressive rather than secure?
facilitatorNotes: Perfumes confuse and drown the senses, flames multiply, and staring forms crowd the walls. Abundance intensifies enclosure.
evidence: drowned the sense in odours

questions.prompt: What separates the command to speak from actual communication in the first dialogue?
facilitatorNotes: Questions repeat, responses are fragmented or inward, and routine plans replace understanding. Being physically together does not ensure exchange.
evidence: Why do you never speak

questions.prompt: How does the pub refrain alter the account of Lil’s suffering?
facilitatorNotes: Closing time cuts through a speaker’s judgmental advice, imposing urgency and routine on reproductive and marital distress. The advice need not be accepted as the poem’s ethical position.
evidence: HURRY UP PLEASE ITS TIME

days.title: The Waste Land III: The Fire Sermon
days.challenge: Distinguish a witness’s perception from a character’s self-serving interpretation.
days.focus: Mechanical routines, sexual indifference, and broken cultural memory.
days.context: Recap of Part II: two interiors, an ornate room with an anxious couple and a London pub conversation about Lil and Albert, ended with the barman’s closing call. The river landscape becomes an industrial city and a sequence of strained encounters. Tiresias is a mythic seer associated with blindness and life in more than one sex. The closing fire imagery juxtaposes Buddhist and Christian traditions without making the poem a single doctrinal statement.
days.contentNote: Contains sexual coercion and assault, bodily imagery, and references to death. Treat the clerk’s interpretation of indifference as a claim the passage exposes, not consent.

excerpt.locator: Complete verse section III. THE FIRE SERMON, 1922 Boni and Liveright edition; begins “THE river’s tent is broken: the last fingers of”; ends “burning”.

blocks.text: III. THE FIRE SERMON

THE river’s tent is broken: the last fingers of leaf
Clutch and sink into the wet bank. The wind
Crosses the brown land, unheard. The nymphs are departed.
Sweet Thames, run softly, till I end my song.
The river bears no empty bottles, sandwich papers,
Silk handkerchiefs, cardboard boxes, cigarette ends
Or other testimony of summer nights. The nymphs are departed.
And their friends, the loitering heirs of city directors;
Departed, have left no addresses.
By the waters of Leman I sat down and wept . . .
Sweet Thames, run softly till I end my song,
Sweet Thames, run softly, for I speak not loud or long.
But at my back in a cold blast I hear
The rattle of the bones, and chuckle spread from ear to ear.

A rat crept softly through the vegetation
Dragging its slimy belly on the bank
While I was fishing in the dull canal
On a winter evening round behind the gashouse
Musing upon the king my brother’s wreck
And on the king my father’s death before him.
White bodies naked on the low damp ground
And bones cast in a little low dry garret,
Rattled by the rat’s foot only, year to year.
But at my back from time to time I hear
The sound of horns and motors, which shall bring
Sweeney to Mrs. Porter in the spring.
O the moon shone bright on Mrs. Porter
And on her daughter
They wash their feet in soda water
Et O ces voix d’enfants, chantant dans la coupole!

Twit twit twit
Jug jug jug jug jug jug
So rudely forc’d.
Tereu

Unreal City
Under the brown fog of a winter noon
Mr. Eugenides, the Smyrna merchant
Unshaven, with a pocket full of currants
C.i.f. London: documents at sight,
Asked me in demotic French
To luncheon at the Cannon Street Hotel
Followed by a weekend at the Metropole.

At the violet hour, when the eyes and back
Turn upward from the desk, when the human engine waits
Like a taxi throbbing waiting,
I Tiresias, though blind, throbbing between two lives,
Old man with wrinkled female breasts, can see
At the violet hour, the evening hour that strives
Homeward, and brings the sailor home from sea,
The typist home at teatime, clears her breakfast, lights
Her stove, and lays out food in tins.
Out of the window perilously spread
Her drying combinations touched by the sun’s last rays,
On the divan are piled (at night her bed)
Stockings, slippers, camisoles, and stays.
I Tiresias, old man with wrinkled dugs
Perceived the scene, and foretold the rest—
I too awaited the expected guest.
He, the young man carbuncular, arrives,
A small house agent’s clerk, with one bold stare,
One of the low on whom assurance sits
As a silk hat on a Bradford millionaire.
The time is now propitious, as he guesses,
The meal is ended, she is bored and tired,
Endeavours to engage her in caresses
Which still are unreproved, if undesired.
Flushed and decided, he assaults at once;
Exploring hands encounter no defence;
His vanity requires no response,
And makes a welcome of indifference.
(And I Tiresias have foresuffered all
Enacted on this same divan or bed;
I who have sat by Thebes below the wall
And walked among the lowest of the dead.)
Bestows one final patronising kiss,
And gropes his way, finding the stairs unlit . . .

She turns and looks a moment in the glass,
Hardly aware of her departed lover;
Her brain allows one half-formed thought to pass:
“Well now that’s done: and I’m glad it’s over.”
When lovely woman stoops to folly and
Paces about her room again, alone,
She smoothes her hair with automatic hand,
And puts a record on the gramophone.

“This music crept by me upon the waters”
And along the Strand, up Queen Victoria Street.
O City city, I can sometimes hear
Beside a public bar in Lower Thames Street,
The pleasant whining of a mandoline
And a clatter and a chatter from within
Where fishmen lounge at noon: where the walls
Of Magnus Martyr hold
Inexplicable splendour of Ionian white and gold.

The river sweats
Oil and tar
The barges drift
With the turning tide
Red sails
Wide
To leeward, swing on the heavy spar.
The barges wash
Drifting logs
Down Greenwich reach
Past the Isle of Dogs.
Weialala leia
Wallala leialala
Elizabeth and Leicester
Beating oars
The stern was formed
A gilded shell
Red and gold
The brisk swell
Rippled both shores
Southwest wind
Carried down stream
The peal of bells
White towers
Weialala leia
Wallala leialala

“Trams and dusty trees.
Highbury bore me. Richmond and Kew
Undid me. By Richmond I raised my knees
Supine on the floor of a narrow canoe.”

“My feet are at Moorgate, and my heart
Under my feet. After the event
He wept. He promised ‘a new start.’
I made no comment. What should I resent?”

“On Margate Sands.
I can connect
Nothing with nothing.
The broken fingernails of dirty hands.
My people humble people who expect
Nothing.”
la la
To Carthage then I came

Burning burning burning burning
O Lord Thou pluckest me out
O Lord Thou pluckest
burning

questions.prompt: How does the empty riverbank preserve traces of vanished social life?
