facilitatorNotes: The list names litter precisely while declaring it absent; departed nymphs and executives’ heirs mix pastoral mythology with modern privilege.
evidence: other testimony of summer nights

questions.prompt: What language prevents treating the clerk’s confidence as evidence of mutual desire?
facilitatorNotes: The typist is tired and indifferent; the narration explicitly distinguishes unopposed from desired contact and exposes his vanity. Absence of resistance is not welcome.
evidence: makes a welcome of indifference

questions.prompt: How do the gramophone and the later river song complicate the hope that music restores connection?
facilitatorNotes: One is automatic after a coercive encounter; later lyric fragments mingle oil, royal history, and damaged voices. Music persists without necessarily repairing experience.
evidence: puts a record on the gramophone

days.title: The Waste Land IV: Death by Water
days.challenge: Interpret a short section through its place within an extended poem.
days.focus: Death’s erasure of commercial identity and the turn from example to address.
days.context: Recap of Part III: Thames scenes, the typist’s encounter observed by Tiresias, and the closing “Burning burning burning.” This brief section returns to the drowned Phoenician anticipated in Part I. Read it several times, mapping its movements and its final change of addressee; use the earlier water warnings as remembered context.
days.contentNote: Describes drowning and a dead body without graphic detail.

excerpt.locator: Complete verse section IV. DEATH BY WATER, 1922 Boni and Liveright edition; begins “PHLEBAS the Phoenician, a fortnight dead, Forgot the cry”; ends “Phlebas, who was once handsome and tall as you.”.

blocks.text: IV. DEATH BY WATER

PHLEBAS the Phoenician, a fortnight dead,
Forgot the cry of gulls, and the deep sea swell
And the profit and loss.
A current under sea
Picked his bones in whispers. As he rose and fell
He passed the stages of his age and youth
Entering the whirlpool.
Gentile or Jew
O you who turn the wheel and look to windward,
Consider Phlebas, who was once handsome and tall as you.

questions.prompt: Why put “profit and loss” beside gulls and sea swell?
facilitatorNotes: Commerce and sensory life are equally forgotten. The pairing reduces the apparent dominance of accounting within a living person’s priorities.
evidence: And the profit and loss

questions.prompt: How does rising and falling in the current become a second kind of passage?
facilitatorNotes: Physical motion accompanies a retrospective passage through age and youth, making chronological identity unstable.
evidence: He passed the stages of his age and youth

questions.prompt: What changes when the poem addresses “you” at the wheel?
facilitatorNotes: The dead man becomes a warning to a living navigator; shared former beauty defeats any easy distance based on religion or apparent control.
evidence: who was once handsome and tall as you

days.title: The Waste Land V: What the Thunder Said
days.challenge: Build a qualified account of an ending whose sounds promise more than its events confirm.
days.focus: Thirst, isolated consciousness, and fragments used to resist ruin.
days.context: Recap of Part IV: ten lines on Phlebas the Phoenician, drowned, ending with an address to “Gentile or Jew.” The final section moves through thirst, ruined cities, possible rain, and fragments of inherited language. The Sanskrit commands are glossed by Eliot as give, sympathize, and control; the closing “Shantih” invokes peace. These clues aid reading but do not settle whether recovery occurs. The 1922 printing reads “Dead mount in mouth,” with the “a” of “mountain” missing; the later Liveright printings consulted (1928, 1930) read the same, so it is kept as printed.
days.contentNote: Includes death, apocalyptic imagery, and religious traditions in a modernist collage.

excerpt.locator: Complete verse section V. WHAT THE THUNDER SAID, 1922 Boni and Liveright edition; begins “AFTER the torchlight red on sweaty faces After the”; ends “Shantih shantih shantih”.

blocks.text: V. WHAT THE THUNDER SAID

AFTER the torchlight red on sweaty faces
After the frosty silence in the gardens
After the agony in stony places
The shouting and the crying
Prison and palace and reverberation
Of thunder of spring over distant mountains
He who was living is now dead
We who were living are now dying
With a little patience

Here is no water but only rock
Rock and no water and the sandy road
The road winding above among the mountains
Which are mountains of rock without water
If there were water we should stop and drink
Amongst the rock one cannot stop or think
Sweat is dry and feet are in the sand
If there were only water amongst the rock
Dead mount in mouth of carious teeth that cannot spit
Here one can neither stand nor lie nor sit
There is not even silence in the mountains
But dry sterile thunder without rain
There is not even solitude in the mountains
But red sullen faces sneer and snarl
From doors of mudcracked houses
If there were water
And no rock
If there were rock
And also water
And water
A spring
A pool among the rock
If there were the sound of water only
Not the cicada
And dry grass singing
But sound of water over a rock
Where the hermit-thrush sings in the pine trees
Drip drop drip drop drop drop drop
But there is no water

Who is the third who walks always beside you?
When I count, there are only you and I together
But when I look ahead up the white road
There is always another one walking beside you
Gliding wrapt in a brown mantle, hooded
I do not know whether a man or a woman
—But who is that on the other side of you?

What is that sound high in the air
Murmur of maternal lamentation
Who are those hooded hordes swarming
Over endless plains, stumbling in cracked earth
Ringed by the flat horizon only
What is the city over the mountains
Cracks and reforms and bursts in the violet air
Falling towers
Jerusalem Athens Alexandria
Vienna London
Unreal

A woman drew her long black hair out tight
And fiddled whisper music on those strings
And bats with baby faces in the violet light
Whistled, and beat their wings
And crawled head downward down a blackened wall
And upside down in air were towers
Tolling reminiscent bells, that kept the hours
And voices singing out of empty cisterns and exhausted wells.

In this decayed hole among the mountains
In the faint moonlight, the grass is singing
Over the tumbled graves, about the chapel
There is the empty chapel, only the wind’s home.
It has no windows, and the door swings,
Dry bones can harm no one.
Only a cock stood on the rooftree
Co co rico co co rico
In a flash of lightning. Then a damp gust
Bringing rain

Ganga was sunken, and the limp leaves
Waited for rain, while the black clouds
Gathered far distant, over Himavant.
The jungle crouched, humped in silence.
Then spoke the thunder
DA
Datta: what have we given?
My friend, blood shaking my heart
The awful daring of a moment’s surrender
Which an age of prudence can never retract
By this, and this only, we have existed
Which is not to be found in our obituaries
Or in memories draped by the beneficent spider
Or under seals broken by the lean solicitor
In our empty rooms
DA
Dayadhvam: I have heard the key
Turn in the door once and turn once only
We think of the key, each in his prison
Thinking of the key, each confirms a prison
Only at nightfall, aetherial rumours
Revive for a moment a broken Coriolanus
DA
Damyata: The boat responded
Gaily, to the hand expert with sail and oar
The sea was calm, your heart would have responded
Gaily, when invited, beating obedient
To controlling hands

I sat upon the shore
Fishing, with the arid plain behind me
Shall I at least set my lands in order?

London Bridge is falling down falling down falling down
Poi s’ascose nel foco che gli affina
Quando fiam ceu chelidon—O swallow swallow
Le Prince d’Aquitaine à la tour abolie
These fragments I have shored against my ruins
Why then Ile fit you. Hieronymo’s mad againe.
Datta. Dayadhvam. Damyata.
Shantih shantih shantih

questions.prompt: How does the imagined sound of water intensify its actual absence?
facilitatorNotes: The accumulating conditional wishes create an almost audible stream before “But there is no water” cancels fulfillment. Sound briefly supplies what the landscape withholds.
evidence: Drip drop drip drop drop drop drop

questions.prompt: Why does thinking about the key confirm a prison instead of opening it?
facilitatorNotes: Each person’s inward repetition may reinforce isolation; the image complicates a simple belief that recognizing confinement is enough to escape.
evidence: each confirms a prison

questions.prompt: Is shoring fragments against ruins a complete restoration?
facilitatorNotes: It can be an act of resistance or provisional order, while the fragments and question about setting lands in order keep repair incomplete. The ending’s peace is an invocation, not a demonstrated social transformation.
evidence: These fragments I have shored against my ruins

days.title: Compensation: What counts as success? (excerpt)
days.challenge: Identify an argument’s hidden premise before evaluating its conclusion.
days.focus: A challenge to a sermon that postpones justice to another life.
days.context: Emerson recalls an ambition to write about compensation and a sermon that sharpened his disagreement about worldly success.
days.contentNote: This 1907 transcription retains nineteenth-century gendered language and bracketed reference numbers. The source’s editorial endnotes are not included; the questions depend on the supplied essay text.

excerpt.locator: Compensation, opening six prose paragraphs; complete source paragraphs 133–138 in the saved paragraph index; opens “Ever since I was a boy, I have wished to write a discourse on Compensation: for it seemed ”; closes “of Compensation; happy beyond my expectation, if I shall truly draw the smallest arc of this circle.”.

questions.prompt: Why call tools, transactions, and greetings documents?
facilitatorNotes: He treats ordinary experience as material from which a moral account can be read. This broadens evidence beyond formal theology.
evidence: the tools in our hands, the bread in our basket

questions.prompt: What premise does Emerson reject in the preacher’s contrast between wicked success and virtuous misery?
facilitatorNotes: The sermon accepts wealth and status as the standard of success. Emerson argues that a different moral standard changes the diagnosis before any future compensation is considered.
evidence: the immense concession that the bad are successful

questions.prompt: What is the force of imagining champagne as a future reward?
facilitatorNotes: The reductive example exposes how the sermon could make virtue deferred access to the pleasures it supposedly rejects. Readers can evaluate whether this is a fair consequence or an exaggerated caricature.
evidence: venison and champagne?

days.title: Why teacher training could not wait — excerpt
days.challenge: Test an apparently orderly proposal against historical constraints and institutional dependencies.
days.focus: The difference between abstract sequence and feasible implementation.
days.context: Du Bois reviews a criticism that manual training should have preceded literacy and higher schooling, then reconstructs why the actual sequence developed differently.
days.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement. Historical racial terminology, generalisations and the author’s reported viewpoints are retained for critical reading, not adopted as the site’s voice. Includes paternalistic historical descriptions of communities and capacity, to be read critically.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, Of the Training of Black Men, the criticism of educational sequence through the development of training schools; UNC transcription of second edition, June1,1903, pp. 94–97; selected paragraphs corresponding to original PG indexes 197–200. Opening “Especially has criticism been directed against the former educational efforts to aid the N”; closing “civilization among a people whose ignorance was not simply of letters, but of life itself.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Du Bois call the proposed order logically complete but historically impossible?
facilitatorNotes: The neat progression assumes teachers and cooperation that did not exist in sufficient numbers. The practical need to train teachers makes advanced institutions a prerequisite for expanding basic schooling.
evidence: That a system logically so complete was historically impossible

questions.prompt: How does the long catalogue of segregated spaces support the educational argument?
facilitatorNotes: It shows that separation is not confined to classrooms or elite social life. A pervasive divided society blocks the everyday leadership and training on which the alternative plan would rely.
evidence: in hospitals and graveyards

questions.prompt: What evidence does he use to defend the institutions, and what additional question could a careful reader ask about it?
facilitatorNotes: He cites trained teachers, reduced illiteracy and the development of further schools. A reader can ask how the figures were obtained or how quality varied without ignoring that these are concrete outcome claims.
evidence: in a single generation they put thirty thousand black teachers in the South

days.title: Compensation: Balance as a universal claim (excerpt)
days.challenge: Evaluate the movement from physical examples to broad moral and political claims.
days.focus: The explanatory reach and possible limits of an extended analogy.
days.context: Emerson assembles paired forces and apparent tradeoffs to argue that advantage always carries a cost.
days.contentNote: This 1907 transcription retains nineteenth-century gendered language and bracketed reference numbers. The source’s editorial endnotes are not included; the questions depend on the supplied essay text. Contains historical scientific simplifications, climate generalizations, and claims about political oppression that readers should critically test.

excerpt.locator: Compensation, polarity through political checks; complete source paragraphs 139–144 in the saved paragraph index; opens “POLARITY, or action and reaction, we meet in every part of nature; in darkness and lig”; closes “pots of Egypt, history honestly confesses that man must have been as free as culture could make him.”.

questions.prompt: How do the needle and the breathing body prepare the claim about human gains and losses?
facilitatorNotes: They establish a pattern of complementary or opposing processes that he then extends to life. Their role is analogical; readers should ask what additional evidence the moral extension would need.
evidence: each thing is a half

questions.prompt: What hidden costs complicate the farmer’s picture of the presidency?
facilitatorNotes: Public position may consume peace and independence while requiring submission to less visible powers. The example distinguishes a conspicuous appearance from actual control.
evidence: the President has paid dear for his White House.

questions.prompt: Do the examples of taxation, harsh penalties, and mild penalties prove that every injustice corrects itself?
facilitatorNotes: They suggest mechanisms of resistance or unintended consequences, but do not establish an exceptionless law. A reasoned response can grant the examples while questioning the universal assurance.
evidence: Though no checks to a new evil appear, the checks exist

days.title: The Sorrow Songs as historical witness — excerpt
days.challenge: Distinguish personal response, historical narrative and a claim about what art can testify to.
days.focus: Cultural memory, misrepresentation and the authority of song.
days.context: Du Bois explains the musical phrases placed before chapters of his book and recalls the Fisk Jubilee Singers. The selection discusses music in prose; listening to an external recording is not required.
days.contentNote: This 1903 text discusses racism and the aftermath of enslavement. Historical racial terminology, generalisations and the author’s reported viewpoints are retained for critical reading, not adopted as the site’s voice. Contains a racial slur in a reported newspaper insult, period cultural stereotypes, and references to enslavement and deprivation.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XIV, Of the Sorrow Songs, opening six prose paragraphs; UNC transcription of second edition, June1,1903, pp. 250–253; selected paragraphs corresponding to original PG indexes 479–484. Opening “THEY that walked in darkness sang songs in the olden days--Sorrow Songs--for they were wea”; closing “ suffering and unvoiced longing toward a truer world, of misty wanderings and hidden ways.”.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for Jubilee Hall to seem made of songs rather than only bricks?
facilitatorNotes: The image connects the building to the singers’ work, fundraising and inherited voices. The later tour narrative gives material grounding to what first appears a purely emotional metaphor.
evidence: To me Jubilee Hall seemed ever made of the songs themselves

questions.prompt: How does the reversal in which the children teach George White to sing change the account of education?
facilitatorNotes: It presents knowledge moving from the children to their teacher as well as in the conventional direction. Their music becomes an achievement he learns to recognise and bring to audiences.
evidence: And then they taught him to sing

questions.prompt: Why does Du Bois concede limited technical knowledge of music before calling the songs a witness?
facilitatorNotes: He locates his interpretive authority in understanding human experience and history rather than specialist terminology. Readers can assess that claim and the limits of using art as evidence without reducing the songs to statistics.
evidence: these songs are the articulate message of the slave to the world

days.title: Walden: Owning a landscape (excerpt)
days.challenge: Follow the shifts between literal purchase, imagined ownership, and aesthetic value.
days.focus: The distinction between possessing land and enjoying it.
days.context: Thoreau recalls surveying possible homes and almost purchasing a farm, then revises the usual definition of wealth.
days.contentNote: Nineteenth-century prose retains original gendered wording, historical allusions, and historical spelling. This is a literary argument to examine, not a universal prescription for how to live. Includes a dismissive generalization about wives.

excerpt.locator: Where I Lived, and What I Lived For, opening six paragraphs; 1854 scan-backed chapter transcription, complete paragraphs 1–6; opens “At a certain season of our life we are accustomed to consider every spot as the possible s”; closes “ uncommitted. It makes but little difference whether you are committed to a farm or the county jail.”. Source: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Walden_(1854)_Thoreau/Where_I_Lived,_and_What_I_Lived_for

questions.prompt: How can he become rich without damaging his poverty?
facilitatorNotes: He gains imagined experience and enjoyment of the landscape without acquiring the financial obligations of ownership. The paradox exposes competing meanings of possession.
evidence: a rich man without any damage to my poverty.

questions.prompt: Why does the poet get the cream while the farmer keeps skimmed milk?
facilitatorNotes: The metaphor values perception and imaginative transformation above a deed. A reader can question the dismissal of agricultural work while explaining this reversal.
evidence: left the farmer only the skimmed milk.

questions.prompt: Why are the owner’s improvements a reason to hurry, rather than an added attraction?
facilitatorNotes: Clearing rocks and old trees would remove the neglected features Thoreau prizes. His desired crop is an experience of the place that cultivation might diminish.
evidence: if I could only afford to let it alone.

days.title: A river that moves the map — excerpt
days.challenge: Distinguish reported measurements, inferences, comparisons and comic personification.
days.focus: The challenge a changing river poses to seemingly stable human boundaries.
days.context: Twain introduces the Mississippi through measurements and examples of its changes. His figures and geographical claims are presented as historical assertions, not an updated reference account.
days.contentNote: Historical memoir and humour; judgments, measurements and language belong to the nineteenth-century narrator and should not be treated as current factual guidance. Includes a brief reference to slavery and state boundaries.

excerpt.locator: Chapter1, The River and Its History, opening ten prose paragraphs; source paragraph indexes 79–88, opening “THE Mississippi is well worth reading about. It is”, closing “few more of them further along in the book.”.

questions.prompt: How do the comparisons with European rivers and countries make the opening claims more than a list of numbers?
facilitatorNotes: The comparisons translate unfamiliar magnitudes into named geographical units and build an impression of exceptional scale. A reader can recognise that rhetorical purpose while still asking how the measurements were obtained.
evidence: The area of its drainage-basin is as great as the combined areas

questions.prompt: What assumption makes the apparently effortless calculation of the new land’s age possible?
facilitatorNotes: It treats a recent rate of land formation as representative of the entire process. The confident phrase invites scrutiny of whether deposition and conditions remained constant across such a long interval.
evidence: without any trouble at all--one hundred and twenty thousand years.

questions.prompt: Why does a cutoff matter to people who have not moved their homes?
facilitatorNotes: A changed course alters access, relative position and potentially jurisdiction. Twain turns physical geography into a question about institutions built around a natural boundary.
evidence: A cut-off plays havoc with boundary lines and jurisdictions

days.title: Sparkles from the Wheel
days.challenge: Evaluate a speaker’s aesthetic response to another person’s work.
days.focus: A small shared spectacle within the moving city.
days.context: A city observer pauses with children beside a knife-grinder. Follow the changes in pace and sound, and consider whether beauty makes the worker more visible or obscures his labor.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “Sparkles from the Wheel”, Walt Whitman Archive ppp.00707, poem elementppp.00919; begins “WHERE the city's ceaseless crowd moves on the livelong”; ends “in tiny showers of gold, Sparkles from the wheel.”.

blocks.text: SPARKLES FROM THE WHEEL.

WHERE the city's ceaseless crowd moves on the livelong day,
Withdrawn I join a group of children watching, I pause aside with them.

By the curb toward the edge of the flagging,
A knife-grinder works at his wheel sharpening a great knife,
Bending over he carefully holds it to the stone, by foot and knee,
With measur'd tread he turns rapidly, as he presses with light but firm hand,
Forth issue then in copious golden jets,
Sparkles from the wheel.

The scene and all its belongings, how they seize and affect me,
The sad sharp-chinn'd old man with worn clothes and broad shoulder-band of leather,
Myself effusing and fluid, a phantom curiously floating, now here absorb'd and arrested,
The group, (an unminded point set in a vast surrounding,)
The attentive, quiet children, the loud, proud, restive base of the streets,
The low hoarse purr of the whirling stone, the light-press'd blade,
Diffusing, dropping, sideways-darting, in tiny showers of gold,
Sparkles from the wheel.

questions.prompt: How does the opening separate the group from the crowd without leaving the city?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker pauses aside while the crowd continues; attention creates a temporary space inside ordinary urban movement.
evidence: I pause aside with them

questions.prompt: Why describe foot, knee, hand, and measured tread before naming the sparks?
facilitatorNotes: The beauty depends on coordinated skilled labor. The physical sequence prevents the spectacle from appearing without a maker.
evidence: With measur'd tread

questions.prompt: What tension remains between the golden sparks and the worker’s worn clothes?
facilitatorNotes: The scene offers beauty but not evidence that the worker’s material condition has improved. The observer is affected; the man continues working.
evidence: old man with worn clothes

days.title: Walden: An inward dawn (excerpt)
days.challenge: Distinguish literal morning from its sustained metaphorical use.
days.focus: Attention as a deliberate remaking of everyday life.
days.context: Thoreau describes his cabin’s apparent remoteness and turns daily awakening into a demand for conscious living.
days.contentNote: Nineteenth-century prose retains original gendered wording, historical allusions, and historical spelling. This is a literary argument to examine, not a universal prescription for how to live.

excerpt.locator: Where I Lived, and What I Lived For, horizon through deliberate living; 1854 scan-backed chapter transcription, complete paragraphs 13–19; opens “Though the view from my door was still more contracted, I did not feel crowded or confined”; closes “ewhat hastily concluded that it is the chief end of man here to "glorify God and enjoy him forever."”. Source: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Walden_(1854)_Thoreau/Where_I_Lived,_and_What_I_Lived_for

questions.prompt: How can a restricted view provide pasture for imagination?
facilitatorNotes: Physical extent and mental freedom are different measures. The distant landscapes and stars enlarge the meaning of his nearby home without claiming it literally moved.
evidence: There was pasture enough for my imagination.

questions.prompt: What changes when a mosquito’s hum becomes an Iliad and Odyssey?
facilitatorNotes: A minor familiar sound gains epic scale through attention. The comparison supports his claim that renewal depends on perception rather than prestigious occasions.
evidence: itself an Iliad and Odyssey in the air

questions.prompt: Why does the final paragraph allow life to prove mean as well as sublime?
facilitatorNotes: Deliberate living is presented as an inquiry whose result should be honestly reported. The desire for intensity does not formally guarantee a flattering conclusion.
evidence: if it proved to be mean

days.title: Ten minutes that awaken a town — excerpt
days.challenge: Track changes in pace, sound and the arrangement of a descriptive scene.
days.focus: Public spectacle and the manufacture of glamour.
days.context: Twain recalls the steamboat arrivals that shaped boyhood aspirations in Hannibal, Missouri. The narrator recreates the scene from adulthood. Twain’s footnote, marked ¹ as in the 1883 printing, follows the paragraph that cites it.
days.contentNote: Historical memoir and humour; judgments, measurements and language belong to the nineteenth-century narrator and should not be treated as current factual guidance. Includes historical racial terminology, reference to racist minstrel entertainment and descriptions of drunkenness.

excerpt.locator: Chapter4, The Boys’ Ambition, opening three prose paragraphs; source paragraph indexes 243–245, opening “WHEN I was a boy, there was but one”, closing “the town drunkard asleep by the skids once more.”.
excerpt.inlineReason: The night gives Twain’s footnote in the form its legacy edition declared, a superscript “¹” at the citing word and the note as a block beginning “¹”; the library work now gives the same note in the corpus note form, “[1]” and “[Footnote 1: …]”. The words are otherwise identical, so the night stays inline.

blocks.text: WHEN I was a boy, there was but one permanent ambition among my comrades in our village¹ on the west bank of the Mississippi River. That was, to be a steamboatman. We had transient ambitions of other sorts, but they were only transient. When a circus came and went, it left us all burning to become clowns; the first negro minstrel show that came to our section left us all suffering to try that kind of life; now and then we had a hope that if we lived and were good, God would permit us to be pirates. These ambitions faded out, each in its turn; but the ambition to be a steamboatman always remained.
¹ Hannibal, Missouri

Once a day a cheap, gaudy packet arrived upward from St. Louis, and another downward from Keokuk. Before these events, the day was glorious with expectancy; after them, the day was a dead and empty thing. Not only the boys, but the whole village, felt this. After all these years I can picture that old time to myself now, just as it was then: the white town drowsing in the sunshine of a summer's morning; the streets empty, or pretty nearly so; one or two clerks sitting in front of the Water Street stores, with their splint-bottomed chairs tilted back against the wall, chins on breasts, hats slouched over their faces, asleep--with shingle-shavings enough around to show what broke them down; a sow and a litter of pigs loafing along the sidewalk, doing a good business in watermelon rinds and seeds; two or three lonely little freight piles scattered about the 'levee;' a pile of 'skids' on the slope of the stone-paved wharf, and the fragrant town drunkard asleep in the shadow of them; two or three wood flats at the head of the wharf, but nobody to listen to the peaceful lapping of the wavelets against them; the great Mississippi, the majestic, the magnificent Mississippi, rolling its mile-wide tide along, shining in the sun; the dense forest away on the other side; the 'point' above the town, and the 'point' below, bounding the river-glimpse and turning it into a sort of sea, and withal a very still and brilliant and lonely one. Presently a film of dark smoke appears above one of those remote 'points;' instantly a negro drayman, famous for his quick eye and prodigious voice, lifts up the cry, 'S-t-e-a-m-boat a-comin'!' and the scene changes! The town drunkard stirs, the clerks wake up, a furious clatter of drays follows, every house and store pours out a human contribution, and all in a twinkling the dead town is alive and moving.

Drays, carts, men, boys, all go hurrying from many quarters to a common center, the wharf. Assembled there, the people fasten their eyes upon the coming boat as upon a wonder they are seeing for the first time. And the boat _is_ rather a handsome sight, too. She is long and sharp and trim and pretty; she has two tall, fancy-topped chimneys, with a gilded device of some kind swung between them; a fanciful pilot-house, a glass and 'gingerbread', perched on top of the 'texas' deck behind them; the paddle-boxes are gorgeous with a picture or with gilded rays above the boat's name; the boiler deck, the hurricane deck, and the texas deck are fenced and ornamented with clean white railings; there is a flag gallantly flying from the jack-staff; the furnace doors are open and the fires glaring bravely; the upper decks are black with passengers; the captain stands by the big bell, calm, imposing, the envy of all; great volumes of the blackest smoke are rolling and tumbling out of the chimneys--a husbanded grandeur created with a bit of pitch pine just before arriving at a town; the crew are grouped on the forecastle; the broad stage is run far out over the port bow, and an envied deckhand stands picturesquely on the end of it with a coil of rope in his hand; the pent steam is screaming through the gauge-cocks, the captain lifts his hand, a bell rings, the wheels stop; then they turn back, churning the water to foam, and the steamer is at rest. Then such a scramble as there is to get aboard, and to get ashore, and to take in freight and to discharge freight, all at one and the same time; and such a yelling and cursing as the mates facilitate it all with! Ten minutes later the steamer is under way again, with no flag on the jack-staff and no black smoke issuing from the chimneys. After ten more minutes the town is dead again, and the town drunkard asleep by the skids once more.

questions.prompt: How does the contrast between permanent and transient ambitions establish the steamboat’s special place?
facilitatorNotes: Other entertainments produce passing desires, but steamboating survives their arrival and departure. The contrast prepares the detailed scene as an explanation of an enduring attraction.
evidence: the ambition to be a steamboatman always remained.

questions.prompt: What changes in the prose when smoke becomes visible above the point?
facilitatorNotes: Still bodies and scattered objects give way to cries, clattering vehicles and converging crowds. The town becomes a collective actor whose movement is organised by the approaching vessel.
evidence: all in a twinkling the dead town is alive and moving.

questions.prompt: How does the explanation of the black smoke complicate the splendour of the arrival?
facilitatorNotes: The impressive smoke is deliberately produced shortly before reaching the town, then disappears after departure. The narrator exposes stagecraft within the remembered admiration rather than simply retracting that admiration.
evidence: a husbanded grandeur created with a bit of pitch pine

days.title: Crossing Brooklyn Ferry
days.challenge: Sustain a long lyric argument whose repetitions change their objects.
days.focus: Poetry’s attempt to create intimacy across historical distance.
days.context: A ferry crossing becomes an address to readers living in later centuries. Trace the nine numbered movements and mark where the speaker shifts from shared sights to shared moral vulnerability.
days.contentNote: Contains frank but non-graphic references to desire, moral failure, and bodily intimacy.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “Crossing Brooklyn Ferry”, Walt Whitman Archive ppp.00707, poem elementppp.00791; begins “1”; ends “or small, you furnish your parts toward the soul.”.

blocks.text: CROSSING BROOKLYN FERRY.

FLOOD-TIDE below me! I see you face to face!
Clouds of the west—sun there half an hour high—I see you also face to face.

Crowds of men and women attired in the usual costumes, how curious you are to me!
On the ferry-boats the hundreds and hundreds that cross, returning home, are more curious to me than you suppose,
And you that shall cross from shore to shore years hence are more to me, and more in my meditations, than you might suppose.

The impalpable sustenance of me from all things at all hours of the day,
The simple, compact, well-join'd scheme, myself disintegrated, every one disintegrated yet part of the scheme,
The similitudes of the past and those of the future,
The glories strung like beads on my smallest sights and hearings, on the walk in the street and the passage over the river,
The current rushing so swiftly and swimming with me far away,
The others that are to follow me, the ties between me and them,
The certainty of others, the life, love, sight, hearing of others.

Others will enter the gates of the ferry and cross from shore to shore,
Others will watch the run of the flood-tide,
Others will see the shipping of Manhattan north and west, and the heights of Brooklyn to the south and east,
Others will see the islands large and small;
Fifty years hence, others will see them as they cross, the sun half an hour high,
A hundred years hence, or ever so many hundred years hence, others will see them,
Will enjoy the sunset, the pouring-in of the flood-tide, the falling-back to the sea of the ebb-tide.

It avails not, time nor place—distance avails not,
I am with you, you men and women of a generation, or ever so many generations hence,
Just as you feel when you look on the river and sky, so I felt,
Just as any of you is one of a living crowd, I was one of a crowd,
Just as you are refresh'd by the gladness of the river and the bright flow, I was refresh'd,
Just as you stand and lean on the rail, yet hurry with the swift current, I stood yet was hurried,
Just as you look on the numberless masts of ships and the thick-stemm'd pipes of steamboats, I look'd.

I too many and many a time cross'd the river of old,
Watched the Twelfth-month sea-gulls, saw them high in the air floating with motionless wings, oscillating their bodies,
Saw how the glistening yellow lit up parts of their bodies and left the rest in strong shadow,
Saw the slow-wheeling circles and the gradual edging toward the south,
Saw the reflection of the summer sky in the water,
Had my eyes dazzled by the shimmering track of beams,
Look'd at the fine centrifugal spokes of light round the shape of my head in the sunlit water,
Look'd on the haze on the hills southward and south-westward,
Look'd on the vapor as it flew in fleeces tinged with violet,
Look'd toward the lower bay to notice the vessels arriving,
Saw their approach, saw aboard those that were near me,
Saw the white sails of schooners and sloops, saw the ships at anchor,
The sailors at work in the rigging or out astride the spars,
The round masts, the swinging motion of the hulls, the slender serpentine pennants,
The large and small steamers in motion, the pilots in their pilot-houses,
The white wake left by the passage, the quick tremulous whirl of the wheels,
The flags of all nations, the falling of them at sunset,
The scallop-edged waves in the twilight, the ladled cups, the frolicsome crests and glistening,
The stretch afar growing dimmer and dimmer, the gray walls of the granite storehouses by the docks,
On the river the shadowy group, the big steam-tug closely flank'd on each side by the barges, the hay-boat, the belated lighter,
On the neighboring shore the fires from the foundry chimneys burning high and glaringly into the night,
Casting their flicker of black contrasted with wild red and yellow light over the tops of houses, and down into the clefts of streets.

These and all else were to me the same as they are to you,
I loved well those cities, loved well the stately and rapid river,
The men and women I saw were all near to me,
Others the same—others who look back on me because I look'd forward to them,
(The time will come, though I stop here to-day and to-night.)

What is it then between us?
What is the count of the scores or hundreds of years between us?

Whatever it is, it avails not—distance avails not, and place avails not,
I too lived, Brooklyn of ample hills was mine,
I too walk'd the streets of Manhattan island, and bathed in the waters around it,
I too felt the curious abrupt questionings stir within me,
In the day among crowds of people sometimes they came upon me,
In my walks home late at night or as I lay in my bed they came upon me,
I too had been struck from the float forever held in solution,
I too had receiv'd identity by my body,
That I was I knew was of my body, and what I should be I knew I should be of my body.

It is not upon you alone the dark patches fall,
The dark threw its patches down upon me also,
The best I had done seem'd to me blank and suspicious,
My great thoughts as I supposed them, were they not in reality meagre?
Nor is it you alone who know what it is to be evil,
I am he who knew what it was to be evil,
I too knitted the old knot of contrariety,
Blabb'd, blush'd, resented, lied, stole, grudg'd,
Had guile, anger, lust, hot wishes I dared not speak,
Was wayward, vain, greedy, shallow, sly, cowardly, malignant,
The wolf, the snake, the hog, not wanting in me,
The cheating look, the frivolous word, the adulterous wish, not wanting,
Refusals, hates, postponements, meanness, laziness, none of these wanting,
Was one with the rest, the days and haps of the rest,
Was call'd by my nighest name by clear loud voices of young men as they saw me approaching or passing,
Felt their arms on my neck as I stood, or the negligent leaning of their flesh against me as I sat,
Saw many I loved in the street or ferry-boat or public assembly, yet never told them a word,
Lived the same life with the rest, the same old laughing, gnawing, sleeping,
Play'd the part that still looks back on the actor or actress,
The same old role, the role that is what we make it, as great as we like,
Or as small as we like, or both great and small.

Closer yet I approach you,
What thought you have of me now, I had as much of you—I laid in my stores in advance,
I consider'd long and seriously of you before you were born.

Who was to know what should come home to me?
Who knows but I am enjoying this?
Who knows, for all the distance, but I am as good as looking at you now, for all you cannot see me?

Ah, what can ever be more stately and admirable to me than mast-hemm'd Manhattan?
River and sunset and scallop-edg'd waves of flood-tide?
The sea-gulls oscillating their bodies, the hay-boat in the twilight, and the belated lighter?
What gods can exceed these that clasp me by the hand, and with voices I love call me promptly and loudly by my nighest name as I approach?
What is more subtle than this which ties me to the woman or man that looks in my face?
Which fuses me into you now, and pours my meaning into you?

We understand then do we not?
What I promis'd without mentioning it, have you not accepted?
What the study could not teach—what the preaching could not accomplish is accomplish'd, is it not?

Flow on, river! flow with the flood-tide, and ebb with the ebbtide!
Frolic on, crested and scallop-edg'd waves!
Gorgeous clouds of the sunset! drench with your splendor me, or the men and women generations after me!
Cross from shore to shore, countless crowds of passengers!
Stand up, tall masts of Mannahatta! stand up, beautiful hills of Brooklyn!
Throb, baffled and curious brain! throw out questions and answers!
Suspend here and everywhere, eternal float of solution!
Gaze, loving and thirsting eyes, in the house or street or public assembly!
Sound out, voices of young men! loudly and musically call me by my nighest name!
Live, old life! play the part that looks back on the actor or actress!
Play the old role, the role that is great or small according as one makes it!
Consider, you who peruse me, whether I may not in unknown ways be looking upon you;
Be firm, rail over the river, to support those who lean idly, yet haste with the hasting current;
Fly on, sea-birds! fly sideways, or wheel in large circles high in the air;
Receive the summer sky, you water, and faithfully hold it till all downcast eyes have time to take it from you!
Diverge, fine spokes of light, from the shape of my head, or any one's head, in the sunlit water!
Come on, ships from the lower bay! pass up or down, white-sail'd schooners, sloops, lighters!
Flaunt away, flags of all nations! be duly lower'd at sunset!
Burn high your fires, foundry chimneys! cast black shadows at nightfall! cast red and yellow light over the tops of the houses!
Appearances, now or henceforth, indicate what you are,
You necessary film, continue to envelop the soul,
About my body for me, and your body for you, be hung our divinest aromas,
Thrive, cities—bring your freight, bring your shows, ample and sufficient rivers,
Expand, being than which none else is perhaps more spiritual,
Keep your places, objects than which none else is more lasting.

You have waited, you always wait, you dumb, beautiful ministers,
We receive you with free sense at last, and are insatiate henceforward,
Not you any more shall be able to foil us, or withhold yourselves from us,
We use you, and do not cast you aside—we plant you permanently within us,
We fathom you not—we love you—there is perfection in you also,
You furnish your parts toward eternity,
Great or small, you furnish your parts toward the soul.

questions.prompt: How do the carefully named sights support the claim that distance “avails not”?
facilitatorNotes: Concrete recurrent experiences make contact imaginable. They are analogies across time, not proof that all future lives or cities remain identical.
evidence: Just as you feel when you look on the river and sky, so I felt

questions.prompt: Why introduce the speaker’s lies, grudges, and suspect thoughts into this celebratory poem?
facilitatorNotes: Confession broadens fellowship beyond ideal moments; future readers are offered recognition of weakness as well as beauty.
evidence: It is not upon you alone the dark patches fall

questions.prompt: How do the commands in section9 revise the earlier catalogue of observed things?
facilitatorNotes: Objects first remembered are now urged to continue serving future people. The poem transforms description into a participatory blessing while admitting that love exceeds complete understanding.
evidence: We fathom you not—we love you

days.title: Walden: Reading as athletic labor (excerpt)
days.challenge: Examine claims about cultural authority without confusing difficulty with automatic greatness.
days.focus: Deliberate reading and the distance between speaking a language and understanding literature.
days.context: Thoreau describes the books he kept near his cabin, acknowledges limited study time, and argues for demanding reading.
days.contentNote: Nineteenth-century prose retains original gendered wording, historical allusions, and historical spelling. This is a literary argument to examine, not a universal prescription for how to live. Includes elitist judgments and a gendered mother-tongue/father-tongue hierarchy.

excerpt.locator: Reading, opening four paragraphs; 1854 scan-backed chapter transcription, complete paragraphs 1–4; opens “With a little more deliberation in the choice of their pursuits, all men would perhaps bec”; closes “ the orator, speaks to the intellect and heart of mankind, to all in any age who can understand him.”. Source: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Walden_(1854)_Thoreau/Reading

questions.prompt: How does the admission about unfinished work qualify the ideal reading life?
facilitatorNotes: House-building and farming interrupt study; even this chosen setting does not remove practical limits. The prospect of future reading sustains him despite incomplete practice.
evidence: made more study impossible.

questions.prompt: Why compare reading with an athlete’s training?
facilitatorNotes: Understanding demands sustained intention and practiced capacities, not only access to words. The analogy makes reading active work rather than passive leisure.
evidence: a training such as the athletes underwent

questions.prompt: What assumption supports the contrast between an orator’s audience and a writer’s future readers?
facilitatorNotes: Written thought is imagined as less dependent on an immediate crowd and more durable across ages. Readers may challenge the hierarchy while explaining the stars-and-clouds comparison.
evidence: to all in any age who can understand him.

days.title: The admired and hated apprentice — excerpt
days.challenge: Read the distance between a jealous child’s reasoning and an adult’s comic presentation.
days.focus: Status, technical language and the desire to be seen.
days.context: After describing the steamboat’s hold on his village, Twain recalls a boy who becomes an apprentice engineer and returns with visible signs of status.
days.contentNote: Historical memoir and humour; judgments, measurements and language belong to the nineteenth-century narrator and should not be treated as current factual guidance. Includes a non-graphic boiler explosion, joking death wishes and exaggerated fantasies of violence.

excerpt.locator: Chapter4, The Boys’ Ambition, the narrator’s father through the chapter’s end; source paragraph indexes 246–248, opening “My father was a justice of the peace, and”, closing “of these mates and clerks and pay for them.”.

questions.prompt: Why do the narrator’s preferred occupations change from cabin-boy to deckhand?
facilitatorNotes: Both roles offer a conspicuous position from which former companions could see him. Visibility and admiration matter before he understands the work itself.
evidence: because he was particularly conspicuous.

questions.prompt: How do greasy clothes and technical vocabulary become social instruments for the returning apprentice?
facilitatorNotes: They display insider knowledge and occupational identity even when they are impractical or unintelligible to others. The narrator’s envy reveals how successfully the performance establishes rank.
evidence: as if he were so used to them that he forgot common people could not understand them.

questions.prompt: What does the reaction to the apprentice’s survival reveal about the child narrator’s moral reasoning?
facilitatorNotes: His disappointment that a rival gains even greater fame exposes jealousy disguised as a complaint against Providence. The adult voice allows the reader to see the selfishness the younger self does not acknowledge.
evidence: the partiality of Providence for an undeserving reptile

days.title: Vigil Strange I Kept on the Field One Night
days.challenge: Read the absence of outward tears alongside repeated acts of physical care.
days.focus: Private mourning and a remembered vigil outside public ceremony.
days.context: A soldier returns after battle to the body of a younger comrade. “Son” and “comrade” name a closeness whose precise biological relation the poem does not settle.
days.contentNote: A soldier mourns and buries a dead comrade; the death is not graphically described.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “Vigil Strange I Kept on the Field One Night”, Walt Whitman Archive ppp.00707, poem elementppp.00863; begins “VIGIL strange I kept on the field one night;”; ends “in his blanket, And buried him where he fell.”.

blocks.text: VIGIL STRANGE I KEPT ON THE FIELD ONE NIGHT.

VIGIL strange I kept on the field one night;
When you my son and my comrade dropt at my side that day,
One look I but gave which your dear eyes return'd with a look I shall never forget,
One touch of your hand to mine O boy, reach'd up as you lay on the ground,
Then onward I sped in the battle, the even-contested battle,
Till late in the night reliev'd to the place at last again I made my way,
Found you in death so cold dear comrade, found your body son of responding kisses, (never again on earth responding,)
Bared your face in the starlight, curious the scene, cool blew the moderate night-wind,
Long there and then in vigil I stood, dimly around me the battlefield spreading,
Vigil wondrous and vigil sweet there in the fragrant silent night,
But not a tear fell, not even a long-drawn sigh, long, long I gazed,
Then on the earth partially reclining sat by your side leaning my chin in my hands,
Passing sweet hours, immortal and mystic hours with you dearest comrade—not a tear, not a word,
Vigil of silence, love and death, vigil for you my son and my soldier,
As onward silently stars aloft, eastward new ones upward stole,
Vigil final for you brave boy, (I could not save you, swift was your death,
I faithfully loved you and cared for you living, I think we shall surely meet again,)
Till at latest lingering of the night, indeed just as the dawn appear'd,
My comrade I wrapt in his blanket, envelop'd well his form,
Folded the blanket well, tucking it carefully over head and carefully under feet,
And there and then and bathed by the rising sun, my son in his grave, in his rude-dug grave I deposited,
Ending my vigil strange with that, vigil of night and battle-field dim,
Vigil for boy of responding kisses, (never again on earth responding,)
Vigil for comrade swiftly slain, vigil I never forget, how as day brighten'd,
I rose from the chill ground and folded my soldier well in his blanket,
And buried him where he fell.

questions.prompt: Why does the first exchange consist only of a look and touch?
facilitatorNotes: Battle prevents sustained attention; the later vigil answers that hurried separation through extended presence.
evidence: One touch of your hand to mine

questions.prompt: Does the absence of tears imply emotional coldness?
facilitatorNotes: Repeated endearments, long watching, and remembered touch show intense attachment; the poem resists equating grief with one visible behavior.
evidence: not a tear, not a word

questions.prompt: What does the careful blanket-folding contribute that an abstract declaration of love would lack?
facilitatorNotes: Concrete, repeated care gives dignity to the dead body despite the rude grave and wartime haste.
evidence: tucking it carefully over head

days.title: Walden: Society in the rain (excerpt)
days.challenge: Track the difference between bodily isolation and felt companionship.
days.focus: Sensory attention and the speaker’s account of loneliness.
days.context: An evening walk, traces left by visitors, and a remembered rainstorm lead Thoreau to reconsider what counts as society.
days.contentNote: Nineteenth-century prose retains original gendered wording, historical allusions, and historical spelling. This is a literary argument to examine, not a universal prescription for how to live. The claims about melancholy are historical personal reflections, not an account of all experiences of depression or solitude.

excerpt.locator: Solitude, opening four prose paragraphs and their closing verse quotation; 1854 scan-backed chapter transcription, complete paragraphs 1–5; opens “This is a delicious evening, when the whole body is one sense, and imbibes delight through”; closes “imely consumes the sad; Few are their days in the land of the living, Beautiful daughter of Toscar."”. Source: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Walden_(1854)_Thoreau/Solitude

questions.prompt: How does rippled but not ruffled connect the speaker’s mood with the pond?
facilitatorNotes: Small movements coexist with underlying composure. The distinction allows active sounds and creatures to belong to repose rather than contradict it.
evidence: my serenity is rippled but not ruffled.

questions.prompt: What do the visitors’ improvised cards reveal about the apparently solitary home?
facilitatorNotes: Flowers, twigs, footprints, and smoke show continuing human contact. Solitude here is not complete separation from a social world.
evidence: a name in pencil on a yellow walnut leaf

questions.prompt: How does rain change the meaning of being alone for this narrator?
facilitatorNotes: The drops and surrounding sounds become signs of kinship, displacing his brief anxiety. Evaluate it as his reported experience; the sweeping claim about melancholy need not describe everyone.
evidence: an infinite and unaccountable friendliness

days.title: The romance acquires working hours — excerpt
days.challenge: Distinguish the young narrator’s confident assumptions from the practical explanations that overturn them.
days.focus: The invisible knowledge and labour behind an admired occupation.
days.context: Unable to carry out a proposed Amazon expedition, the young narrator persuades Horace Bixby to teach him Mississippi piloting. A cub is an apprentice.
days.contentNote: Historical memoir and humour; judgments, measurements and language belong to the nineteenth-century narrator and should not be treated as current factual guidance. Includes harsh verbal treatment of an apprentice.

excerpt.locator: Chapter6, A Cub-pilot’s Experience, the apprenticeship agreement through the first midnight summons; source paragraph indexes 265–275, opening “I soon discovered two things. One was that a”, closing “real and work-like about this new phase of it.”.

questions.prompt: What makes the description of learning the river as a small enterprise ironic?
facilitatorNotes: The task covers more than a thousand miles, and the older narrator states that awareness of its demands might have prevented him from beginning. The adjective belongs to youthful confidence, not a measured assessment.
evidence: the small enterprise of 'learning' twelve or thirteen hundred miles

questions.prompt: Why does Bixby steer near the shore when the apprentice thinks distance from it is safer?
facilitatorNotes: Upstream navigation uses the slower water near the bank; downstream travel benefits from the stronger current. The practical explanation shows why safety cannot be judged from distance alone.
evidence: the easy water was close ashore and the current outside

questions.prompt: How does the midnight summons revise the narrator’s idea of steamboat romance?
facilitatorNotes: He knew boats travelled at night without considering the workers required to operate them. The joke exposes a gap between noticing a service and imagining its human cost.
evidence: somebody had to get up out of a warm bed to run them.

days.title: The Artilleryman’s Vision
days.challenge: Distinguish present surroundings from an involuntary-seeming reconstruction of past violence.
days.focus: Sensory memory, excitement, and the distance between home and battle.
days.context: A former soldier lies awake beside his sleeping family as a battle returns in vivid mental images. The poem supplies an experience of war memory, not a clinical diagnosis.
days.contentNote: Includes combat, wounded soldiers, and disturbing recurrent war imagery.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “The Artilleryman’s Vision”, Walt Whitman Archive ppp.00707, poem elementppp.00875; begins “WHILE my wife at my side lies slumbering, and”; ends “bursting in air, and at night the vari-color'd rockets.”.

blocks.text: THE ARTILLERYMAN'S VISION.

WHILE my wife at my side lies slumbering, and the wars are over long,
And my head on the pillow rests at home, and the vacant midnight passes,
And through the stillness, through the dark, I hear, just hear, the breath of my infant,
There in the room as I wake from sleep this vision presses upon me;
The engagement opens there and then in fantasy unreal,
The skirmishers begin, they crawl cautiously ahead, I hear the irregular snap! snap!
I hear the sounds of the different missiles, the short t-h-t! t-h-t! of the rifle-balls,
I see the shells exploding leaving small white clouds, I hear the great shells shrieking as they pass,
The grape like the hum and whirr of wind through the trees, (tumultuous now the contest rages,)
All the scenes at the batteries rise in detail before me again,
The crashing and smoking, the pride of the men in their pieces,
The chief-gunner ranges and sights his piece and selects a fuse of the right time,
After firing I see him lean aside and look eagerly off to note the effect;
Elsewhere I hear the cry of a regiment charging, (the young colonel leads himself this time with brandish'd sword,)
I see the gaps cut by the enemy's volleys, (quickly fill'd up, no delay,)
I breathe the suffocating smoke, then the flat clouds hover low concealing all;
Now a strange lull for a few seconds, not a shot fired on either side,
Then resumed the chaos louder than ever, with eager calls and orders of officers,
While from some distant part of the field the wind wafts to my ears a shout of applause, (some special success,)
And ever the sound of the cannon far or near, (rousing even in dreams a devilish exultation and all the old mad joy in the depths of my soul,)
And ever the hastening of infantry shifting positions, batteries, cavalry, moving hither and thither,
(The falling, dying, I heed not, the wounded dripping and red I heed not, some to the rear are hobbling,)
Grime, heat, rush, aide-de-camps galloping by or on a full run,
With the patter of small arms, the warning s-s-t of the rifles, (these in my vision I hear or see,)
And bombs bursting in air, and at night the vari-color'd rockets.

questions.prompt: Why begin with the infant’s almost inaudible breath?
facilitatorNotes: The quiet domestic sound sharpens the contrast with the imagined cannon and establishes a present from which memory displaces attention.
evidence: the breath of my infant

questions.prompt: How do the imitated rifle sounds affect the account of remembering?
facilitatorNotes: They bring the reader into immediate auditory experience; the past seems enacted rather than reported at a safe distance.
evidence: the short t-h-t! t-h-t

questions.prompt: How does “devilish exultation” complicate a simple account of fear?
facilitatorNotes: The memory includes pride and battle excitement as well as violence; not attending to the wounded exposes the narrowed consciousness of combat.
evidence: a devilish exultation

days.title: Walden: Room for conversation (excerpt)
days.challenge: Interpret humorous exaggeration without losing the practical criticism beneath it.
days.focus: Hospitality measured by attention rather than buildings or dinners.
days.context: Thoreau explains how he welcomes company in a small cabin and why both space and simplicity matter to conversation.
days.contentNote: Nineteenth-century prose retains original gendered wording, historical allusions, and historical spelling. This is a literary argument to examine, not a universal prescription for how to live.

excerpt.locator: Visitors, opening five prose paragraphs and closing Spenser quotation; 1854 scan-backed chapter transcription, complete paragraphs 1–6; opens “I think that I love society as much as most, and am ready enough to fasten myself like a b”; closes “ was; Rest is their feast, and all things at their will: The noblest mind the best contentment has."”. Source: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Walden_(1854)_Thoreau/Visitors

questions.prompt: What do the three chairs make visible about forms of companionship?
facilitatorNotes: The increasing number represents solitude, friendship, and society. The limited furniture does not set a strict limit on guests; it exposes the mismatch between house size and social richness.
evidence: one for solitude, two for friendship, three for society.

questions.prompt: Why might closeness prevent people from hearing each other?
facilitatorNotes: The waves and sailing images suggest thought needs room to develop without interference. The paradox concerns reflective attention, beyond literal volume.
evidence: they break each other's undulations.

questions.prompt: How does the account of meals challenge customary hospitality?
facilitatorNotes: Ceremony and elaborate feeding can burden a visit or imply that it is troublesome. Thoreau values shared thought and contentment, though his joke about sympathizing with hungry guests invites debate.
evidence: You need not rest your reputation on the dinners you give.

days.title: A plantation found in the dark — excerpt
days.challenge: Follow changing judgments while distinguishing luck from knowledge the observer lacks.
days.focus: Evidence, expertise and resistance to revising a belief.
days.context: The apprentice has begun learning from Bixby but has failed to record the river landmarks. At night, he doubts that the experienced pilot can identify the required landing.
days.contentNote: Historical memoir and humour; judgments, measurements and language belong to the nineteenth-century narrator and should not be treated as current factual guidance. Contains a derogatory racial label and dialect representation, insults and reported profanity.

excerpt.locator: Chapter6, A Cub-pilot’s Experience, the first night’s navigation through arrival at Jones’s plantation; source paragraph indexes 276–310, opening “It was a rather dingy night, although a fair”, closing “And I fully believed it was an accident, too.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Bixby’s question about which end of the plantation first weaken the apprentice’s confidence in his own judgment?
facilitatorNotes: The question reveals precise local knowledge beyond simply recognising a plantation. Bixby also knows how the present water level affects access, so expertise includes changing conditions.
evidence: The stumps there are out of water at this stage

questions.prompt: How does the narrator’s prompt answer that he does not know produce comedy?
facilitatorNotes: He briefly congratulates himself for the speed of a reply when the relevant issue is its content. The mismatch dramatises how far he remains from understanding what a pilot must know.
evidence: I was gratified to be able to answer promptly, and I did.

questions.prompt: What evidence challenges the final claim that the successful landing was accidental?
facilitatorNotes: Bixby predicts the landing, identifies its usable end and manages the approach before confirmation from shore. The narrator calls this luck because accepting expertise would require revising his beliefs and learning obligations.
evidence: And I fully believed it was an accident, too.

days.title: Dirge for Two Veterans
days.challenge: Connect stanza shape, changing light, and a procession’s approach.
days.focus: Public ritual transformed into personal participation in mourning.
days.context: A father and son are being buried together after falling in battle. Read the short opening and closing lines of each stanza aloud alongside the longer middle lines.
days.contentNote: A funeral poem for two soldiers killed in battle.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “Dirge for Two Veterans”, Walt Whitman Archive ppp.00707, poem elementppp.00872; begins “THE last sunbeam Lightly falls from the finish'd Sabbath,”; ends “my soldiers, my veterans, My heart gives you love.”.

blocks.text: DIRGE FOR TWO VETERANS.

THE last sunbeam
Lightly falls from the finish'd Sabbath,
On the pavement here, and there beyond it is looking,
Down a new-made double grave.

LO, the moon ascending,
Up from the east the silvery round moon,
Beautiful over the house-tops, ghastly, phantom moon,
Immense and silent moon.

I see a sad procession,
And I hear the sound of coming full-key'd bugles,
All the channels of the city streets they're flooding,
As with voices and with tears.

I hear the great drums pounding,
And the small drums steady whirring,
And every blow of the great convulsive drums,
Strikes me through and through.

For the son is brought with the father,
(In the foremost ranks of the fierce assault they fell,
Two veterans son and father dropt together,
And the double grave awaits them.)

Now nearer blow the bugles,
And the drums strike more convulsive,
And the daylight o'er the pavement quite has faded,
And the strong dead-march enwraps me.

In the eastern sky up-buoying,
The sorrowful vast phantom moves illumin'd,
('Tis some mother's large transparent face,
In heaven brighter growing.)

O strong dead-march you please me!
O moon immense with your silvery face you soothe me!
O my soldiers twain! O my veterans passing to burial!
What I have I also give you.

The moon gives you light,
And the bugles and the drums give you music,
And my heart, O my soldiers, my veterans,
My heart gives you love.

questions.prompt: How does the poem move from seeing a grave to being enveloped by the march?
facilitatorNotes: The procession approaches through city streets while sound intensifies; the speaker becomes physically and emotionally involved.
evidence: the strong dead-march enwraps me

questions.prompt: What does imagining the moon as a mother’s face add to the father-and-son burial?
facilitatorNotes: It brings maternal mourning into a military ceremony and links the immense sky to intimate family loss.
evidence: some mother's large transparent face

questions.prompt: Why end with the heart’s gift after listing light and music?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker contributes something distinct from the environment and instruments; parallel phrasing makes love part of the collective tribute.
evidence: My heart gives you love

days.title: Walden: Two fishes with one hook (excerpt)
days.challenge: Follow shifts between physical sensation and speculative thought.
days.focus: Silence, sound, and an encounter that interrupts abstraction.
days.context: These three paragraphs recount company on the pond and solitary fishing at night, linking practical food gathering with reflection.
days.contentNote: Nineteenth-century prose retains original gendered wording, historical allusions, and historical spelling. This is a literary argument to examine, not a universal prescription for how to live. Includes catching fish for food.

excerpt.locator: The Ponds, companionship and night-fishing paragraphs; 1854 scan-backed chapter transcription, complete paragraphs 2–4; opens “Occasionally, after my hoeing was done for the day, I joined some impatient companion who ”; closes “ into this element which was scarcely more dense. Thus I caught two fishes as it were with one hook.”. Source: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Walden_(1854)_Thoreau/The_Ponds

questions.prompt: How can the older fisherman’s limited hearing contribute to unbroken harmony?
facilitatorNotes: The companionship depends on shared activity and compatible silence rather than verbal agreement. The psalm and philosophy coexist without being argued into identity.
evidence: far more pleasing to remember than if it had been carried on by speech.

questions.prompt: What changes between the earlier adventures and the present home by the shore?
facilitatorNotes: The earlier visits end in a return to human haunts; the narrator now inhabits the place that once seemed an excursion. The contrast makes familiarity part of the changing experience.
evidence: But now I had made my home by the shore.

questions.prompt: What are the two fishes caught by one hook?
facilitatorNotes: One is literal food; the other is an insight or renewed contact with nature when the line interrupts cosmic speculation. Several formulations are defensible if grounded in that movement.
evidence: interrupt your dreams and link you to Nature again.

days.title: The crossing after sunset — excerpt
days.challenge: Track suspense through clocks, silences, sounding calls and controlled action.
days.focus: How a narrator renders expert performance through an inexperienced witness.
days.context: Bixby’s boat has visiting pilots aboard. A delay threatens to force a stop before the dangerous Hat Island crossing, and the apprentice watches how experienced observers respond.
days.contentNote: Historical memoir and humour; judgments, measurements and language belong to the nineteenth-century narrator and should not be treated as current factual guidance. Describes danger to a vessel and potential loss of life, without injury.

excerpt.locator: Chapter7, A Daring Deed, the grounding delay through the chapter’s end; source paragraph indexes 332–358, opening “Next morning I felt pretty rusty and low-spirited. We”, closing “the Shadow of Death, but he's a lightning pilot!'”.

questions.prompt: Why is the approaching darkness more serious downstream than upstream?
facilitatorNotes: A strong current pushes the boat toward hazards and reduces its ability to resist them. The explanation supplies a practical basis for the suspense rather than relying only on frightened language.
evidence: a boat was too nearly helpless, with a stiff current pushing behind her

questions.prompt: How do the unused door handle and the gathered pilots convey a decision without explicit explanation?
facilitatorNotes: The guests expect a stop, then notice that Bixby continues. Their suspended departures and silent convergence let the reader infer both surprise and growing admiration.
evidence: let the knob turn back again.

questions.prompt: Why does the account add the invisible wreck after the successful crossing?
facilitatorNotes: The retrospective detail makes the precision and stakes intelligible to a reader who could not see the route. It converts general admiration into an explanation of what had to be avoided.
evidence: a sunken and invisible wreck

days.title: Reconciliation
days.challenge: Explain a shift from universal claims to a single intimate action.
days.focus: Recognition of shared humanity and the limits of posthumous reconciliation.
days.context: The speaker approaches an enemy’s coffin. Reread the long opening statement and the final sequence of movements; consider what can and cannot be reconciled after death.
days.contentNote: An enemy soldier’s body lies in a coffin; the speaker kisses the dead face.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “Reconciliation”, Walt Whitman Archive ppp.00707, poem elementppp.00882; begins “WORD over all, beautiful as the sky, Beautiful that”; ends “with my lips the white face in the coffin.”.

blocks.text: RECONCILIATION.

WORD over all, beautiful as the sky,
Beautiful that war and all its deeds of carnage must in time be utterly lost,
That the hands of the sisters Death and Night incessantly softly wash again, and ever again, this soil'd world;
For my enemy is dead, a man divine as myself is dead,
I look where he lies white-faced and still in the coffin—I draw near,
Bend down and touch lightly with my lips the white face in the coffin.

questions.prompt: What is unsettling about calling the loss of all war’s deeds beautiful?
facilitatorNotes: The claim can welcome an end to violence but also raises a question about forgetting suffering. The poem’s tender gesture does not settle that tension.
evidence: war and all its deeds of carnage

questions.prompt: What changes when “enemy” is followed by “a man divine as myself”?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker recognizes equal value across the wartime division; the comparison undermines a hierarchy of worthy and unworthy bodies.
evidence: a man divine as myself

questions.prompt: Why move from looking to drawing near, bending, and kissing?
facilitatorNotes: Each action reduces distance and makes recognition bodily. Yet the enemy cannot answer, so the scene is not a reciprocal agreement.
evidence: I draw near

days.title: Walden: What color is the pond? (excerpt)
days.challenge: Organize a long descriptive paragraph by changing viewpoint, light, distance, and proposed causes.
days.focus: Observation as a correction to a single fixed description.
days.context: Thoreau offers a sustained account of Walden’s dimensions, clarity, and changing colors.
days.contentNote: Nineteenth-century prose retains original gendered wording, historical allusions, and historical spelling. This is a literary argument to examine, not a universal prescription for how to live. Historical physical explanations should be read as the author’s observations and hypotheses.

excerpt.locator: The Ponds, complete paragraph beginning “The scenery of Walden”; 1854 scan-backed chapter transcription, complete paragraphs 5–5; opens “The scenery of Walden is on a humble scale, and, though very beautiful, does not approach ”; closes “agnified and distorted withal, produces a monstrous effect, making fit studies for a Michael Angelo.”. Source: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Walden_(1854)_Thoreau/The_Ponds

questions.prompt: Why is one color name inadequate for Walden?
facilitatorNotes: Distance, angle, weather, depth, and background alter the perceived color. Distinguish these conditions instead of treating the descriptions as careless contradictions.
evidence: one when viewed at a distance, and another, more proper, close at hand.

questions.prompt: What observation challenges the explanation that green water merely reflects leaves?
facilitatorNotes: The same green appears against a sand-bank and before leaves unfold. He proposes a different color mixture while marking it as tentative.
evidence: before the leaves are expanded

questions.prompt: How does the glass of water limit what the speaker can claim?
facilitatorNotes: A small quantity looks colorless even though the pond is green or blue. He explicitly leaves the required quantity untested, allowing description and uncertainty to coexist.
evidence: How large a body of Walden water would be required to reflect a green tint I have never proved.

days.title: The shape in the pilot’s head — excerpt
days.challenge: Distinguish changes in appearance from physical changes in the riverbank.
days.focus: Mental models, perception and the need to update knowledge.
days.context: The apprentice has memorised many place names and begins to feel capable. Bixby introduces another demand: recognising and navigating the river under different conditions of light. Twain’s footnote, marked ¹ as in the 1883 printing, follows the paragraph that cites it.
days.contentNote: Historical memoir and humour; judgments, measurements and language belong to the nineteenth-century narrator and should not be treated as current factual guidance. Includes figurative death wishes and a teacher’s insults.

excerpt.locator: Chapter8, Perplexing Lessons, opening through the changing banks report; source paragraph indexes 361–379, opening “At the end of what seemed a tedious while,”, closing “over again in a different way every twenty-four hours.”.
excerpt.inlineReason: The night gives Twain’s footnote in the form its legacy edition declared, a superscript “¹” at the citing word and the note as a block beginning “¹”; the library work now gives the same note in the corpus note form, “[1]” and “[Footnote 1: …]”. The words are otherwise identical, so the night stays inline.

blocks.text: At the end of what seemed a tedious while, I had managed to pack my head full of islands, towns, bars, 'points,' and bends; and a curiously inanimate mass of lumber it was, too. However, inasmuch as I could shut my eyes and reel off a good long string of these names without leaving out more than ten miles of river in every fifty, I began to feel that I could take a boat down to New Orleans if I could make her skip those little gaps. But of course my complacency could hardly get start enough to lift my nose a trifle into the air, before Mr. Bixby would think of something to fetch it down again. One day he turned on me suddenly with this settler--
'What is the shape of Walnut Bend?'

He might as well have asked me my grandmother's opinion of protoplasm. I reflected respectfully, and then said I didn't know it had any particular shape. My gunpowdery chief went off with a bang, of course, and then went on loading and firing until he was out of adjectives.

I had learned long ago that he only carried just so many rounds of ammunition, and was sure to subside into a very placable and even remorseful old smooth-bore as soon as they were all gone. That word 'old' is merely affectionate; he was not more than thirty-four. I waited. By and by he said--

'My boy, you've got to know the _shape _of the river perfectly. It is all there is left to steer by on a very dark night. Everything else is blotted out and gone. But mind you, it hasn't the same shape in the night that it has in the day-time.'
'How on earth am I ever going to learn it, then?'
'How do you follow a hall at home in the dark. Because you know the shape of it. You can't see it.'
'Do you mean to say that I've got to know all the million trifling variations of shape in the banks of this interminable river as well as I know the shape of the front hall at home?'
'On my honor, you've got to know them _better _than any man ever did know the shapes of the halls in his own house.'
'I wish I was dead!'
'Now I don't want to discourage you, but--'
'Well, pile it on me; I might as well have it now as another time.'

'You see, this has got to be learned; there isn't any getting around it. A clear starlight night throws such heavy shadows that if you didn't know the shape of a shore perfectly you would claw away from every bunch of timber, because you would take the black shadow of it for a solid cape; and you see you would be getting scared to death every fifteen minutes by the watch. You would be fifty yards from shore all the time when you ought to be within fifty feet of it. You can't see a snag in one of those shadows, but you know exactly where it is, and the shape of the river tells you when you are coming to it. Then there's your pitch-dark night; the river is a very different shape on a pitch-dark night from what it is on a starlight night. All shores seem to be straight lines, then, and mighty dim ones, too; and you'd _run _them for straight lines only you know better.
