days.context: Jurgis, Jonas, and Marija seek their first packinghouse jobs; Antanas is older and less physically strong. Attend to the difference between the family’s celebration and the narrator’s hints about what employers value.
days.contentNote: Includes slaughterhouse blood and entrails, employment discrimination, and a racist comparison to Indigenous people.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 4, Wikisource 1906 Doubleday, Page transcription, chapter paragraphs 2–5; begins “Promptly at seven the next morning Jurgis reported for”; ends “saying that it would be his turn another day.”.

questions.prompt: Why does waiting obediently at the door expose Jurgis to abuse?
facilitatorNotes: He follows the instruction as he understands it, while the boss assumes unstated knowledge. The mismatch reveals unequal control over communication.
evidence: had meant for him to enter, but had not said this

questions.prompt: How does the narrator’s comment about the forelady interrupt Marija’s triumph?
facilitatorNotes: It forecasts that good nature and strength make her exploitable, a meaning she does not yet understand.
evidence: as she was destined to understand later

questions.prompt: What makes Antanas’s brave smile painful rather than simply optimistic?
facilitatorNotes: The family has been told that the industry discards even long-serving older men; he is seeking entry to a system that rejects his age.
evidence: the men who had grown old in their own service

days.title: Walden: Alone in a crowded place (excerpt)
days.challenge: Separate physical proximity, intellectual attention, and emotional loneliness.
days.focus: Solitude as a state of mind and a possible cost to relationships.
days.context: Thoreau describes the mind’s observing capacity, then compares a student’s concentration with a farmer’s work.
days.contentNote: Nineteenth-century prose retains original gendered wording, historical allusions, and historical spelling. This is a literary argument to examine, not a universal prescription for how to live. The final anecdote mentions dying of exhaustion and hunger; the passage’s views of solitude are the author’s, not universal mental-health claims.

excerpt.locator: Solitude, reflective doubleness through imagined company; 1854 scan-backed chapter transcription, complete paragraphs 12–15; opens “With thinking we may be beside ourselves in a sane sense. By a conscious effort of the min”; closes “lly cheered by a like but more normal and natural society, and come to know that we are never alone.”. Source: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Walden_(1854)_Thoreau/Solitude

questions.prompt: What danger accompanies the ability to observe one’s own experience from a distance?
facilitatorNotes: Detachment may support reflection but also weaken responsiveness to friends. The paragraph explicitly qualifies its own attraction to the spectator position.
evidence: This doubleness may easily make us poor neighbors and friends sometimes.

questions.prompt: How does the student-farmer comparison expose a double standard?
facilitatorNotes: The farmer accepts absorbed outdoor work but mistakes intellectual work indoors for inactivity or loneliness. Both can labor in a field, literally or metaphorically, and both seek recreation afterward.
evidence: the student, though in the house, is still at work in his field

questions.prompt: What does the stale-cheese image criticize about frequent meetings?
facilitatorNotes: Repetition without fresh experience can reduce the value people bring to one another. A response can question his proposed sparsity of society while identifying the criticism of empty routine.
evidence: a new taste of that old musty cheese

days.title: The association that helped its opponents first — excerpt
days.challenge: Follow the economic incentives of apprentices, employers, current members and nonmembers.
days.focus: How an organisation can create benefits it does not initially capture.
days.context: Twain moves from individual expertise to the pilots’ attempt to organise collectively. This excerpt ends during the association’s difficult early period, before later reversals.
days.contentNote: Historical memoir and humour; judgments, measurements and language belong to the nineteenth-century narrator and should not be treated as current factual guidance. Includes dismissive historical language about older and disabled workers.

excerpt.locator: Chapter15, The Pilots’ Monopoly, the association’s introduction through its initial exclusion from employment; source paragraph indexes 643–647, opening “Having now set forth in detail the nature of”, closing “which that poor martyr had to put up with.”.

questions.prompt: Why can growing steamboat business coincide with falling pilot wages in this account?
facilitatorNotes: The number of trained or licensed pilots rises as existing pilots take apprentices for unpaid help and family advancement. Increased labour supply can outpace increased demand.
evidence: Too many pilots were being 'made.'

questions.prompt: How do the pension and burial provisions shape early membership?
facilitatorNotes: They attract unemployed and retired pilots who gain immediate support, while employed pilots can avoid dues and risk. The benefits make membership valuable for people the employers are least eager to hire.
evidence: the initiation fee was only twelve dollars, and no dues required from the unemployed.

questions.prompt: Why do the outsiders’ rising wages create a particularly sharp irony?
facilitatorNotes: Excluding association members reduces the available workforce and helps raise nonmembers’ pay, while the organisers remain without jobs. The outcome initially appears to reward ridicule rather than solidarity.
evidence: not one of whom received a particle of benefit from it.

days.title: The Jungle: the house advertisement
days.challenge: Separate an advertisement’s emotional associations from its stated financial terms.
days.focus: Domestic aspiration and the assumptions hidden in a plausible budget.
days.context: After finding work, the family studies an advertisement for a home. Read its visual and verbal promises against the conditional language in their calculations.
days.contentNote: The narrator mocks Lithuanian words and makes assumptions about family roles; evaluate those as historical rhetoric.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 4, Wikisource 1906 Doubleday, Page transcription, chapter paragraphs 6–8; begins “Their good luck, they felt, had given them the”; ends “of this district should live the way they did.”.

questions.prompt: Why combine a house with embracing spouses, a cradle, and a cherub?
facilitatorNotes: The placard sells safety, family love, and a future as well as a building; the details invite emotional identification before scrutiny of terms.
evidence: a smiling cherub

questions.prompt: What uncertainty is concealed inside “if they had employment”?
facilitatorNotes: Their ability to keep paying depends on steady future earnings, which current success does not guarantee.
evidence: if they had employment

questions.prompt: How does the final mention of one day’s earnings qualify Jurgis’s assurance?
facilitatorNotes: It shows a long-term decision resting on a very brief prosperous experience; the narrator makes optimism intelligible but fragile.
evidence: a dollar and fifty-seven cents in a single day

days.title: Tender Buttons: Glass, glitter, and a cushion (selection)
days.challenge: Read once for sounds, again for repeated words, and a third time for relations between titles and descriptions.
days.focus: Difference and change inside apparently familiar domestic objects.
days.context: The opening three pieces of Objects make ordinary names the starting points for language that resists ordinary description. The reading time includes three passes and brief annotation.
days.contentNote: Experimental prose poetry uses disrupted grammar, unexpected associations, and repetition. No single hidden paraphrase is required; support interpretations with specific verbal patterns.

excerpt.locator: Objects, first three complete titled prose poems; complete source paragraphs 19–35 in the saved paragraph index; opens “A CARAFE, THAT IS A BLIND GLASS.”; closes “ is not like a same thing that has stripes, it is not even more hurt than that, it has a little top.”.

questions.prompt: What tension does blind glass create with spectacle and pointing in the opening piece?
facilitatorNotes: The title’s blocked vision meets words associated with seeing and indicating. Discuss how these cues complicate expectations that a named object will be transparently pictured.
evidence: an arrangement in a system to pointing

questions.prompt: How does the correction after There is no search affect the voice in Glazed Glitter?
facilitatorNotes: The assertion immediately gives way to renewed possibility. Repeated there is produces motion in the thinking voice even when a stable referent remains uncertain.
evidence: But there is, there is that hope

questions.prompt: What links the cushion’s cover with the repeated language of change?
facilitatorNotes: Cover, appearance, color, and costume make surfaces active sites of difference. A strong interpretation follows these recurrences without forcing every sentence into one literal cushion description.
evidence: Supposing you do not like to change

days.title: A shared information system changes the trade — excerpt
days.challenge: Trace how an information practice changes safety, bargaining power and employment.
days.focus: Collective knowledge and the costs of exclusion.
days.context: The pilots’ association has placed locked report boxes at river landings and supplied members with forms and keys. Members record changing channels; nonmembers cannot use the same system. Underwriters are insurers.
days.contentNote: Historical memoir and humour; judgments, measurements and language belong to the nineteenth-century narrator and should not be treated as current factual guidance. Describes vessel accidents without graphic injury.

excerpt.locator: Chapter15, The Pilots’ Monopoly, daily report forms through the underwriters’ decision; source paragraph indexes 668–675, opening “These blanks were filled up, day by day, as”, closing “their decision among themselves and upon plain business principles.”.

questions.prompt: What makes the sample report useful beyond its statement of water depth?
facilitatorNotes: It links depth to precise visual alignments, steering actions and newly observed hazards. A later pilot can act on the information, not merely learn that a crossing is difficult.
evidence: New snag just where you straighten down; go above it.

questions.prompt: How does the hundred-eyes comparison alter the earlier image of an individual pilot’s memory?
facilitatorNotes: Expertise now depends on coordinated observations by many people, made recent and accessible through reports. Individual skill remains necessary but no longer supplies all the relevant evidence alone.
evidence: a hundred sharp eyes to watch it for him

questions.prompt: Why do insurers become decisive without necessarily conspiring with the association?
facilitatorNotes: The reported difference in accident risk gives them a business reason to require association pilots. That safety incentive also increases the association’s power and disadvantages outsiders.
evidence: upon plain business principles.

days.title: The Jungle: reading the contract
days.challenge: Distinguish a contract’s formal validity from whether its consequences are understood.
days.focus: Language barriers, social pressure, and incomplete reassurance.
days.context: The family has agreed to consider a house purchase. Unable to leave work, Jurgis sends relatives with Jokubas to read the papers; they seek legal advice when the wording alarms them.
days.contentNote: Includes acute distress and Jurgis’s threat to kill the agent; the passage ends without an attack.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 4, Wikisource 1906 Doubleday, Page transcription, chapter paragraphs 16–29; begins “They were to come on the morrow, and he”; ends “stepmother in the next room, sobbing softly to themselves.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Elzbieta feel embarrassed about reading the agreement carefully?
facilitatorNotes: She fears that scrutiny insults the agent’s honesty, so politeness works against informed consent.
evidence: they doubted his honesty

questions.prompt: Does the lawyer greeting the agent by name prove a conspiracy?
facilitatorNotes: It understandably alarms the buyers, but acquaintance alone proves no collusion. Distinguish their fear from evidence the scene supplies.
evidence: greet the agent by his first name

questions.prompt: What danger remains inside the second lawyer’s reassuring explanation?
facilitatorNotes: The rental form makes eviction easier after missed payments. “So long as they paid” is a substantial condition rather than a guarantee of security.
evidence: to make it easier to turn the party out

days.title: Tender Buttons: A box, coffee, and darkening color (selection)
days.challenge: Compare sound-driven links with ordinary cause-and-effect syntax on three deliberate readings.
days.focus: How repetition and color disrupt an expected explanation.
days.context: These neighboring pieces move among containers, coffee, dirt, and elegance. Read the prose aloud softly on the second pass to hear its shifts.
days.contentNote: Experimental prose poetry uses disrupted grammar, unexpected associations, and repetition. No single hidden paraphrase is required; support interpretations with specific verbal patterns.

excerpt.locator: Objects, A Box through Nothing Elegant, four complete titled prose poems; complete source paragraphs 36–50 in the saved paragraph index; opens “A BOX.”; closes “ it, if inside is let in and there places change then certainly something is upright. It is earnest.”.

questions.prompt: How does the repeated out of form make the first Box sound explanatory while troubling ordinary explanation?
facilitatorNotes: The syntax promises causes and results, but kindness/redness and selection/cattle do not form obvious causal relations. Sound, association, and the promise of order become visible.
evidence: Out of kindness comes redness

questions.prompt: What happens as sight, slighter, simpler, and sounder recur in A Piece of Coffee?
facilitatorNotes: The sequence changes by sound as well as meaning, repeatedly suggesting a reason without stabilizing one. Readers should identify actual verbal transitions rather than label the whole piece random.
evidence: the same sight slighter

questions.prompt: How does the unfinished-sounding end of Coffee change the force of its repeated May sentences?
facilitatorNotes: Each qualification loosens certainty, and the final preposition leaves expectation suspended. The effect can be compared with the next poem’s confident makes statements.
evidence: May not be strange to.

days.title: A river a million miles long — excerpt
days.challenge: Distinguish arithmetic within a model from the assumptions that make a model applicable.
days.focus: Satire of confident conclusions drawn from a narrow range of evidence.
days.context: After discussing river travel, Twain explains cutoffs and constructs an intentionally absurd projection from reported changes in river length. The figures are historical source claims, not modern measurements.
days.contentNote: Historical memoir and humour; judgments, measurements and language belong to the nineteenth-century narrator and should not be treated as current factual guidance. Contains an implied threat against people who deliberately cut through a riverbank.

excerpt.locator: Chapter17, Cut-offs and Stephen, opening through the comic extrapolation; source paragraph indexes 703–709, opening “THESE dry details are of importance in one particular.”, closing “conjecture out of such a trifling investment of fact.”.

questions.prompt: How can a short ditch change the value of two plantations in opposite directions?
facilitatorNotes: A new channel brings one property to the navigable bank while leaving the other beside an abandoned course. The example shows that a physical shortcut redistributes economic advantage.
evidence: quadrupling its value

questions.prompt: Where does the projection move from reported past change to an unsupported assumption?
facilitatorNotes: It extends a recent average rate unchanged across immense past and future periods. The arithmetic does not establish that cutoffs could keep shortening a river without physical limits.
evidence: by what had occurred in a given time in the recent past

questions.prompt: How do the precise date next November and the shared mayor intensify the satire?
facilitatorNotes: They supply confident detail to impossible consequences, exposing the false certainty rather than correcting it with another measurement. The jokes target the disproportion between evidence and conjecture.
evidence: such wholesale returns of conjecture out of such a trifling investment of fact.

days.title: The Jungle: speeding up the gang
days.challenge: Compare a general principle with the personal case that tests it.
days.focus: Competition, collective action, and the first cracks in self-reliance.
days.context: Jurgis begins to learn how the work pace is set and why fellow workers organize. His father’s job search introduces a case that his confidence in individual effort cannot easily explain.
days.contentNote: Contains demeaning comparisons, class hostility, and a brief reference to childhood beating.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 5, Wikisource 1906 Doubleday, Page transcription, chapter paragraphs 8–16; begins “This was the first time in his life that”; ends “strange things kept coming to Jurgis's notice every day!”.

questions.prompt: Why are specially paid pacemakers important to the whole line?
facilitatorNotes: Their speed sets a standard others must match, while waiting applicants make refusal risky; the system is coordinated rather than each worker choosing a pace.
evidence: speeding up the gang

questions.prompt: How does Antanas expose an inconsistency in Jurgis’s judgment of less able workers?
facilitatorNotes: Jurgis dismisses the unfit in general but knows his father’s reliability and labor history. Affection reveals facts his general rule excludes.
evidence: consigned the unfit to destruction

questions.prompt: How does Jurgis avoid Tamoszius’s explanation at the end?
facilitatorNotes: He attacks the speaker as weak and lazy instead of answering the account of incentives and graft. Yet repeated strange events make that dismissal unstable.
evidence: Tamoszius was simply another of the grumblers

days.title: Tender Buttons: Containers, counts, and a plate (selection)
days.challenge: Reread for counting, conditional syntax, and the unstable relation between a container and its contents.
days.focus: Domestic arrangement as a problem made by language.
days.context: Umbrella, cloak, stamp, box, and plate supply a sequence of titles. The reading time includes marking repeated structural words and testing two possible emphases aloud.
days.contentNote: Experimental prose poetry uses disrupted grammar, unexpected associations, and repetition. No single hidden paraphrase is required; support interpretations with specific verbal patterns. Includes references to cigarettes as objects.

excerpt.locator: Objects, Mildred’s Umbrella through A Plate, five complete titled prose poems; complete source paragraphs 51–72 in the saved paragraph index; opens “MILDRED'S UMBRELLA.”; closes “hange to incline each way, a plan that has that excess and that break is the one that shows filling.”.

questions.prompt: How does the Red Stamp sentence delay arriving at a result?
facilitatorNotes: Its accumulating if-clauses repeatedly reopen the condition before reaching the catalogue. The syntax can make classification feel necessary and also difficult to complete.
evidence: they need a catalogue.

questions.prompt: What changes when one, two, and three are placed on the table?
facilitatorNotes: The repeated structure promises countable order, but shifting covers, lengths, and corners complicate it. Explain the effect of the sequence without treating it as a solvable arithmetic puzzle.
evidence: The three are on the table.

questions.prompt: How does the lamp-and-cake series complicate a single sign of glass?
facilitatorNotes: The expanding list repeatedly denies exclusivity, making meaning relational and provisional. Compare that expansion with the apparent boundedness of a plate.
evidence: The lamp and the cake and the cover

days.title: How the Other Half Lives: the boundary line (excerpt)
days.challenge: Separate quoted testimony and statistics from Riis’s own moral verdicts in a reformer’s opening argument.
days.focus: How a documentary investigation defines its audience, its evidence, and its assignment of blame.
days.context: Jacob A. Riis (1849–1914), a Danish immigrant who became a New York police reporter, published this documentary study of Lower Manhattan tenement housing in 1890, illustrated with his own photographs. The Introduction states the book’s central claim before the chapters that follow tour the tenements.
days.contentNote: Riis writes as a reformer addressing comfortable readers; his generalizations about poverty, crime, and the morals of the poor reflect 1890 assumptions that the discussion examines rather than adopts.

excerpt.locator: Introduction, first four paragraphs (PG 45502); opens “Long ago it was said that "one half of the world does not know how the other half lives."”; closes “even though it gives it claim upon our utmost patience and tenderest charity.”.

questions.prompt: Riis opens with a proverb and then says the half “on top” did not know “because it did not care.” What does he say finally forced the “upper half” to inquire, and what does that suggest about the readers he expects?
facilitatorNotes: Crowding and violent “upheavals” made ignorance too costly; the implied readers are the comfortable half, addressed through self-interest as well as conscience. Some students will hear a warning about social unrest, others a deliberate shaming of indifference; both readings fit the wording.
evidence: It did not know because it did not care.
then the upper half fell to inquiring what was the matter

questions.prompt: Riis cites the Prison Association secretary’s testimony and figures such as “three-fourths” of New Yorkers and “thirty-seven thousand” tenant houses. Which claims in these paragraphs rest on quoted records or numbers, and which are Riis’s own interpretation?
facilitatorNotes: The counts and the testimony are presented as public record; conclusions such as “there is no way out” and “a storm-centre forever of our civilization” are Riis’s. Note that the testimony’s link between homes and crime is itself an interpretation by the witness, quoted rather than demonstrated. A student may reasonably trust the statistics while questioning the causal claims.
evidence: To-day three-fourths of its people live in the tenements
drawn from the plain public records
the boundary line of the Other Half lies through the tenements

questions.prompt: In the last paragraph Riis calls the tenement system “the child of our own wrong,” yet lists the tenements as “hot-beds of the epidemics” and “nurseries of pauperism and crime.” Does his language present tenement dwellers as victims, as threats, or as both? Whom does he hold responsible?
facilitatorNotes: Responsibility falls on “the community that gave it no other choice” and on “public neglect and private greed.” Yet the list of evils casts the poor as a source of contagion endangering the rich. Students may defend this double rhetoric as persuasive strategy or criticize it as dehumanizing; ask which words carry each effect.
evidence: the community that gave it no other choice
That we have to own it the child of our own wrong does not excuse it
the evil offspring of public neglect and private greed

days.title: The Jungle: the house’s former occupants
days.challenge: Assess an embedded narrator’s evidence without treating vividness as verification.
days.focus: Repeated dispossession and the uncertain authority of neighborhood memory.
days.context: An older neighbor recounts the history of the family’s house and the neighborhood’s successive immigrant groups. Her knowledge includes firsthand experience, hearsay, and uncertain explanation.
days.contentNote: Includes workplace deaths, child neglect and abuse, tuberculosis, ethnic stereotyping, and a threat of collective violence.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 6, Wikisource 1906 Doubleday, Page transcription, chapter paragraphs 5–13; begins “About a block away from them there lived another”; ends “red stain wherever he had spit upon the floor.”.

questions.prompt: Why can paying for a house count as “fooling the company”?
facilitatorNotes: The neighbor argues that repeated default and resale are built into the business model; successful payment frustrates expected repeat profit.
evidence: fooling the company

questions.prompt: What evidence and limitations support her account of the house’s cost?
facilitatorNotes: She cites her son’s connection to a contractor and her own similar purchase; these are relevant but partly secondhand, not a presented ledger.
evidence: her son belonged to a political organization with a contractor

questions.prompt: How does the discussion of consumption mix causal reasoning with superstition?
facilitatorNotes: Construction and rooms are suspected alongside the phase of the moon, while childhood illness is explicitly uncertain. The narrator finally asks how much is exaggeration.
evidence: How much of it was exaggeration—who could tell

days.title: Tender Buttons: Lines, colors, and a chair (selection)
days.challenge: Use multiple readings to hear repeated questions and trace claims about lines, placement, and boundaries.
days.focus: What an object title seems to promise and what the prose actually supplies.
days.context: These pieces pass from a bottle to clothes, a piano, and a chair. Annotate the words that appear to define an object and those that unsettle the definition.
days.contentNote: Experimental prose poetry uses disrupted grammar, unexpected associations, and repetition. No single hidden paraphrase is required; support interpretations with specific verbal patterns.

excerpt.locator: Objects, A Seltzer Bottle through A Chair, six complete titled prose poems; complete source paragraphs 73–94 in the saved paragraph index; opens “A SELTZER BOTTLE.”; closes “y, if it is why is there no complexion, why is there no rubbing, why is there no special protection.”.

questions.prompt: How does the recurring suppose in A Seltzer Bottle affect the status of its description?
facilitatorNotes: It creates a chain of hypothetical constructions rather than a settled inventory. The final present and constant arrive after language that has made the object difficult to fix.
evidence: suppose the rest of the message is mixed

questions.prompt: What does the repeated final line of A Long Dress do that a conventional color description would not?
facilitatorNotes: It makes distinction itself the subject, repeating with a small change in emphasis. The preceding unstable color equations make the boundary line unusually important.
evidence: A line just distinguishes it.

questions.prompt: How do measurement, arrangement, and suitability shape A Chair without yielding a clear picture?
facilitatorNotes: They imply social and spatial rules around seating while withholding a straightforward visual portrait. A response should show how at least two repeated terms create this pressure.
evidence: Practice measurement, practice the sign

days.title: How the Other Half Lives: how the first tenements were made (excerpt)
days.challenge: Follow a historical narrative that weaves an 1857 legislative report’s language into the author’s own account.
days.focus: How property becomes “opportunity”: the economic logic of subdividing old houses.
days.context: Jacob A. Riis (1849–1914), a Danish immigrant who became a New York police reporter, published this documentary study of Lower Manhattan tenement housing in 1890, illustrated with his own photographs. Chapter I traces the tenement to the former homes of wealthy families near the East River, converted after the War of 1812 as trade and immigration swelled the city.
days.contentNote: Riis writes as a reformer addressing comfortable readers; his generalizations about poverty, crime, and the morals of the poor reflect 1890 assumptions that the discussion examines rather than adopts.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, Genesis of the Tenement, first three paragraphs (PG 45502); opens “The first tenement New York knew bore the mark of Cain from its birth”; closes “with here and there one of the original rear tenements.”.

questions.prompt: According to Riis and the report he quotes, how did the tenant-house change from “a real blessing” for the working poor into something the report calls “evils more destructive than wars”? Put the stages in order.
facilitatorNotes: Business growth made the old houses valuable; owners and agents partitioned large rooms “without regard to light or ventilation”; the dark bedroom appeared; rents were set high and repairs neglected. Some students will emphasize population pressure, others the owners’ choices; Riis includes both but weights the second.
evidence: the tenant-house became a real blessing to that class of industrious poor
the necessities of the poor became the opportunity of their wealthier neighbors
without regard to light or ventilation

questions.prompt: The report says landlords “urged the filthy habits of the tenants as an excuse.” How does Riis use this to answer the claim that tenants caused the conditions? Is the same report’s description of the tenants consistent with that answer?
facilitatorNotes: The report assigns responsibility to the owners’ tolerance of conditions. Yet it also calls tenants “loose in morals, improvident in habits, degraded,” so the document shifts blame while keeping contemptuous language. Students might instead read that phrase as a description of conditions rather than character; ask what the adjectives judge.
evidence: the proprietors frequently urged the filthy habits of the tenants as an excuse for the condition of their property
loose in morals, improvident in habits, degraded, and squalid as beggary itself

questions.prompt: In the last paragraph a Dutch burgher’s garden becomes “an alley” and “a ‘court.’” How does this single lot condense Riis’s history, and which short sentence states the motive behind every change?
facilitatorNotes: The before-and-after image (gate, shell-paved walk, extra stories added “another story, and another”) turns a citywide process into one visible place. The motive sentence is “It was rent the owner was after.” Some readers may detect nostalgia for an idealized Knickerbocker past; that tension is worth naming.
evidence: It was rent the owner was after
The shell-paved walk had become an alley

days.title: The Jungle: interest and a child’s wages
days.challenge: Follow financial details into an ethical consequence without assuming legal form ensures fairness.
days.focus: Hidden costs, child labor, and a calculation that restores hope at a price.
days.context: The family discovers a charge it had not understood in the house agreement. Its response reshapes Ona’s and Stanislovas’s work; track the causal chain from contract to household decision.
days.contentNote: Depicts exploitative child labor and dangerous working conditions.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 6, Wikisource 1906 Doubleday, Page transcription, chapter paragraphs 14–29; begins “And yet all these things were as nothing to”; ends “two were very much in love with each other.”.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a term being in the deed and the buyers knowing it?
facilitatorNotes: The text treats written inclusion as legally sufficient while showing practical non-understanding; the agent benefits from that gap.
evidence: They had not been intended to know it

questions.prompt: Why is the employer’s care to “comply with the law” ironic?
facilitatorNotes: A glance at a false age document allows the child to work; formal paperwork replaces attention to the child’s actual age and welfare.
evidence: the packers were very careful to comply with the law

questions.prompt: What does the final return to balanced figures leave out?
facilitatorNotes: The child’s wages cover interest, but the cost includes education, daylight, health, and constrained future. Financial equivalence is not an unchanged life.
evidence: just about as they had been before

days.title: Tender Buttons: Showing, mending, and making a mark (selection)
days.challenge: Reread short pieces in sequence, tracking the repeated verbs show, mean, and change.
days.focus: The gap between seeing a sign and knowing what it establishes.
days.context: The sequence includes containers, cloth, water, paper, and a drawing. Its short units invite comparison rather than a search for one continuous plot.
days.contentNote: Experimental prose poetry uses disrupted grammar, unexpected associations, and repetition. No single hidden paraphrase is required; support interpretations with specific verbal patterns. Contains historical references to Japanese culture and gendered wording.

excerpt.locator: Objects, A Frightful Release through A Drawing, twelve complete titled prose poems; complete source paragraphs 95–122 in the saved paragraph index; opens “A FRIGHTFUL RELEASE.”; closes “s, best to make bitter, best to make the length tall and nothing broader, anything between the half.”.

questions.prompt: What does the purse’s chain establish, and what does the final limitation withhold?
facilitatorNotes: It shows openness but is denied wider explanatory power. The repeated showed directs attention to the limits of evidence within a seemingly simple description.
evidence: that is all that it showed.

questions.prompt: How does the shift from broken cup to broken plate disturb the account of mending?
facilitatorNotes: An apparent clarification changes the object instead of merely explaining it. The repair language can be read alongside the poem’s own unstable joins, without assuming a single symbolic solution.
evidence: that is to say a plate is broken

questions.prompt: What effect does best to say becoming best to show have in A Drawing?
facilitatorNotes: Verbal explanation moves toward visual marking, but neither settles the object’s meaning. The repetition gives the paragraph procedural energy while its instructions remain unusual.
evidence: best to say it best to show sudden places

days.title: How the Other Half Lives: what is a tenement? (excerpt)
days.challenge: Compare a legal definition, an official description, and the author’s own counts and predictions.
days.focus: Definitions as evidence, and the shift from documentation to warning.
days.context: Jacob A. Riis (1849–1914), a Danish immigrant who became a New York police reporter, published this documentary study of Lower Manhattan tenement housing in 1890, illustrated with his own photographs. Chapter II describes the public-health “awakening” of the 1860s, when fear of cholera led to a Board of Health that began regulating new buildings. This excerpt asks what that regulation achieved.
days.contentNote: Riis’s closing images of “mob-rule and wrath” reflect fears of urban unrest common among his middle-class readers; consider how they function as persuasion.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, The Awakening, from the paragraph beginning “The determined effort to head it off” to the end of the chapter (PG 45502), two illustration captions omitted; closes “what will the harvest be?”.

questions.prompt: Riis says the era of the air-shaft “has not solved the problem of housing the poor” but “has made good use of limited opportunities.” What did regulation control, and what did it leave untouched?
facilitatorNotes: Sanitary law governs new houses only; old buildings and overcrowding remain, and poverty “compels” crowding. Students may debate whether Riis’s claim that tenements “will exist in New York forever” is realism or resignation.
evidence: Over the new houses sanitary law exercises full control. But the old remain.
The outrageous overcrowding, too, remains.

questions.prompt: Riis gives both the law’s definition of a tenement and the description given when it was “last arraigned before the bar of public justice.” Why does he need both, and which details of the second matter most to his argument?
facilitatorNotes: The legal definition includes flats and apartment-houses “with which we have nothing to do,” so he narrows to the typical tenement: dark closets for bedrooms, no through ventilation, a saloon’s side-door. The courtroom metaphor treats the building as a defendant. Students may choose different details as most damning; ask them to justify the choice.
evidence: The law defines it as a house
a set of rooms consists of one or two dark closets, used as bedrooms
no direct through ventilation is possible

questions.prompt: The Crosby Street count of “101 adults and 91 children” now “no longer excites even passing attention.” How does Riis turn readers’ numbness to numbers into an argument, and how does the final paragraph’s warning change the kind of appeal he makes?
facilitatorNotes: If figures that once caused a sensation are now ignored, the problem has outgrown public outrage. The closing paragraph moves from sympathy to fear and self-interest, citing the Sub-Treasury’s guns and asking “what will the harvest be?” Some will call this prophetic urgency; others fearmongering about the poor.
evidence: It no longer excites even passing attention
hold them at their mercy in the day of mob-rule and wrath
what will the harvest be?

days.title: The Jungle: what respectable poetry leaves out
days.challenge: Connect concrete incidents to the narrator’s explicit argument about literary subject matter.
days.focus: The limits of personal protection and the representability of poverty.
days.context: The narrative returns to life after the wedding. A streetcar rule, adulterated goods, and an infestation turn the couple’s desire for security into repeated encounters with unequal power.
days.contentNote: Includes child mistreatment, illness, food contamination, and vermin. Claims about products belong to the historical novel, not present-day product information.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 7, Wikisource 1906 Doubleday, Page transcription, chapter paragraphs 2–11; begins “All summer long the family toiled, and in the”; ends “one more misery for the rest of their days.”.

questions.prompt: How does the transfer rule defeat Jurgis’s attempt to keep Ona dry?
facilitatorNotes: He pays for transport, but an undisclosed procedural requirement denies her transfer. Care and expenditure cannot control the company’s terms.
evidence: the passenger must ask for the transfer

questions.prompt: Why ask what knowing about adulteration would help if alternatives are unavailable?
facilitatorNotes: The question challenges the idea that information alone ensures consumer choice; poverty and location restrict practical options.
evidence: what good would it have done them

questions.prompt: What argument about literature emerges from the failed insect powder?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator insists that petty, humiliating suffering deserves attention even when it lacks conventional dignity or pathos. The scene tests a tradition of ennobling anguish.
evidence: not admitted into the vocabulary of poets

days.title: Tender Buttons: Surfaces and small transformations (selection)
days.challenge: Read the miniature pieces three times, comparing lists, commands, and repeated color words.
days.focus: Scale, surfaces, and the changing grammatical lives of ordinary names.
days.context: The sequence moves among weather, fabric, flowers, and colors. Read across the boundaries while preserving each printed title as a separate starting point.
days.contentNote: Experimental prose poetry uses disrupted grammar, unexpected associations, and repetition. No single hidden paraphrase is required; support interpretations with specific verbal patterns.

excerpt.locator: Objects, Water Raining through A Brown, sixteen complete titled prose poems; complete source paragraphs 123–155 in the saved paragraph index; opens “WATER RAINING.”; closes “A brown which is not liquid not more so is relaxed and yet there is a change, a news is pressing.”.

questions.prompt: How does A Petticoat compress a changing surface into a list?
facilitatorNotes: White, disgrace, ink, and rosy charm move between color, judgment, stain, and attraction without explanatory links. The reader must account for that movement rather than simply name a garment.
evidence: A light white, a disgrace, an ink spot, a rosy charm.

questions.prompt: What changes when A Time to Eat places pleasant and tyrannical in the same chain?
facilitatorNotes: The accumulation lets routine appear comforting and controlling at once. Repeated and gives equal grammatical weight to terms that ordinary description might separate.
evidence: habitual and tyrannical and authorised

questions.prompt: How do the agents trimming the feather transform the meaning of trimmed?
facilitatorNotes: Light and sound-like volumes join more concrete forces, extending the verb beyond a person cutting an object. Compare the assurance of cohesive with the variety of the listed agents.
evidence: it is trimmed by the light and the bug and the post

days.title: How the Other Half Lives: inside a Cherry Street tenement (excerpt)
days.challenge: Track a second-person guided tour and decide what the reader is directed to see, hear, and judge.
days.focus: Documentary immersion, causal claims, and the moral categories Riis draws.
days.context: Jacob A. Riis (1849–1914), a Danish immigrant who became a New York police reporter, published this documentary study of Lower Manhattan tenement housing in 1890, illustrated with his own photographs. Here Riis leads the reader into a tenement on Cherry Street in the old Fourth Ward of the Lower East Side.
days.contentNote: This passage describes a young child dying of measles in an unventilated tenement; it is not graphic but is distressing. Riis also renders speech in dialect and draws moral distinctions among the poor that the discussion can question.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, The Down Town Back-Alleys, from “Enough of them everywhere. Suppose we look into one?” through “the first and the best evidence of a desire to be honest.” (PG 45502), one illustration caption omitted.

questions.prompt: Riis writes in the present tense and addresses “you” (“Be a little careful, please!”). Name three things the reader is directed to notice before reaching the dying child. What does this tour achieve that a statistical report cannot?
facilitatorNotes: Darkness, the slamming hall-door, the sinks in the hallway, the squeaking pump, the saloon’s smell. The tour makes the reader a witness who physically experiences the building; it also lets Riis control the order of perception. Students may note that the guided “you” leaves little room to see the scene differently.
evidence: Hear the pump squeak! It is the lullaby of tenement-house babes.
The smell of it has followed you up.

questions.prompt: Riis concludes, “That dark bedroom killed it.” Is that claim supported by what the passage shows? What would a skeptical health inspector want to know before accepting it?
facilitatorNotes: Riis assigns cause to the built environment, after stressing the absence of fresh air. An inspector might ask about medical care, nutrition, crowding, and how measles spread in the building. The claim is plausible but compressed; some students will treat it as rhetoric, others as a defensible causal argument.
evidence: With half a chance it might have lived; but it had none. That dark bedroom killed it.

questions.prompt: The father asks, “need we complain--such as we?” and Riis repeats, “Such as we!” How does Riis reinterpret the father’s words? How does his closing claim about the clothes-line divide the poor into categories, and is that division fair?
facilitatorNotes: The father’s resignation becomes Riis’s accusation of a city that teaches people to expect nothing. The clothes-line sentence praises “honest poverty” but implies that others are paupers lacking a desire to be honest; it reassures middle-class readers that some poor deserve help. Students may defend it as sympathetic or criticize it as moralizing.
evidence: If we cannot keep the baby, need we complain--such as we?
The true line to be drawn between pauperism and honest poverty is the clothes-line.

days.title: The Jungle: Marija’s uncertain future
days.challenge: Track how a comic love story is interrupted by an economic pattern.
days.focus: Artistic expression, affection, and seasonal employment.
days.context: Marija’s courtship with the violinist Tamoszius develops as her can-painting wages seem to promise a home. An abrupt factory closure tests the security of those plans.
days.contentNote: Includes possessive jealousy and a brief report of domestic violence in neighborhood gossip.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 8, Wikisource 1906 Doubleday, Page transcription, chapter paragraphs 2–11; begins “Yet even by this deadly winter the germ of”; ends “done by a person who did not know English.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Tamoszius become eloquent with the violin after struggling to speak?
facilitatorNotes: Music gives his emotional life an expressive form; the family’s response makes that interiority visible beyond his awkward conversation.
evidence: the soul of him would flame up and become eloquent

questions.prompt: What does comparing the factory to planets and seasons reveal about Marija’s expectation?
facilitatorNotes: She assumes permanence and regularity in an institution controlled by production and orders; its shutdown exposes a mistaken scale of certainty.
evidence: a thing akin to the planets and the seasons

questions.prompt: How do the other women revise the meaning of a high weekly wage?
facilitatorNotes: They average earnings over unemployment as well as busy weeks. The advertised or remembered peak wage misrepresents annual security.
evidence: your pay was really only half what you thought

days.title: Tender Buttons: Naming, steadiness, and echoes (selection)
days.challenge: Spend three slow passes on the short sequence, once aloud; annotate reversals and changed repetitions.
days.focus: Names and familiar objects that fail to secure a stable meaning.
days.context: A person’s name, a sound, a table, shoes, and animal titles form this compact sequence. The reading time is for rereading and comparing its verbal patterns.
days.contentNote: Experimental prose poetry uses disrupted grammar, unexpected associations, and repetition. No single hidden paraphrase is required; support interpretations with specific verbal patterns. Contains brief violent imagery involving an elephant and the historical word “crazy.”

excerpt.locator: Objects, A Little Called Pauline through A White Hunter, six complete titled prose poems; complete source paragraphs 156–179 in the saved paragraph index; opens “A LITTLE CALLED PAULINE.”; closes “A white hunter is nearly crazy.”.

questions.prompt: How does anything in Pauline’s opening qualify the apparently specific name in the title?
facilitatorNotes: The body substitutes an indefinite term for the proper name, making the act of naming more conspicuous than an identifiable portrait. Shudders gives that uncertainty a bodily response.
evidence: A little called anything shows shudders.

questions.prompt: How does the table’s supposed steadiness coexist with revision and shaking?
facilitatorNotes: Repeated means promises a definition, but the definition includes change and an unstable stand. Readers can hear the repetition trying to establish what the words keep revising.
evidence: a stand where it did shake.

questions.prompt: Why does the repeated monkey/donkey line matter beneath the title A Dog?
facilitatorNotes: Sound likeness offers a relation while the title introduces a different animal. The mismatch asks the reader to attend to how a phrase moves and returns rather than expect a zoological description.
evidence: A little monkey goes like a donkey.

days.title: How the Other Half Lives: children of the tenements (excerpt)
days.challenge: Weigh a reported dialogue, an anecdote, a satirical comparison, and charity statistics as different kinds of evidence.
days.focus: How Riis argues for rescuing children, and the prejudices his rhetoric relies on.
days.context: Jacob A. Riis (1849–1914), a Danish immigrant who became a New York police reporter, published this documentary study of Lower Manhattan tenement housing in 1890, illustrated with his own photographs. He drew on police and charity records; the Children’s Aid Society, founded in 1853, ran lodging-houses and sent children to farm families in the West.
days.contentNote: Describes neglected and abandoned children. Riis uses the phrase “little Hottentots,” a dismissive colonial-era term for the Khoekhoe people of southern Africa.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XV, The Problem of the Children, from “A little fellow who seemed clad in but a single rag” through “did their efforts flag for ever so brief a time.” (PG 45502).

questions.prompt: The interview at Police Headquarters is reported almost as a script. What does each of the boy’s answers reveal, and why might Riis let questions and answers stand with little commentary?
facilitatorNotes: Church, school, and bread are the questioner’s assumed markers of a normal childhood; each answer exposes their absence, and the beer answer leads the police to the saloon and his “home.” The bare dialogue lets readers draw the conclusion themselves; some students will notice the comic tone and ask whether it softens or sharpens the point.
evidence: We don't have no clothes to go to church.
We don't buy no bread; we buy beer

questions.prompt: Riis contrasts New York’s “home-heathen” with missionaries abroad who spent “one year and sixty thousand dollars” converting one girl. What is his argument about priorities, and how does the language of the comparison affect a modern reader’s judgment of it?
facilitatorNotes: The argument is that charity should attend to neglected children at home first. Its force depends on mocking foreign people with a racial label, so the satire aims at missionaries but borrows contempt for Africans. Students may argue the satire targets misdirected charity; ask whether that excuses the terms.
evidence: our home-heathen that are growing up in New York's streets to-day
they might come to New York with a good deal better prospect of success

questions.prompt: In the final paragraph Riis cites the Children’s Aid Society and the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children. Does he present these numbers as evidence of success or of danger? Which phrase decides it for you?
facilitatorNotes: Both: the numbers show what organized effort has done and also the scale of the “crop” the tenements produce, so any slackening would be dangerous. The financial argument (“a wiser investment”) appeals to taxpayers. Students may weigh the metaphor of harvest differently.
evidence: a wiser investment than to have let them grow up thieves and thugs
the cause for apprehension that would exist did their efforts flag for ever so brief a time

days.title: The Jungle: paid hours and union hopes
days.challenge: Analyze how a wage rule allocates time and risk between workers and employers.
days.focus: Unequal accounting of labor and the promise and limits of collective action.
days.context: A seasonal slowdown leaves workers waiting without pay, then working late at speed. Jurgis begins to support the union, but the family initially expects more from membership than it can deliver.
days.contentNote: Describes exploitation and exposure to severe cold in industrial work.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 8, Wikisource 1906 Doubleday, Page transcription, chapter paragraphs 12–16; begins “The men upon the killing-beds felt also the effects”; ends “proceeded to discuss the election of a recording secretary.”.

questions.prompt: Why can fewer paid hours produce a longer and more exhausting day?
facilitatorNotes: Workers must remain available while unpaid, then complete late-arriving work; they bear both waiting time and unpredictable hours.
evidence: not more than two hours' work to his credit

questions.prompt: How are minutes treated differently when a worker is late and when an hour is unfinished?
facilitatorNotes: One minute late loses an hour, while fifty minutes at the end may earn nothing. The apparent unit of an hour is applied asymmetrically.
evidence: they did not pay for any fraction of an hour

questions.prompt: Why include the factory closure just after union membership brings happiness?
facilitatorNotes: It checks the belief that joining alone ends all troubles. Collective organization offers agency but not immediate control of every economic decision.
evidence: belonging to a union meant an end of all their troubles

days.title: Tender Buttons: Books and broken definitions (selection)
days.challenge: Reread for the voices of assertion, command, supposition, and correction; try contrasting stresses aloud.
days.focus: Language that seems to explain while repeatedly changing direction.
days.context: The closing Objects sequence places eyes, a shawl, a book, a pencil, and a dress beside phrases that sound like interrupted speech.
days.contentNote: Experimental prose poetry uses disrupted grammar, unexpected associations, and repetition. No single hidden paraphrase is required; support interpretations with specific verbal patterns. Includes brief threatening-sounding phrases without a developed scene of violence.

excerpt.locator: Objects, A Leave through This Is the Dress, Aider, seven complete titled prose poems; complete source paragraphs 180–209 in the saved paragraph index; opens “A LEAVE.”; closes “A jack in kill her, a jack in, makes a meadowed king, makes a to let.”.

questions.prompt: What happens to a reader’s expectations when Suppose an Eyes repeatedly uses suppose and that is to say?
facilitatorNotes: These forms promise clarification but keep reopening or redirecting it. The unusual title and repeated clauses make the process of proposing meaning visible.
evidence: Suppose it is within a gate

questions.prompt: How do commands interrupt the insistence that Book was there?
facilitatorNotes: Stop it and later cover up break a descriptive rhythm with directions whose addressee is uncertain. The shift creates voices or competing impulses without requiring an invented narrative.
evidence: Book was there. Stop it, stop it

questions.prompt: What can be heard in the final dress piece that a plain paraphrase would lose?
facilitatorNotes: Aider, whow, and muncher produce repeated vowel and consonant patterns and urgent stop-start motion. Demonstrate a pattern aloud and explain its effect while acknowledging that its referents remain uncertain.
evidence: aider whow, aider stop the muncher

days.title: How the Other Half Lives: working women, wages, and fines (excerpt)
days.challenge: Follow a chapter that moves from quoted testimony and two individual cases to wage statistics, then test the economic argument against the cases.
days.focus: Wages, fines, and child labor: how documentary detail exposes the gap between law and practice.
days.context: Jacob A. Riis (1849–1914), a Danish immigrant who became a New York police reporter, published this documentary study of Lower Manhattan tenement housing in 1890, illustrated with his own photographs. The couplet he quotes is from Thomas Hood’s 1843 protest poem “The Song of the Shirt.” Riis draws on newspaper reports, a city mission journal, and an 1889–1890 investigation by the Working Women’s Society of New York into the pay and conditions of saleswomen in large stores.
days.contentNote: The opening reports two suicides of impoverished women, quoting their last written words, and refers to prostitution in period terms (“the paths of shame,” “the wages of sin”).

excerpt.locator: Chapter XX, The Working Girls of New York, from the chapter’s opening “Of the harvest of tares, sown in iniquity” through “seeing to it that the law was respected by the owners.” (PG 45502), including the quoted couplet.

questions.prompt: Before giving any wage figures, Riis quotes the Working Women’s Society and the last words of two women. Why open with these cases, and how does the Society’s reasoning about men’s and women’s wages prepare his later argument?
facilitatorNotes: The individual testimony makes the stakes concrete before the statistics; Riis calls the cases typical, with “many parallels,” which students may question as evidence drawn from two examples. The Society argues that women’s wages have no floor because prostitution is always available as an alternative; Riis later adds that partly supported women set wages the rest must accept. Both explain why pay can fall below subsistence.
evidence: woman's wages have no limit, since the paths of shame are always open to her
I would have done any honest work, even to scrubbing
It is a story that has many parallels

questions.prompt: Riis argues that “the very fact that some need not starve on their wages condemns the rest to that fate.” Explain the reasoning. Why does he put the “everlasting law of supply and demand” in quotation marks?
facilitatorNotes: Women partly supported by families can accept lower pay, which sets the wage for those who must live on it alone. The quotation marks distance Riis from a phrase used to excuse low wages, a “convenient gag for public indignation.” Some students may defend the market explanation as accurate while rejecting its use as an excuse.
evidence: the very fact that some need not starve on their wages condemns the rest to that fate
that serves as such a convenient gag for public indignation

questions.prompt: Which store example most persuasively shows unfairness: the girl fined after $167 in sales, the fines for sitting down, or the dismissals for “too long service”? Defend your choice.
facilitatorNotes: Each works differently: the sales comparison shows pay unrelated to value; the seat fines show a law obeyed in form and defeated in practice; the dismissals show employers avoiding raises. Accept any choice supported by the text and its irony.
evidence: yet for some trivial mistake the girl was fined sixty cents out of her two dollars
The seats were there, but the girls were fined when found using them.
was too long service

questions.prompt: In the last paragraph, how does Riis show that child-labor laws existed on paper but not in practice? What does his emphasis on the word “guessed” add?
facilitatorNotes: Children are told to lie about their age; truant officers came once a year and the children returned within a month; one inspector oversaw some twelve thousand factories whose number is only guessed. The emphasis exposes that the state does not even know what it claims to regulate. Students might note Riis’s sarcasm in calling enforcement “so efficient.”
evidence: but in a month's time they were all back in their places
Up till this summer, a single inspector was charged with the duty of keeping the run of them all

days.title: The Jungle: learning the forms of democracy
days.challenge: Distinguish participation with understanding from the outward performance of civic procedures.
days.focus: Literacy, political education, and the machinery of patronage.
days.context: The union motivates Jurgis to learn English and reconsider earlier experiences of naturalization and voting. The narrator’s account links political favors to control over neighborhood resources.
days.contentNote: Includes electoral corruption, animal fighting references, and a political club’s appropriation of Indigenous labels. This is the novel’s historical depiction, not voting guidance.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 9, Wikisource 1906 Doubleday, Page transcription, chapter paragraphs 2–7; begins “One of the first consequences of the discovery of”; ends “hairs, and this also the packers gather and clean.”.

questions.prompt: Why does union participation make literacy newly urgent for Jurgis?
facilitatorNotes: He wants to understand meetings and contribute, giving reading a concrete public purpose rather than merely private advancement.
evidence: to be able to take part in them

questions.prompt: What irony separates the oath from the claim that he is the President’s equal?
facilitatorNotes: He cannot understand the oath and is being mobilized by others; ceremonial equality coexists with manipulation and dependence.
evidence: an oath of which he did not understand a word

questions.prompt: How can Scully’s good wages and job recommendations strengthen the corrupt system described?
facilitatorNotes: Material benefits create loyalty and silence around graft. A patron can genuinely help individuals while sustaining exploitative control.
evidence: A note signed by him was equal to a job

days.title: Tender Buttons: Rooms, centres, and arrangements (excerpt)
days.challenge: Read the entire passage three times, tracing centre, change, and arrangement while resisting a forced room diagram.
days.focus: Spatial language as both promise and disruption of order.
days.context: Unlike the individually titled Objects pieces, Rooms proceeds in an extended sequence. This excerpt begins at the section’s opening and ends after a completed paragraph about family terms.
days.contentNote: Experimental prose poetry uses disrupted grammar, unexpected associations, and repetition. No single hidden paraphrase is required; support interpretations with specific verbal patterns.

excerpt.locator: Rooms, opening fourteen paragraphs; complete source paragraphs 466–479 in the saved paragraph index; opens “Act so that there is no use in a centre. A wide action is not a width. A preparation is gi”; closes “there was a decision. Replacing a casual acquaintance with an ordinary daughter does not make a son.”.

questions.prompt: How does the first instruction challenge the conventional role of a centre?
facilitatorNotes: It asks for action without use in a centre, then the later paragraphs repeatedly return to centres. That tension makes organization an ongoing problem rather than an absent subject.
evidence: Act so that there is no use in a centre.

questions.prompt: What is the effect of asserting no change alongside spreading, placing, and disturbance?
facilitatorNotes: Stable-sounding declarations coexist with processes that rearrange a scene. Readers can compare exact recurrences and explain how the prose makes stasis difficult to maintain.
evidence: Any change was in the ends of the centre.

questions.prompt: How does the sister/mister passage connect sound resemblance with a refusal of substitution?
facilitatorNotes: The rhyme-like terms resemble one another but are explicitly distinguished; acquaintance, daughter, and son also resist simple exchange. The paragraph tests whether verbal proximity can establish equivalence.
evidence: The sister was not a mister.

days.title: How the Other Half Lives: what law, opinion, and landlords have done (excerpt)
days.challenge: Evaluate an assessment organized by agent (law, public sentiment, landlords) and the principle it rests on.
days.focus: Reform as a problem of perception, responsibility, and business.
days.context: Jacob A. Riis (1849–1914), a Danish immigrant who became a New York police reporter, published this documentary study of Lower Manhattan tenement housing in 1890, illustrated with his own photographs. Near the end of the book he assesses twenty years of reform: tenement-house laws, the Health Department’s powers, and early “model tenement” experiments.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXIV, What Has Been Done, from the opening question through “Sentiment, having prompted the effort, forgot to stand aside and let business make it.” (PG 45502), one illustration with its captions omitted.

questions.prompt: Riis organizes this excerpt by agent: the law, public sentiment, and the landlord. What verdict does he give each, and which sentence best captures his view of public sentiment?
facilitatorNotes: The law did “what it could,” banning lot-covering barracks and rear tenements; public sentiment is fitful, roused only by outrage or epidemic; landlords mostly yielded “not always gracefully,” with honorable exceptions. Students may differ on whether Riis is fair to the authorities.
evidence: The law has done what it could.
it has slumbered peacefully until some flagrant outrage on decency
the landlord has done his share; chiefly perhaps by yielding

questions.prompt: Riis contrasts a landlord who would never “shed the blood of a fellow-man by actual violence” with the same man fighting an order to repair his plumbing. What is his point about how people recognize harm?
facilitatorNotes: Slow, indirect harm does not register as violence, so a person can kill tenants by neglect without feeling guilty. Riis calls this a failure of “mental sight” requiring education. Some students may connect this to modern debates about structural or environmental harm.
evidence: It is apparently the slowness of the process that obscures his mental sight.
to make him see that he has no right to slowly kill his neighbors, or his tenants, by making a death-trap of his house

questions.prompt: Riis insists that housing the poor “must be business” and that “Any charity scheme merely turns him into a pauper.” What does he assume about dignity and about markets? What in the excerpt supports the claim, and what is missing?
facilitatorNotes: He assumes a fair exchange preserves the tenant’s self-respect and that well-managed housing can pay. Support here is mostly assertion and appeal to European experience; the data come in later chapters. There is also tension with his own account that business created the tenements. Arguments for public housing or charity are defensible alternatives.
evidence: The business of housing the poor, if it is to amount to anything, must be business
the workman has a just claim to a decent home, and the right to demand it
Any charity scheme merely turns him into a pauper

days.title: The Jungle: what the packers sold, and what the workers bore
days.challenge: Weigh gossip, report, and the narrator’s own claims as kinds of evidence, and follow how the closing catalogue builds to its final sentence.
days.focus: Adulterated food, captured regulation, and the cost written on workers’ bodies.
days.context: Recap: in Chapter IX the union has made Jurgis curious about how Packingtown is governed; he has learned how votes are bought and how the boss Scully serves the packers, including over the sewer called “Bubbly Creek.” These closing paragraphs of the chapter report what the men say about the meat and about their own bodies.
days.contentNote: Describes diseased and adulterated meat, severe workplace injuries, and workers’ deaths in rendering vats in vivid detail.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IX, Wikisource 1906 Doubleday, Page transcription, chapter paragraphs 8–12 (end of chapter); begins “And there were things even stranger than this, according”; ends “out to the world as Durham's Pure Leaf Lard!”.
excerpt.inlineReason: The night omits the footnote callout after “henchmen of the local political machine!” in its first paragraph, which its legacy edition did not declare; the library work keeps the callout as “[1]” (the note, the inspection regulations, follows the chapter). The words are otherwise identical, so the night stays inline.

blocks.text: And there were things even stranger than this, according to the gossip of the men. The packers had secret mains, through which they stole billions of gallons of the city's water. The newspapers had been full of this scandal—once there had even been an investigation, and an actual uncovering of the pipes; but nobody had been punished, and the thing went right on. And then there was the condemned meat industry, with its endless horrors. The people of Chicago saw the government inspectors in Packingtown, and they all took that to mean that they were protected from diseased meat; they did not understand that these hundred and sixty-three inspectors had been appointed at the request of the packers, and that they were paid by the United States government to certify that all the diseased meat was kept in the state. They had no authority beyond that; for the inspection of meat to be sold in the city and state the whole force in Packingtown consisted of three henchmen of the local political machine! And shortly afterward one of these, a physician, made the discovery that the carcasses of steers which had been condemned as tubercular by the government inspectors, and which therefore contained ptomaines, which are deadly poisons, were left upon an open platform and carted away to be sold in the city; and so he insisted that these carcasses be treated with an injection of kerosene—and was ordered to resign the same week! So indignant were the packers that they went farther, and compelled the mayor to abolish the whole bureau of inspection; so that since then there has not been even a pretence of any interference with the graft. There was said to be two thousand dollars a week hush-money from the tubercular steers alone; and as much again from the hogs which had died of cholera on the trains, and which you might see any day being loaded into box-cars and hauled away to a place called Globe, in Indiana, where they made a fancy grade of lard.

Jurgis heard of these things little by little, in the gossip of those who were obliged to perpetrate them. It seemed as if every time you met a person from a new department, you heard of new swindles and new crimes. There was, for instance, a Lithuanian who was a cattle-butcher for the plant where Marija had worked, which killed meat for canning only; and to hear this man describe the animals which came to his place would have been worth while for a Dante or a Zola. It seemed that they must have agencies all over the country, to hunt out old and crippled and diseased cattle to be canned. There were cattle which had been fed on "whiskey-malt," the refuse of the breweries, and had become what the men called "steerly"—which means covered with boils. It was a nasty job killing these, for when you plunged your knife into them they would burst and splash foul-smelling stuff into your face; and when a man's sleeves were smeared with blood, and his hands steeped in it, how was he ever to wipe his face, or to clear his eyes so that he could see? It was stuff such as this that made the "embalmed beef" that had killed several times as many United States soldiers as all the bullets of the Spaniards; only the army beef, besides, was not fresh canned, it was old stuff that had been lying for years in the cellars.

Then one Sunday evening, Jurgis sat puffing his pipe by the kitchen stove, and talking with an old fellow whom Jonas had introduced, and who worked in the canning-rooms at Durham's; and so Jurgis learned a few things about the great and only Durham canned goods, which had become a national institution. They were regular alchemists at Durham's; they advertised a mushroom-catsup, and the men who made it did not know what a mushroom looked like. They advertised "potted chicken,"—and it was like the boarding-house soup of the comic papers, through which a chicken had walked with rubbers on. Perhaps they had a secret process for making chickens chemically—who knows? said Jurgis's friend; the things that went into the mixture were tripe, and the fat of pork, and beef suet, and hearts of beef, and finally the waste ends of veal, when they had any. They put these up in several grades, and sold them at several prices; but the contents of the cans all came out of the same hopper. And then there was "potted game” and "potted grouse," "potted ham," and "devilled ham"—de-vyled, as the men called it. "De-vyled" ham was made out of the waste ends of smoked beef that were too small to be sliced by the machines; and also tripe, dyed with chemicals so that it would not show white; and trimmings of hams and corned beef; and potatoes, skins and all; and finally the hard cartilaginous gullets of beef, after the tongues had been cut out. All this ingenious mixture was ground up and flavored with spices to make it taste like something. Anybody who could invent a new imitation had been sure of a fortune from old Durham, said Jurgis's informant; but it was hard to think of anything new in a place where so many sharp wits had been at work for so long; where men welcomed tuberculosis in the cattle they were feeding, because it made them fatten more quickly; and where they bought up all the old rancid butter left over in the grocery-stores of a continent, and "oxidized" it by a forced-air process, to take away the odor, rechurned it with skim-milk, and sold it in bricks in the cities! Up to a year or two ago it had been the custom to kill horses in the yards—ostensibly for fertilizer; but after long agitation the newspapers had been able to make the public realize that the horses were being canned. Now it was against the law to kill horses in Packingtown, and the law was really complied with—for the present, at any rate. Any day, however, one might see sharp-horned and shaggy-haired creatures running with the sheep—and yet what a job you would have to get the public to believe that a good part of what it buys for lamb and mutton is really goat's flesh!

There was another interesting set of statistics that a person might have gathered in Packingtown—those of the various afflictions of the workers. When Jurgis had first inspected the packing-plants with Szedvilas, he had marvelled while he listened to the tale of all the things that were made out of the carcasses of animals, and of all the lesser industries that were maintained there; now he found that each one of these lesser industries was a separate little inferno, in its way as horrible as the killing-beds, the source and fountain of them all. The workers in each of them had their own peculiar diseases. And the wandering visitor might be sceptical about all the swindles, but he could not be sceptical about these, for the worker bore the evidence of them about on his own person—generally he had only to hold out his hand.

There were the men in the pickle-rooms, for instance, where old Antanas had gotten his death; scarce a one of these that had not some spot of horror on his person. Let a man so much as scrape his finger pushing a truck in the pickle-rooms, and he might have a sore that would put him out of the world; all the joints in his fingers might be eaten by the acid, one by one. Of the butchers and floorsmen, the beef-boners and trimmers, and all those who used knives, you could scarcely find a person who had the use of his thumb; time and time again the base of it had been slashed, till it was a mere lump of flesh against which the man pressed the knife to hold it. The hands of these men would be criss-crossed with cuts, until you could no longer pretend to count them or to trace them. They would have no nails,—they had worn them off pulling hides; their knuckles were swollen so that their fingers spread out like a fan. There were men who worked in the cooking-rooms, in the midst of steam and sickening odors, by artificial light; in these rooms the germs of tuberculosis might live for two years, but the supply was renewed every hour. There were the beef-luggers, who carried two-hundred-pound quarters into the refrigerator-cars; a fearful kind of work, that began at four o'clock in the morning, and that wore out the most powerful men in a few years. There were those who worked in the chilling-rooms, and whose special disease was rheumatism; the time-limit that a man could work in the chilling-rooms was said to be five years. There were the wool-pluckers, whose hands went to pieces even sooner than the hands of the pickle-men; for the pelts of the sheep had to be painted with acid to loosen the wool, and then the pluckers had to pull out this wool with their bare hands, till the acid had eaten their fingers off. There were those who made the tins for the canned-meat; and their hands, too, were a maze of cuts, and each cut represented a chance for blood-poisoning. Some worked at the stamping-machines, and it was very seldom that one could work long there at the pace that was set, and not give out and forget himself, and have a part of his hand chopped off. There were the "hoisters," as they were called, whose task it was to press the lever which lifted the dead cattle off the floor. They ran along upon a rafter, peering down through the damp and the steam; and as old Durham's architects had not built the killing-room for the convenience of the hoisters, at every few feet they would have to stoop under a beam, say four feet above the one they ran on; which got them into the habit of stooping, so that in a few years they would be walking like chimpanzees. Worst of any, however, were the fertilizer-men, and those who served in the cooking-rooms. These people could not be shown to the visitor,—for the odor of a fertilizer-man would scare any ordinary visitor at a hundred yards, and as for the other men, who worked in tank-rooms full of steam, and in some of which there were open vats near the level of the floor, their peculiar trouble was that they fell into the vats; and when they were fished out, there was never enough of them left to be worth exhibiting,—sometimes they would be overlooked for days, till all but the bones of them had gone out to the world as Durham's Pure Leaf Lard!

questions.prompt: Sinclair keeps marking his sources: “according to the gossip of the men,” “said Jurgis’s friend,” “There was said to be.” Why might a novel signal hearsay so openly, and does it weaken or strengthen the case? How does the paragraph beginning “There was another interesting set of statistics” rank the kinds of evidence?
facilitatorNotes: Open attribution lets the narrator report scandals without claiming to have witnessed them, and positions the reader as an investigator. The later paragraph separates swindles a visitor “might be sceptical about” from injuries a worker carries “on his own person,” so Sinclair himself grades the evidence. Students may find the hearsay a weakness or an honest documentary method.
evidence: And there were things even stranger than this, according to the gossip of the men.
And the wandering visitor might be sceptical about all the swindles, but he could not be sceptical about these

questions.prompt: How does the account of the meat inspectors explain why the public’s trust was misplaced? Compare it with the inspector the family watched on their tour of Durham’s hog rooms.
facilitatorNotes: The federal inspectors were appointed “at the request of the packers” and certified only meat for interstate sale; city inspection was a few political “henchmen,” and the one physician who acted was forced out. The earlier inspector chatted while carcasses passed. Both scenes show oversight that lends authority without protection; students may debate how far a novel’s claims should be checked against historical records.
evidence: they did not understand that these hundred and sixty-three inspectors had been appointed at the request of the packers
and was ordered to resign the same week!
