questions.prompt: The final paragraph catalogues trades and their injuries, from the pickle-rooms to the hoisters, and ends with the fertilizer-men and the tank-rooms. Why end on “Durham’s Pure Leaf Lard!”? What does that closing irony accomplish that a statistic could not?
facilitatorNotes: The brand name returns from the advertising signs of the tour, turning consumers into unwitting participants and making the abstraction of “afflictions” concrete. The cumulative catalogue builds pressure toward the last clause. Some readers judge the ending sensational; others see it as the novel’s most effective documentary stroke. Both responses can be argued from the text.
evidence: the worker bore the evidence of them about on his own person—generally he had only to hold out his hand
till all but the bones of them had gone out to the world as Durham's Pure Leaf Lard!

days.title: Tender Buttons: A changing window and a final fountain (excerpt)
days.challenge: Reread for sound substitutions and the long final accumulation; compare the ending’s rhythm with its earlier short questions.
days.focus: Closure that gathers a sequence without fixing one final paraphrase.
days.context: These are the final paragraphs of Rooms and of Tender Buttons. They repeatedly return to weather, windows, change, and claims about what words mean.
days.contentNote: Experimental prose poetry uses disrupted grammar, unexpected associations, and repetition. No single hidden paraphrase is required; support interpretations with specific verbal patterns. Includes passing references to suffering, drowning, and sacrifice.

excerpt.locator: Rooms, final twenty paragraphs of the book; complete source paragraphs 531–550 in the saved paragraph index; opens “A bridge a very small bridge in a location and thunder, any thunder, this is the capture o”; closes “ere is incredible justice and likeness, all this makes a magnificent asparagus, and also a fountain.”.

questions.prompt: How do window and willow make sound part of the passage’s spatial change?
facilitatorNotes: The related sounds nearly reproduce one another while designating different things. The earlier claim about another spelling draws attention to letters as material that can alter the scene.
evidence: A willow and no window

questions.prompt: What does the repeated it means more than that do to the promise of clearness?
facilitatorNotes: Each assertion expands or qualifies the preceding meaning. Clearness becomes an active, unsettled process rather than a final dictionary statement.
evidence: it means more than that

questions.prompt: How does the final paragraph arrive at asparagus and a fountain?
facilitatorNotes: The accumulating notwithstanding clauses defer completion, then repeated care organizes a final gathering. The surprising objects provide a verbal arrival without resolving every association; discuss the ending’s effect rather than demand a single decoded message.
evidence: all this makes a magnificent asparagus, and also a fountain.

days.title: How the Other Half Lives: how the case stands (excerpt)
days.challenge: Classify a numbered summary into checkable facts, value claims, and predictions, then test it against an illustrative scene.
days.focus: How a documentary book turns evidence into a program of reform.
days.context: Jacob A. Riis (1849–1914), a Danish immigrant who became a New York police reporter, published this documentary study of Lower Manhattan tenement housing in 1890, illustrated with his own photographs. In the final chapter Riis restates his case as numbered propositions and turns to remedies.
days.contentNote: Riis’s description of an Italian mother and her children on a tenement roof repeats an ethnic stereotype that recurs in his book; discussion can examine how such details function in his argument.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXV, How the Case Stands, from the opening question “What, then, are the bald facts” through “while the enemy it pursues is putting the best foot foremost.” (PG 45502).

questions.prompt: Riis sums up his case as eight numbered “bald facts.” Which are factual claims that could be checked, which are value judgments, and which are predictions?
facilitatorNotes: II and the rent claim in IV can be investigated; “entitle it … as a right” in IV and VI are value claims; III and VIII are predictions about the city’s future; VII promises a proof to follow. Students may classify borderline items differently; the point is to see that “facts” here includes argument.
evidence: II. That it is not housed decently.
IV. That it pays high enough rents to entitle it to be so housed, as a right.
VII. That it will pay to do it.

questions.prompt: The Mott Street landlord paints his row and adds “a gorgeous tin cornice” dated 1890. What does Riis use the scene to argue? How does his description of the people on the roof sit with proposition V, that tenants are “in advance of” their houses?
facilitatorNotes: Cosmetic improvement is not reform. But the stereotyped image of the Italian mother shifts attention to tenants’ habits, contradicting his own proposition that tenants are better than their houses. Students may read the detail as realism or as prejudice doing persuasive work.
evidence: His way was to give the wretched pile a coat of paint
That was a landlord's way, and will not get us out of the mire.
the condition of the tenants is in advance of the condition of the houses which they occupy

questions.prompt: Riis suggests the State might regulate rents as it regulates elevated-railway fares, adding, “I throw out the suggestion, knowing quite well that it is open to attack.” Why might he present the idea so cautiously, and how does it fit his rule that reform must make a bad tenement unprofitable?
facilitatorNotes: Rent regulation challenged landlords’ property rights and the business principle he praised; hedging protects his credibility with readers. It fits the rule by targeting the profit that drives crowding. Students may judge the caution as prudent or as a weakness in his program.
evidence: I throw out the suggestion, knowing quite well that it is open to attack.
reform by law must aim at making it unprofitable to own a bad tenement
